Guide/Single-page view

Accenture 2026 — The Complete Preparation Guide

Everything in one file. Built from a 31-file pack by build_single.py, which is why it can be rebuilt rather than maintained by hand.

What this is, and what it leaves out

The pack measured only 7% verbatim duplication — its files do not repeat each other, they cover different material or the same topic in different words. So this is not a concatenation with the repeats stripped. For every topic it takes the canonical treatment and drops the files that were superseded, and the list of what was dropped and why is at the end of this document. Nothing was removed silently.

On the numbers here

Values marked as verified were produced by executing them — subnet arithmetic through Python's ipaddress, SQL against a real database, C compiled and run, puzzles solved by exhaustive search. Where sources disagree, both are shown rather than one being picked. No official Accenture source was ever obtained; everything here is secondary.

🟣 Updated in this edition — checked against a real extracted paper

This edition was cross-checked, section by section, against ~120 questions extracted from a recent Accenture test (screenshots of an actual sitting, plus its rendered answer keys). What changed: Part 1 gains the real paper's evidence on the section split; Part 4 gains the topics the paper shows that no syllabus listed (Docker file/networking/volume questions, OAuth 2.0, web-tech MCQs, MySQL triggers, concurrency anomalies, Suite B / EAP methods, MS Office and Excel dynamic-array items); Part 5 gains the paper's real SQL, frontend and DSA coding tasks, fully worked; Part 6 gains every workable real question, worked out (RP-numbered). What the paper settled: OOP, DBMS/SQL and OS theory DO appear in the technical MCQ round — that dispute is closed. What it could not settle: cut-off percentages, and whether C++ is offered in the coding round (the paper does prove C++ is examined as an MCQ topic). The supplied final syllabus now controls Round 1: psychometric test, then memory/quick-fire maths/shortest-path games; the legacy verbal/critical/abstract section was removed entirely. Duplicate technical passes and repeated timed-mock copies were also removed, and every removal is recorded at the end of this document. Nothing was corrected silently.

Part 1 — How the assessment works

What you are sitting, in what order, and the rules that decide the result

Source: your placement-training deck. This supersedes every inferred pattern in the rest of this pack. Where my earlier research disagreed with it, the deck wins and I have said so explicitly below.

The three assessment rounds

1. Online Written Assessment   ──► 4 sections, 125 questions, 175 minutes
2. Communication Assessment
3. Interview Round

Online Written Assessment — the four sections

Round Section Questions Time Elimination?
1a Behavioural Assessment 54 20 min ❌ The only non-elimination section
1b Cognitive Assessment (game-based) 3–4 20 min ✅ Yes
2 Technical Assessment (MCQ) 45 45 min ✅ Yes
3 Coding Assessment 3 60 min ✅ Yes

"Only the Behavioural Round is not an elimination round." Everything else can end your candidacy. That single line reorders your preparation: the behavioural section is 54 of the 125 questions — 43% of the paper — and it cannot eliminate you. Do not spend real preparation time on it. Spend it on the 48 questions that can.

A note on the arithmetic

The deck states 125 questions / 175 minutes overall, but the four listed sections sum to ~106 questions / 145 minutes (54 + 4 + 45 + 3 = 106; 20 + 20 + 45 + 60 = 145).

The missing ~19 questions and 30 minutes almost certainly belong to the Communication Assessment, which independent drive listings put at exactly 30 minutes and around 20 questions. So the 175-minute figure is the whole online sitting including communication, not just the four written sections.

This does not change anything you do — it just means don't be surprised when the timer says 175 and your four sections only account for 145.

What this deck CONFIRMED, and what it CORRECTED

Confirmed (my research had these right)

  • Traditional Quant / Logical / Verbal aptitude is gone, replaced by game-based questions
  • Behavioural section of 54 questions
  • Technical MCQ: 45 questions / 45 minutes
  • Coding: 3 questions / 60 minutes, split DSA + SQL + Web
  • Communication assessment is a separate round

Corrected — five topics I did not have

The Technical Assessment syllabus is broader than any source I found online. These five appear on the official list and in none of my earlier research:

Topic Why it matters
Wifi Security A named topic in its own right — WEP/WPA/WPA2/WPA3, not general networking
DevOps Entirely absent from every prep site I checked
OOPs I had said this was interview-only. I was wrong — it is an MCQ topic
Operating System Same — I had it as interview-only. It is on the MCQ list
CPU, Memory Computer organisation/architecture — registers, cache, RAM/ROM

Also corrected: SQL is tested twice — once as MCQ in Round 2, once as a full query in Round 3. I had it only in the coding round.

Where the deck differs from other sources

Point Deck Other sources I follow
Cognitive questions 3–4 "3 games" Deck
Cognitive time 20 min 40 min combined with behavioural Deck (20 + 20 separately)
Behavioural elimination Not eliminating "non-elimination but contributes" Deck — but see below

⚠️ One caveat on the behavioural round. The deck says it does not eliminate. A first-hand candidate account separately reports that the Communication score influenced final role and package. Non-eliminating is not the same as unscored — answer the behavioural section consistently and honestly rather than randomly.

⚠️ C++ — conflicting evidence, and the safe play

The official job posting lists Backend as Java, Dotnet, Python, C++, C#. But three first-hand reports of the actual October 2025 test say C++ was not offered: "You could code in Java, Python, or C#", and asked directly, the OP explained "major campuses were not allowed to code in cpp… they are mentioning it as backend, not DSA."

🟣 Real-paper update (this edition). A captured recent test examines C++ as an MCQ topic — a C++ protected-inheritance code question appears in the technical round — but the capture includes no coding-round language menu, so the coding question stays open. Read C++ (especially access specifiers and inheritance) so the MCQ cannot blindside you; code in whichever backend language you are fastest in.

Safe play: be ready in Java or Python. If C++ appears, use it. Do not walk in with C++ as your only option.

Frontend: HTML · CSS · React.js · Vue.js — but every account says you only modify existing code, so vanilla JS is enough.

Round 1 — Behavioural & Cognitive

Part 3 🆕

Marks-per-hour, re-ranked against the confirmed syllabus

The official topic list changes the ordering from my earlier estimate. Here it is again with the real weights.

Rank Topic Est. Q Effort Why
1 PseudoCode ~8–10 Medium Largest single technical block; the deck lists it 2nd of 9
2 Coding Q1 (DSA) 1 of 3 High Eliminating, and the tier differentiator
3 SQL (MCQ + coding) ~5 + 1 Medium Tested twice. Best combined return in the paper
4 OOPs ~5 Low — you have the guide Pure recall from material you already own
5 Operating System ~5 Low — you have the guide Same
6 Common Apps & MS Office ~5 Very low Cheapest marks in the paper. One hour, done
7 Network Security & Cloud ~5 Low Guide + cloud models
8 CPU, Memory ~4 Low Small, closed syllabus — very learnable
9 Wifi Security ~3 Very low Four protocols, one table. Highest marks-per-minute on the list
10 DevOps ~3 Low Closed syllabus: Docker, Jenkins, CI/CD, Git
11 Coding Q3 (Web) 1 of 3 Medium Reported easiest of the three coding questions
12 Cognitive games 3–4 Low ceiling Cannot be studied much; remove surprise only
— Behavioural 54 ~zero Non-eliminating. 43% of the paper, and you should spend almost no time on it

The headline: the four "you already have it" topics (OOPs, OS, plus SQL and network security from your guides) plus the three tiny closed-syllabus topics (Wifi Security, CPU/Memory, DevOps) are together worth roughly 25 of the 45 technical questions and can be covered in about two focused days.

Suggested schedule

Day 1 — the free marks (all gap topics, all small) MS Office (1 h) · Wifi Security (45 min) · CPU & Memory (1 h) · DevOps (1.5 h) · Cloud service models (45 min) → ROUND2

Day 2 — revise what you already own OOPs (2 h) + OS (2 h) from cs_funda, skimming the Interview Questions and Revision Notes sections rather than re-reading in full.

Day 3 — PseudoCode Part 6, the practice bank — the 202-question bank plus the 18 real-paper items (RP37–RP54), timed at 1 min each.

Day 4–5 — SQL, twice over cs_funda/DBMS for the MCQ side, then write queries by hand for Round 3. Joins and subqueries first — they are the largest module in Accenture's own pre-onboarding curriculum.

Day 6–7 — Coding Part 5 in Java or Python in whichever backend language you are fastest in — C++ included, then Web coding.

Day 8 — Communication + one full mock.

The behavioural section needs 15 minutes of reading, once. Round 1 guide.

Final scope correction — use the verified four-round syllabus

The supplied first-hand syllabus screenshot is the controlling scope for this guide. It supersedes older web pages and earlier conflict notes that described a legacy verbal/critical/abstract/numerical paper. Do not study that legacy paper for this exam.

Round Confirmed content What to prepare
1. Psychometric Test Standard personality/behavioural assessment consistency, integrity, collaboration, learning, resilience; answer honestly and quickly
2. Gamified Assessment memory game · quick-fire maths game · shortest-path grid puzzle visual recall, mental arithmetic/order comparison, grid path planning
3. Brutal Technical Assessment pseudocode · MS Office · cloud · computer networks · cybersecurity · OOPs · Java/Python OOP · JavaScript frontend scenario-heavy technical MCQs and code reading
4. Coding Round simple array DSA · SQL joins over 2–3 tables/schemas · JavaScript frontend/UI task one timed DSA solution, schema reading and joins, DOM/CSS/JS implementation

Evidence from the extracted question set

The extracted paper contains 120 numbered items including duplicates, image-only stubs and coding-task summaries. Its usable question weight is concentrated in:

Observed cluster Approx. captured items Relevance
Pseudocode / bitwise / loops / arrays / recursion 19 direct Round 3 match; highest repeated cluster
Networking / Wi-Fi / firewalls / cryptography / security 25+ direct Round 3 match; scenario-heavy
Cloud / containers / DevOps / REST 20+ direct Round 3 match, including cloud-native variants
SQL / DBMS MCQs and coding tasks 15+ Round 3 SQL theory plus Round 4 join task
OOP / Java / Python / JavaScript / HTML/CSS 20+ direct Round 3 OOP/frontend plus Round 4 frontend
MS Office 5 direct Round 3 match
OS / CPU / hardware 8+ present in the extracted paper; retained as evidence-backed CS fundamentals, not expanded as a separate exam round

The count is intentionally approximate: repeated questions, blurry image-only items and cross-topic questions make false precision misleading. The guide now keeps only the legacy-free scope above. Image-only topics are retained only when the extracted paper actually names them; unsupported legacy aptitude chapters are removed from the rendered study guide.

Exam mechanics you must know before you plan your prep

Rule Detail Why it changes your prep
45 questions / 45 minutes one shared clock across all sections 60 seconds per question, average. No section has its own timer
Sub-sectional cut-offs you must clear the overall technical cut-off AND a cut-off in every individual section ⚠️ You cannot trade sections. A perfect networking score does not rescue a failed MS Office section. This is the single most important fact on this page
Inter- and intra-sectional movement allowed you may move between sections and between questions Do a fast first pass for the easy marks in every section, then return. Never let the clock die inside one section
No negative marking in the MCQ round wrong ≠ penalty Answer all 45. Never leave a blank
Elimination round failing it ends the process —
Difficulty: rated High / Moderate scenario-worded, not one-liners Expect "A company needs X, which should they use?" rather than "Define X"

⚠️ Negative marking exists in the Round-1 cognitive GAMES (the official deck's game screens say marks are subtracted for wrong attempts). It does not exist in this technical MCQ round or the coding round. Don't carry the wrong habit across.

The section split — four sources, none of them agreeing

All four agree the paper is 45 questions in 45 minutes. They do not agree on how those 45 are divided:

Block PrepInsta (2026 page) PlacementPreparation Question-bank PDF First-hand Oct-2025 sitting
Common Applications / MS Office 12 12 — 7
Pseudocode (+ OOPs) 22 18 — 10
Networking + Security + Cloud (+ DevOps) 11 10 ~41% 14
OS + DBMS + CPU + CS basics not listed not listed ~5% 14
Total 45 40 — 45

Read this table honestly: two independent public syllabi say the paper has three sections and no CS-fundamentals block at all. One question bank says that block is ~5%. The only person who actually sat the paper says it was 31% — and the official placement deck backs them up, in its own words:

"Revise basics from Operating Systems, Networking, and DBMS."

🎯 The safe reading

Part A (Networking/Security/Cloud) is large under every source — study it first. Part B is somewhere between 0% and 31%. Two sources say it may not appear; two say it is a third of the paper. The cost of preparing it and not needing it is one day. The cost of skipping it and meeting a 14-question block — with a sub-sectional cut-off on it — is the offer. So prepare it.

Study Part A first, but give Part B a full day.

The real extracted paper — the section split, what it settles, what it changes

Part 2 — Start here — plain-English primers

Read these before the reference sections. Written from zero, with worked examples and the trap that catches everyone

P1. How to trace pseudocode without paper

This is the single highest-value skill in the whole technical assessment, because Accenture gives you no rough paper and pseudocode is the section every source rates Hard.

What the section actually is

You are shown eight to twenty lines of code — either Accenture's language-neutral dialect (Integer a, Set x = 5, Print, End for) or plain C — and asked one of three questions:

  1. What does it print?
  2. What does variable x hold at the end?
  3. How many times does the loop run?

That is the whole section. There is no theory to learn. There is only one skill: following instructions exactly, in your head, without drifting.

Why people get these wrong

Two mistakes cause almost all of the loss, and neither is about not knowing the language:

Mistake What it looks like
Reading instead of executing You glance at the loop, decide "it sums 1 to 5", and answer 15 — when the loop actually starts at 0 or stops one early
Skipping the branch that does nothing An else that doesn't run this pass still ends the if. Miss that and every later line shifts

Both come from the same root: your brain wants to understand the code, and understanding is not the task. Executing is the task.

The method — a mental table

Give every variable a column. Give every pass through the loop a row. Fill the table in mechanically, one cell at a time, without looking ahead.

Integer i, sum
Set sum = 0
for(i = 1; i <= 5; i++)
    Set sum = sum + i
End for
Print sum
pass i test i <= 5 sum after the body
— — — 0
1 1 true 1
2 2 true 3
3 3 true 6
4 4 true 10
5 5 true 15
6 6 false → exit 15

Prints 15. ✅ computed

That took longer than guessing. It also cannot be wrong. Do this for the first two questions and you will find you can do it in your head by the third — the table becomes a habit, and the habit is what survives the pressure.

The four traps, in the order they cost marks

1. Off-by-one in the loop bound. i < 5 runs 5 times (i = 0,1,2,3,4). i <= 5 starting at 1 runs 5 times. i <= 5 starting at 0 runs 6 times. ✅ Always write down the first and last value of i before anything else.

2. Integer division. In C and in Accenture's dialect, 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5. ✅ The fractional part is discarded, not rounded — so 9 / 2 is 4, and -7 / 2 is -3 on modern compilers (truncation toward zero). This single rule changes the answer to a large share of arithmetic questions.

3. Pre- versus post-increment. j = i++ gives j the old value of i. j = ++i gives j the new one. Starting from i = 5:

statement i after j after
j = i++ 6 5
j = ++i 6 6

✅ both compiled and run.

⚠️ A warning about practice sites. Many show printf("%d %d", i++, ++i) with a confident answer. That expression is undefined behaviour in C — two unsequenced changes to i in one statement — and different compilers genuinely print different things. If you see it with an answer, the site is wrong. Accenture's pseudocode uses sequenced statements, so the table above is the form you will meet.

4. The dangling else. An else binds to the nearest unmatched if, not to the one that lines up visually. When indentation and braces disagree, the braces win.

Where to go next

The full dialect reference, the ranked trap list and 32 practice questions are in the Pseudocode section.

P2. Subnetting from zero

This is the only calculation in the paper. It looks like maths. It is actually just counting in binary, and once you see that, it stops being hard.

Why subnets exist at all

A company gets one block of IP addresses. Putting every machine in one flat block is bad for two reasons: a broadcast reaches everything (noisy), and anyone inside can reach anything (unsafe). So you cut the block into smaller blocks — subnets — and put a router between them. Now traffic is contained and access can be controlled.

🟢 A real Accenture question asks why cloud providers subnet a VPC. The answer is isolation and control — not "to get more addresses". Subnetting never creates addresses. It only divides the ones you have, and it actually loses a couple per subnet.

The one idea

An IPv4 address is 32 bits. The prefix — the /24 in 192.168.1.0/24 — says how many of those bits are fixed and identify the network. The rest are free and identify the host.

192.168.1.0/24
└──────┬─────┘
   24 bits fixed (network)   →   32 − 24 = 8 bits free (host)

8 free bits means 2⁸ = 256 addresses in the block. Two of them are reserved:

  • the all-zeros host address is the network address (the block's name)
  • the all-ones host address is the broadcast address

So usable hosts = 2^(32 − prefix) − 2. For a /24 that is 256 − 2 = 254. ✅

The table to memorise

Prefix Mask Block size Usable hosts
/24 255.255.255.0 256 254
/25 255.255.255.128 128 126
/26 255.255.255.192 64 62
/27 255.255.255.224 32 30
/28 255.255.255.240 16 14
/29 255.255.255.248 8 6
/30 255.255.255.252 4 2

✅ whole table computed. Learn the block-size column — 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4 — and everything else follows.

Two shortcuts that remove the arithmetic:

  • last mask octet = 256 − block size. Block 64 → mask octet 192. ✅
  • Subnets start at multiples of the block size. Block 64 → networks at .0, .64, .128, .192.

Worked: which subnet is a host in?

Question: 192.168.10.77/26 — what is the network address and the broadcast?

  1. /26 → block size 64.
  2. Multiples of 64: 0, 64, 128, 192.
  3. 77 falls between 64 and 127 → network = 192.168.10.64.
  4. Broadcast is one below the next block: 128 − 1 → 192.168.10.127.
  5. Usable range: .65 to .126, which is 62 hosts. ✅

All four values computed with Python's ipaddress.

Worked: the other direction

Question: a department needs 200 hosts. What prefix?

You need 200 usable, so 202 addresses including the two reserved. The smallest power of two ≥ 202 is 256 = 2⁸, so you need 8 host bits → prefix 32 − 8 = /24, giving 254 usable. ✅

A /25 gives only 126, which is not enough. Always add the 2 before rounding up — forgetting it is the classic error, and it changes the answer whenever the requirement is 2 short of a power of two (126, 254, 510…).

Where to go next

The class table, private ranges, APIPA and 8 more worked subnets are in Network · Security · Cloud, section A4.

P3. The OSI model, told as one packet's journey

Seven layers, memorised as a list, is why people find OSI boring and then get the scenario questions wrong. Here is the same thing as a story.

You type a URL and press enter

Layer What happens to your data here Unit Device
7 Application Your browser writes an HTTP request: GET /index.html Data —
6 Presentation It is encrypted (TLS) and maybe compressed Data —
5 Session The conversation with that server is opened and tracked Data —
4 Transport Split into pieces, each stamped with a port (443) so the right program gets it. TCP adds sequence numbers Segment —
3 Network Each piece gets source and destination IP so it can cross networks Packet Router
2 Data Link Each piece gets MAC addresses for the next hop on this cable Frame Switch
1 Physical It becomes electricity, light or radio Bits Cable, hub

At the other end the same seven steps run in reverse, peeling one header off at a time, until the server's web software receives exactly the bytes you sent.

Mnemonic, top down: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

The three things they actually test

1. Which device is at which layer. This is the most-asked OSI question, and it has a clean logic: a device operates at the layer of the address it reads.

  • Hub — reads nothing, just repeats electricity → Layer 1
  • Switch — reads MAC addresses → Layer 2
  • Router — reads IP addresses → Layer 3
  • Firewall — reads ports (L4) and can read content (L7) → Layer 3–7

2. Which unit is at which layer. Segment (4) → Packet (3) → Frame (2) → Bits (1). Notice it goes down in the order the words get smaller in your head. A question saying "which PDU does a router forward?" wants packet.

3. Where encryption lives. TLS is usually placed at the Presentation layer (6) in OSI terms, though in the real TCP/IP stack it sits between transport and application. Exam answer: Layer 6.

Switch versus router — the scenario question

🟢 "Two computers on the same office LAN need to talk. Which device?" → Switch. Same network, MAC addresses are enough, no routing needed.

🟢 "A computer needs to reach a server in another building on a different network." → Router. Different networks means you need IP.

One sentence that answers most of them: a switch moves traffic within a network, a router moves traffic between networks.

Where to go next

The full seven-layer table with protocols per layer, and the TCP/IP four-layer mapping, are in Network · Security · Cloud, sections A1–A2.

P4. TCP vs UDP, in plain words

The analogy that actually holds

TCP is a phone call. You dial, the other person picks up, you both confirm you can hear each other, and then you talk. If a sentence is missed, they say "sorry, again?" and you repeat it. Slower to start, but nothing is lost.

UDP is shouting across a room. You just shout. Maybe they heard, maybe they didn't. You never find out and you never repeat yourself. Nothing is guaranteed, and it is very fast.

The comparison they test

TCP UDP
Connection Connection-oriented — handshake first Connectionless — just send
Reliability Guaranteed delivery, acknowledgements, retransmission None
Ordering In-order, using sequence numbers No ordering
Speed Slower Faster
Header size 20 bytes 8 bytes
Flow control Yes (windowing) No
Used by HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, SSH DNS, DHCP, video streaming, VoIP, online games

Why anyone would choose to lose data

This is the bit that confuses people. Why use UDP at all?

Because for live media, a late packet is worse than a lost one. In a video call, a frame that arrives 400 ms late is useless — the moment has passed. TCP would stop everything to retransmit it, freezing your call to deliver a frame nobody needs. UDP drops it and moves on, and you get a momentary glitch instead of a freeze.

Rule for the exam: if the scenario says live, real-time, streaming, voice, game, or broadcast — the answer is UDP. If it says file, page, email, transfer, or must arrive — the answer is TCP.

The three-way handshake

Guaranteed to appear. Three messages, in this order:

  1. SYN — client: "can we talk? my sequence number starts at X"
  2. SYN-ACK — server: "yes, and mine starts at Y; I acknowledge your X"
  3. ACK — client: "I acknowledge your Y"

Now the connection is open. Closing uses four messages (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK), because each side shuts its own direction independently.

The trap: the question sometimes asks for the number of messages. Opening = 3. Closing = 4.

P5. Cloud service models, without the buzzwords

The one analogy worth knowing

You want pizza.

Model What you get Pizza version
On-premises You buy and run everything You grow the wheat and build the oven
IaaS You rent the machine; you install and manage everything on it You buy a frozen pizza; you use your own oven
PaaS You get a place to run your code; the provider handles the machine and OS You order delivery; you supply the table and drinks
SaaS You just use the finished software You eat at the restaurant

The rule the exam actually tests

As you go IaaS → PaaS → SaaS, you manage less and control less.

You manage IaaS PaaS SaaS
Your data ✔ ✔ ✔
Your application ✔ ✔ ✘
Runtime, middleware ✔ ✘ ✘
Operating system ✔ ✘ ✘
Virtualization, servers, storage, network ✘ ✘ ✘

The OS row is the giveaway. Almost every "which model is this?" question can be answered by asking: who patches the operating system? You → IaaS. Not you → PaaS or SaaS.

Examples they use

Examples
IaaS AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine
PaaS Heroku, Azure App Service, Google App Engine, AWS Elastic Beanstalk
SaaS Gmail, Google Workspace, Salesforce, Dropbox, Office 365

🟢 "In which model does the customer control the OS and applications but not the underlying infrastructure?" → IaaS.

The five characteristics, in plain words

NIST lists five. Translated:

  1. On-demand self-service — you click a button, you get a server. No phone call.
  2. Broad network access — reachable over the network, from any normal device.
  3. Resource pooling — one physical machine is shared between many customers (multi-tenancy). This is what makes it cheap.
  4. Rapid elasticity — capacity grows and shrinks automatically with demand.
  5. Measured service — you are billed for what you used, metered.

Elasticity vs scalability — a favourite distinction. Scalability is can it grow? Elasticity is does it grow and shrink automatically, right now, with demand? Elasticity implies automatic and bidirectional.

P6. Encryption and hashing — the difference that decides the question

Two operations that look similar and are not

Encryption is reversible. You scramble data so it can be unscrambled later by someone with the key. The whole point is getting it back.

Hashing is one-way. You turn data into a fixed-size fingerprint that cannot be turned back. The whole point is not getting it back.

Therefore: passwords are hashed, never encrypted. If a site can email you your existing password, it stored it reversibly, and that is a defect. This is the most common exam framing of the distinction.

Symmetric vs asymmetric

Symmetric Asymmetric
Keys One shared secret key A pair — public + private
Same key encrypts and decrypts? Yes No — public encrypts, private decrypts
Speed Fast Slow (roughly 100–1000× slower)
The hard problem Getting the key to the other person safely Solved — you can publish the public key
Algorithms AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman
Key sizes AES 128 / 192 / 256 bits RSA 1024 / 2048 / 4096 bits

How HTTPS uses both — the question behind the question

Asymmetric is too slow for a whole page, and symmetric can't safely share its key over the internet. So TLS uses both:

  1. The server sends its certificate containing its public key.
  2. Your browser and the server use asymmetric crypto to agree on a fresh symmetric key, which nobody watching can derive.
  3. Everything after that is encrypted with the fast symmetric key.

One line for the exam: asymmetric to exchange the key, symmetric for the data.

Hashing details they ask

Algorithm Output Status
MD5 128 bits Broken — collisions are easy. Never for security
SHA-1 160 bits Broken/deprecated
SHA-256 256 bits Current standard
bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 varies Designed to be slow — the right choice for passwords

Salt is a random value added to each password before hashing, so two people with the same password get different hashes. It defeats precomputed rainbow tables.

Why "slow" is a feature: an attacker who steals your database wants to try billions of guesses. SHA-256 is fast, so billions is cheap. bcrypt is deliberately expensive, so the same attack takes centuries.

Digital signatures — the reverse

Signing uses the pair backwards: you encrypt a hash of the message with your private key, and anyone can decrypt it with your public key. If it decrypts, only you could have sent it. That gives authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation — but not confidentiality, since anyone can read it.

P7. SQL joins, actually explained

Joins are where the coding round's database question lives, and where most people guess.

The setup

students                     courses
+----+--------+-----------+  +-----+-----------+
| id | name   | course_id |  | id  | title     |
+----+--------+-----------+  +-----+-----------+
| 1  | Anu    | 10        |  | 10  | Maths     |
| 2  | Bala   | 20        |  | 20  | Physics   |
| 3  | Chitra | NULL      |  | 30  | Chemistry |
+----+--------+-----------+  +-----+-----------+

Chitra has no course. Chemistry has no student. Those two rows are the entire point of joins — what happens to them decides which join you need.

The four

Join Keeps Result on the data above
INNER only rows that match on both sides Anu-Maths, Bala-Physics → 2 rows
LEFT all left rows, plus matches + Chitra-NULL → 3 rows
RIGHT all right rows, plus matches + NULL-Chemistry → 3 rows
FULL OUTER everything from both → 4 rows

✅ all four counts executed against a real database.

Read the question for the word "all". "List all students, including those not enrolled" → the word all attached to the left table means LEFT JOIN. If it said "students who are enrolled", that is INNER.

Two more you should recognise

SELF JOIN — a table joined to itself, used for hierarchies. "Find each employee and their manager" joins employees to employees on e.manager_id = m.id.

CROSS JOIN — every row paired with every row. 3 students × 3 courses = 9 rows. Almost always a mistake when it appears by accident (a missing ON clause).

The NULL trap that ends interviews

NULL means unknown, and unknown compared to anything is not true:

Expression Result
NULL = NULL not true — returns no rows
NULL <> 5 not true
WHERE x IS NULL ✔ the correct test
COUNT(*) counts all rows, NULLs included
COUNT(column) skips NULLs
AVG(column), SUM(column) skip NULLs (so AVG is over non-NULL rows only)

✅ every row executed on SQLite.

The nastiest version: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM emp) returns zero rows if any manager_id is NULL — because id <> NULL is never true. Use NOT EXISTS instead. ✅ reproduced.

WHERE vs HAVING

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after.

SELECT dept, AVG(sal)
FROM emp
WHERE sal > 30000          -- throws out low earners FIRST
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2        -- then keeps only departments with 3+ of them

You cannot put an aggregate in WHERE, because at that moment the groups do not exist yet. That is the whole rule.

Second-highest salary — the classic

SELECT MAX(sal) FROM emp WHERE sal < (SELECT MAX(sal) FROM emp);

Reads as: the largest salary that is smaller than the largest salary. Handles duplicates correctly, which the LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 version does not.

P8. Big-O without the maths

What it is measuring

Big-O answers one question: as the input gets bigger, how much worse does this get? It deliberately ignores constants and hardware, because those change and the shape does not.

The ladder, best to worst

Notation Name n = 1,000 means roughly Typical source
O(1) constant 1 step array index, hash lookup
O(log n) logarithmic 10 steps binary search
O(n) linear 1,000 steps one loop over the data
O(n log n) linearithmic ~10,000 steps merge sort, quick sort average
O(n²) quadratic 1,000,000 steps two nested loops
O(2ⁿ) exponential astronomically bad naive recursion on subsets

✅ step counts computed by running the loops.

The gap that matters: at n = 1,000, linear is a thousand steps and quadratic is a million. That factor is why "it worked on the example but timed out on the hidden tests" happens in the coding round.

How to read it off code in five seconds

  • One loop over n → O(n)
  • Two nested loops over n → O(n²)
  • A loop that halves n each pass (n = n / 2) → O(log n)
  • A loop over n containing a halving loop → O(n log n)
  • Two loops one after another (not nested) → still O(n) — you add, then keep the biggest term

The nested-loop trap: for i in 0..n: for j in i+1..n: looks like half the work, and it is — it runs n(n−1)/2 times. For n = 10 that is exactly 45 iterations ✅. But n²/2 is still O(n²), because constants are dropped.

Sorting, the table they ask from

Algorithm Average Worst Space Stable?
Bubble O(n²) O(n²) O(1) Yes
Selection O(n²) O(n²) O(1) No
Insertion O(n²) O(n²) O(1) Yes
Merge O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n) Yes
Quick O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) No
Heap O(n log n) O(n log n) O(1) No

The two facts most asked: quick sort's worst case is O(n²) (already-sorted input with a bad pivot), and merge sort is the one that needs O(n) extra space.

Binary search — the one to be careful with

Worst case is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes, not log₂ n.

n probes
100 7
1,000 10
1,024 11
10,000 14

✅ counted by running the search. The 1,024 row is the trap — people answer 10 because 2¹⁰ = 1024, but you need one more probe to finish.

And it only works on sorted data. A question that gives you an unsorted array and asks for binary search is testing whether you noticed.

P9. OOPs — the four pillars, explained once properly

Encapsulation

Bundle the data and the methods that act on it, and hide the data. Fields go private; access goes through methods.

Why: an object can then guarantee its own rules. A BankAccount with a private balance can refuse a withdrawal that would go negative. If balance were public, anyone could set it to −5000 and no rule could stop them.

Abstraction

Show what it does, hide how. You call car.start() without knowing about the starter motor.

Encapsulation vs abstraction — the distinction they test: encapsulation is about hiding data; abstraction is about hiding complexity. Encapsulation is the mechanism, abstraction is the intent.

Inheritance

A class reuses another class's members. Dog extends Animal gets everything Animal has, and adds or changes what it needs. This is an is-a relationship — a dog is an animal.

Type Shape
Single A → B
Multilevel A → B → C
Hierarchical A → B and A → C
Multiple B and C → D — not allowed for classes in Java

The diamond problem is why Java forbids multiple class inheritance: if B and C both override a method from A, and D extends both, which one does D get? Java's answer: use interfaces, which carry no state to conflict.

Polymorphism

One name, many behaviours. Two kinds, and the difference is the single most-asked OOPs question:

Overloading Overriding
Where Same class Parent and child class
Signature Must differ (parameters) Must be identical
Return type Can differ Must match (or be covariant)
Resolved Compile time Run time
Also called Static / early binding Dynamic / late binding

One sentence: overloading is same name different parameters in one class; overriding is same signature redefined in a subclass.

Abstract class vs interface

Abstract class Interface
Instantiate? No No
Method bodies Yes, can have both Only default/static (Java 8+)
Fields Any, including state public static final constants
Inherit how many? One Many
Use when Classes are closely related and share code Unrelated classes share a capability

The rule of thumb: an abstract class says "is a kind of"; an interface says "is able to". Bird is a kind of Animal (abstract class), and is able to Fly (interface).

P10. Operating systems — the five things they actually ask

Process vs thread

Process Thread
Memory Its own address space Shares the process's memory
Creation cost Heavy Light
Crash impact Isolated — one dies, others live One thread crashing can kill the process
Communication Needs IPC (pipes, sockets) Just shared variables

Why threads share memory: it makes communication instant, and it is also why threads need locks and processes usually do not.

Deadlock — the four conditions

All four must hold at once. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

  1. Mutual exclusion — a resource can be held by only one at a time
  2. Hold and wait — you hold one and wait for another
  3. No preemption — it cannot be taken from you
  4. Circular wait — A waits for B, B waits for A

The most practical fix is breaking circular wait: make everyone acquire resources in the same fixed order. If everybody locks A before B, no cycle can form.

Mutex vs semaphore

Mutex = a key to one toilet. One person in, and the same person must return the key. Ownership matters.

Semaphore = a bowl of n keys to a car park. Up to n cars in; any attendant can put a key back. It is a counter, not an owner.

Mutex is binary and owned. A counting semaphore allows n. A binary semaphore looks like a mutex but has no ownership — that is the exam distinction.

Paging vs segmentation

Paging Segmentation
Divides memory into Fixed-size pages Variable-size segments
Sized by The hardware The program's logical parts (code, stack, heap)
Suffers Internal fragmentation External fragmentation
Visible to the programmer No Yes

Internal fragmentation = wasted space inside a block you were given (a 4 KB page holding 100 bytes). External = free space exists but is split into pieces too small to use.

Page replacement — the calculable one

Reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2:

Frames FIFO faults LRU faults
3 10 9
4 7 6

✅ all four simulated. Work them by drawing the frames and stepping through — there is no shortcut, and the marks come from being careful rather than clever.

Belady's anomaly: with FIFO, adding more frames can increase faults. It sounds impossible, which is exactly why it is asked. LRU and Optimal never suffer it. (On this particular string FIFO does improve with more frames — Belady needs a specially chosen string.)

P11. Excel — the five formulas that carry the section

MS Office is rated the easiest section and has its own cut-off, which makes it the best marks-per-minute in the paper. Excel is most of it.

Absolute vs relative references — learn this first

A1 is relative: copy the formula down and it becomes A2, A3. $A$1 is absolute: it stays A1 wherever you copy it. $A1 locks the column only; A$1 locks the row only.

The dollar sign locks whatever comes straight after it. That one sentence answers every reference question.

Where it matters: a tax rate in one cell that every row must multiply by. Use $B$1, or copying the formula down will silently point at B2, B3 and give you wrong answers with no error message.

VLOOKUP

=VLOOKUP(what_to_find, where_to_look, which_column, exact_or_near)

Three things they test:

  1. The lookup value must be in the first column of the range. VLOOKUP cannot look left.
  2. The column number is counted from the start of the range, not from column A.
  3. The last argument: FALSE (or 0) = exact match — almost always what you want. TRUE requires the data to be sorted and returns approximate matches.

INDEX + MATCH is the answer to "look up a value to the left of the key", because VLOOKUP structurally cannot.

COUNT family

Function Counts
COUNT cells containing numbers only
COUNTA cells that are not empty (any type)
COUNTBLANK empty cells
COUNTIF cells meeting one condition
COUNTIFS cells meeting several

The COUNT vs COUNTA distinction is asked constantly: COUNT ignores text, COUNTA does not.

The error values

Error Means
#DIV/0! divided by zero or by an empty cell
#VALUE! wrong type — text where a number belongs
#REF! the reference is gone — you deleted the row it pointed at
#NAME? Excel doesn't recognise the name — usually a misspelt function
#N/A a lookup found nothing
#NUM! a number that is invalid or too large

#REF! vs #NAME? is the pair they test: #REF! is a broken cell reference, #NAME? is a broken function name.

Order of operations

Excel follows normal maths: brackets, then ^, then * and /, then + and −. =2+3*4 is 14, not 20. ✅ Percentage and negation bind tighter than everything else, so =-2^2 is 4 in Excel — it negates first — which differs from most programming languages.

P12. The seven-minute version

If you have almost no time, this is what to carry in.
Rounds Behavioural + games → Technical MCQ 45 Q/45 min → Coding 3 Q/60 min → Communication → Interview
Cut-offs Overall and every sub-section. You cannot skip a section
Negative marking Games: yes. MCQ and coding: no — answer everything
Navigation You can move between sections. Take the easy marks everywhere first
Usable hosts 2^(32−prefix) − 2. /24=254, /26=62, /27=30, /30=2
Devices Hub L1, Switch L2 (MAC), Router L3 (IP)
PDUs Segment 4, Packet 3, Frame 2, Bits 1
TCP vs UDP Reliable/ordered/slow vs fast/lossy. DNS, DHCP, streaming = UDP
Handshake SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK (3). Close is 4
Ports FTP 20/21, SSH 22, SMTP 25, DNS 53, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443
Service models Who patches the OS? You → IaaS. Not you → PaaS/SaaS
Crypto Symmetric = one key, fast, AES. Asymmetric = key pair, slow, RSA. HTTPS uses both
Hashing One-way. Passwords are hashed, never encrypted. SHA-256, salted
Joins The word "all" in the question means an OUTER (usually LEFT) join
NULL NULL = NULL is not true. Use IS NULL. COUNT(*) counts them, COUNT(col) does not
WHERE vs HAVING WHERE before grouping, HAVING after
Binary search ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 probes. n=1024 → 11, not 10
Overload vs override Same class + different params + compile time · vs · subclass + same signature + run time
Deadlock Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait
Excel $ The dollar locks whatever follows it
Integer division 7/2 is 3. Truncates, never rounds
Pseudocode Trace with a table. Do not read and guess

Part 3 — Round 1 — behavioural and the cognitive games

54 behavioural items in 20 minutes, then the games. The games deduct marks

PART A — The gamified set

Screenshot-confirmed Round 2 scope

The supplied final syllabus describes three game families. Prepare these before any other aptitude-style material:

  1. Memory game — briefly study a grid or sequence, then reproduce the positions or order after it disappears. Chunk rows/columns and encode positions verbally.
  2. Quick-fire maths game — compare or calculate small arithmetic expressions under a short timer. Estimate first, calculate only when two values are close, and keep moving instead of writing long solutions.
  3. Shortest-path grid puzzle — find the route in the fewest legal steps. Mark the start and target, estimate the Manhattan lower bound, then avoid loops and count each move exactly once.

The older classic-puzzle material below is retained only as method practice where it overlaps these families. It is not a separate verbal, critical-reasoning or numerical-aptitude round in the verified syllabus.

Covered in full in Round 1 — Behavioural & Cognitive. The short version:

1. Select Bubbles (mental arithmetic). Bubbles like 17×3, 54, 8², 120÷2, 7×7; select them in ascending order of value. Order them, do not compute them — you need to know 17×3 sits between 50 and 55, not that it is 51. Compute exactly only the pair you cannot separate by magnitude. ✅ Verified ascending order: 7×7 (49) → 17×3 (51) → 54 → 120÷2 (60) → 8² (64).

2. Path Finder. Reach a target by rotating or re-laying tiles. Find the target first and work backwards; count the Manhattan minimum |r₁−r₂| + |c₁−c₂| before touching anything, so you know whether a detour is forced. ✅ From (2,1) to (5,7) that is 9 moves.

3. Memory Maze. A grid you study, then reproduce. Encode positions as a path or shape, never as individual cells — working memory holds 4–7 items, and a shape is one.

Three tricks worth ten minutes each, all verified:

  • ×5 → halve, then ×10. 86 × 5 = 43 × 10 = **430** ✅
  • ×11 (two digits) → outer digits, sum in the middle. 72 × 11 → 7_(9)_2 = **792** ✅
  • squares ending in 5 → n(n+1) then append 25. 35² = 3×4=12 → **1225** ✅ · 65² = 6×7=42 → **4225** ✅

What it is

A personality/psychometric questionnaire. No technical questions. You are shown a statement and asked how much you agree, typically on a five-point scale:

Highly Disagree · Disagree · Neutral · Agree · Highly Agree

Six core competencies are being measured (from the official deck):

  1. Collaboration
  2. Leadership
  3. Problem-solving
  4. Continuous learning
  5. Business ethics
  6. Emotional resilience

The pacing problem — this is the real difficulty

54 questions in 20 minutes is 22 seconds per question. That is the entire challenge. There is no time to deliberate, and deliberation is not what is being measured anyway. Read, react, move.

If you run out of time, unanswered items are worse than instinctive ones. Keep moving at pace.

How these instruments actually score you

Three mechanisms worth understanding, because they determine the only real advice here:

1. Consistency checks. The same trait is probed several times in differently-worded items, sometimes reversed. If you "Highly Agree" that you enjoy teamwork and then "Highly Agree" that you prefer working entirely alone, the instrument flags an inconsistency. Inconsistency is the main way people score badly on these.

2. Social-desirability detection. Answering every item at the maximum socially-desirable extreme ("I am always calm, always ethical, always leading") reads as impression management rather than as a strong candidate. Real people have a texture.

3. Reverse-scored items. Some statements are written so that disagreeing is the positive answer. You cannot just pick "Highly Agree" down the page.

The six worked examples from the official deck

These are the exact items shown in your training deck, with the ideal response and the competency each maps to. Study the pattern, not the answers — the real test will use different wording.

# Statement Ideal answer Competency
1 "I remain calm and focused when I have to complete an important task within a short deadline." Highly Agree Pressure Handling
2 "I prefer working with people who think exactly the same way I do." Disagree Teamwork / Adaptability
3 "When I receive constructive feedback, I use it to improve my future performance." Highly Agree Feedback / Growth Mindset
4 "If I make a mistake at work, I prefer to keep it to myself unless someone notices it." Highly Disagree Accountability / Integrity
5 "I am comfortable learning a new technology even when I have little prior experience with it." Highly Agree Adaptability / Learning
6 "When a teammate is struggling, I usually take over their task instead of discussing the problem with them." Disagree Collaboration

The pattern these six reveal

Look at which ones are reverse-scored — items 2, 4 and 6. Half the sample items require disagreement. That is the single most useful thing on this page: you cannot sail through agreeing with everything.

Now read what separates them:

  • Items 1, 3, 5 are positively framed — they describe resilience, coachability and adaptability. Agree strongly.
  • Item 2 sounds harmless ("I like working with like-minded people") but codes as low tolerance for diverse viewpoints. Disagree.
  • Item 4 is the integrity trap. Concealing a mistake until noticed is an accountability failure, and integrity items are usually scored hardest. This is the one item type where the extreme answer (Highly Disagree) is right.
  • Item 6 is the subtlest and most instructive. Taking over a struggling teammate's work sounds helpful — that is exactly why it is a trap. It codes as rescuing instead of collaborating: it removes their learning opportunity and creates a single point of failure. The collaborative behaviour is to discuss the problem with them.

Generalise item 6. Whenever a statement offers a helpful-sounding action that bypasses communication, the ideal answer is to disagree. Accenture is a consulting and delivery organisation; communicating and escalating properly is the behaviour being selected for.

The decision rules

Apply these at 22 seconds a question:

  1. Integrity items → answer at the extreme. Hiding mistakes, cutting corners, misreporting, bending rules "just this once" — Highly Disagree, no hesitation.
  2. Learning and feedback items → strongly positive. Willingness to learn unfamiliar technology and to act on criticism are core to a fresher role.
  3. Anything that avoids communication → negative. Working around a colleague, silently fixing someone's work, not raising a blocker, not telling a manager about a slip.
  4. Anything that avoids diversity of thought → negative. Preferring people who think like you, dismissing unfamiliar approaches.
  5. Pressure and resilience items → positive, but do not claim to be never affected by anything.
  6. Leave a little texture. Use the full scale. Reserve "Highly" for items you truly hold — especially integrity items — and use plain Agree/Disagree elsewhere. An all-extremes profile reads as gamed.
  7. Be consistent. If a theme returns in different words, answer it the same way. The instrument is checking.

What NOT to do

  • Do not try to reverse-engineer a "perfect" profile. These instruments are built to detect that, and it is the most common way to score badly.
  • Do not leave items blank chasing perfection on earlier ones.
  • Do not overthink 22-second questions. Your first reaction is usually both the honest answer and the consistent one.

Bottom line: read the six patterns above, then answer honestly and fast. This section cannot eliminate you. Move on.

What changed

The supplied final syllabus confirms three game families: memory, quick-fire maths, and a shortest-path grid puzzle. This is not a verbal, critical-reasoning or numerical-aptitude paper.

This is the single biggest time-saver in your entire preparation. Conventional placement prep is roughly 40% quantitative aptitude — time-speed-distance, profit-and-loss, percentages, permutations. None of it is on this paper. Do not study it.

The three games in the verified syllabus

The screenshot-confirmed scope is more reliable than older candidate variants.

Game What it is Timing
1. Memory game Study a sequence/grid briefly, then reproduce or identify it short timed rounds
2. Quick-fire maths Compare or calculate small expressions under time pressure short timed rounds
3. Shortest-path grid Find the route in the least legal steps short timed rounds

🔴 The games ELIMINATE. The psychometric does not.

"From my test center, around 3–4 people got eliminated after this round, so the gamified part was elimination-based, while psychometric wasn't."

Practical rule: accuracy matters more than reckless speed. Use the timer, but do not guess blindly when a move or calculation can be checked.

The verified syllabus explicitly includes memory, quick-fire maths and shortest-path grid practice. Prepare all three families rather than treating memory as optional.

Memory and recall puzzles

The verified syllabus explicitly includes memory. You are shown a sequence, grid or set of symbols, it disappears, and you reproduce or identify it.

If it does appear: you are shown a sequence, grid or set of symbols, it disappears, and you reproduce or identify it.

Technique — chunking. Working memory holds roughly 4–7 items. Grouping beats raw memorisation:

  • 4 9 2 7 1 5 8 3 → remember 4927 · 1583 (two chunks, not eight items)
  • For grids, encode positions as a shape or path, not as individual cells.
  • Say the sequence to yourself sub-vocally — the phonological loop holds it longer.

Do not blink past the display phase. Look at the whole field first, then chunk.

Quick-fire maths

🔴 The task is to ORDER results, not to compute them exactly. That is the key tactic and it is worth more than any arithmetic drill:

You are shown bubbles like 17×3, 54, 8², 120÷2 and must select them in ascending order of their value. You do not need the exact value of 17×3 — you need to know it sits between 50 and 55. Estimate magnitude, order, move.

Where exactness IS required: when two bubbles are close (51 vs 17×3 = 51). Compute only the pair you cannot separate by magnitude.

Have these automatic so nothing costs you thinking time:

Have memorised Why
Tables to 20 Removes the most common hesitation
Squares to 25 169, 196, 225, 256, 289, 324, 361, 400, 441, 484, 529, 576, 625
Cubes to 12 512, 729, 1000, 1331, 1728
Powers of 2 to 1024 Appears in pattern games too
Percentage↔fraction 12.5%=1/8 · 25%=1/4 · 33⅓%=1/3 · 37.5%=3/8 · 62.5%=5/8 · 75%=3/4

Practise against a 15-second timer, not untimed. The constraint is the test. Accuracy is weighted — these games typically track error rate, not just throughput, so wild guessing to inflate volume backfires.

What to have automatic:

Have memorised Why
Tables to 20 Removes the most common hesitation
Squares to 25 169, 196, 225, 256, 289, 324, 361, 400, 441, 484, 529, 576, 625
Cubes to 12 512, 729, 1000, 1331, 1728
Powers of 2 to 1024 Appears in pattern games too
Percentage↔fraction 12.5% = 1/8 · 25% = 1/4 · 33⅓% = 1/3 · 37.5% = 3/8 · 62.5% = 5/8 · 75% = 3/4

Three mental-arithmetic tricks worth ten minutes each:

  • ×5 → halve, then ×10. 86 × 5 = 43 × 10 = 430
  • ×11 (two digits) → outer digits, sum in the middle. 72 × 11 → 7_(7+2)_2 = 792
  • Squares ending in 5 → n5² = n(n+1) then append 25. 35² = 3×4=12 → 1225

Grid / shortest-path puzzles

Navigate a grid under constraints — reach a target, avoid obstacles, minimum moves, sometimes collecting items in order.

Technique:

  1. Find the target first, then work backwards toward the start. Backward search prunes far more branches than forward wandering.
  2. Count the minimum moves before you touch anything. On an open grid, minimum steps from (r₁,c₁) to (r₂,c₂) is |r₁−r₂| + |c₁−c₂| (Manhattan distance). If your route is longer than that, you are detouring — check whether an obstacle actually forces it.
  3. Obstacles usually create exactly one viable corridor. Find the pinch point.
  4. Expect the rules to change between levels — a new obstacle type, a move limit, a reversed goal. This is deliberate: adaptability is part of what is scored. Re-read the prompt on every level.

How the games are scored — and what follows from it

Reports consistently say these instruments track decision process, not just final answers: accuracy under pressure, consistency across levels, and how you adapt when rules shift.

Practical consequences:

  • Accuracy over speed. A slower correct answer beats fast guessing.
  • Consistency matters. Erratic performance — brilliant then careless — reads worse than steady competence.
  • Do not panic on a hard level. Some are designed to be unfinishable within the time; how you behave when stuck is itself a signal. Keep making sensible moves.
  • Read every prompt. The rule change is the test.

Preparation ceiling — and the honest limit here

A couple of hours removes the surprise factor. Beyond that, returns collapse.

✅ Now partly verified. A first-hand account of the October 2025 assessment gives the three games, their timings, and the fact that this part eliminates — that is reflected above. Still unverified: the exact scoring model (whether process is weighted alongside accuracy), and whether the game set varies by campus.

One correction worth stating plainly: I earlier wrote that the games were "3–4 questions" and had a low preparation ceiling. The arithmetic game is 25 questions at 15 seconds each and people were eliminated at this stage. It deserves more than the token effort I originally suggested.

Prioritise the arithmetic game — it is the one part that responds directly to practice, and the reported bar is 20 of 25. Still do not trade coding practice for game practice: the technical round is 45 questions and the coding round decides your tier.

Round 1 checklist

These six statements are the exact items shown in the official training deck, with the response the deck marks as ideal and the competency each maps to. The real paper is 54 items in 20 minutes — about 22 seconds each. Six is what exists; nobody has published the other 48, and inventing them would teach a pattern that is not real.

⚠️ This round is not scored right or wrong

A behavioural instrument measures alignment with the competencies an employer selects for. "Matching the deck" is not the same as being correct, and this round is the one part of the assessment that does not eliminate. What it can do is flag you as inconsistent, so answer as one person would.

The real difficulty is pace. 22 seconds an item means first instinct, no deliberating. Use this to feel that cadence.

Three of the six are reverse-scored — half the sample requires disagreement. ✅ counted. You cannot sail through agreeing with everything, and that is the single most useful thing on this page.

Pressure handling

Q1. "I remain calm and focused when I have to complete an important task within a short deadline."

  • A) Highly Agree
  • B) Agree
  • C) Disagree
  • D) Highly Disagree
Answer & explanation

Answer: A) Highly Agree

Competency: Pressure handling. Positively framed and central to a delivery role. The deck marks the strong endorsement, not the hedge.

Teamwork and adaptability

Q2. "I prefer working with people who think exactly the same way I do."

  • A) Highly Agree
  • B) Agree
  • C) Disagree
  • D) Highly Disagree
Answer & explanation

Answer: C) Disagree

Competency: Teamwork / adaptability. Reverse-scored. It sounds harmless — liking like-minded colleagues — but it codes as low tolerance for diverse viewpoints.

Note the deck marks Disagree, not Highly Disagree: preferring some common ground is human. Save the extremes for the integrity items.

Feedback and growth

Q3. "When I receive constructive feedback, I use it to improve my future performance."

  • A) Disagree
  • B) Highly Agree
  • C) Agree
  • D) Highly Disagree
Answer & explanation

Answer: B) Highly Agree

Competency: Feedback / growth mindset. Coachability is one of the things a graduate programme is most explicitly selecting for.

Accountability and integrity

Q4. "If I make a mistake at work, I prefer to keep it to myself unless someone notices it."

  • A) Agree
  • B) Disagree
  • C) Highly Agree
  • D) Highly Disagree
Answer & explanation

Answer: D) Highly Disagree

Competency: Accountability / integrity. Reverse-scored. This is the integrity trap, and the one item type where the extreme answer is the right one. Concealing a mistake until someone notices is an accountability failure, and integrity items are usually scored hardest.

Learning and adaptability

Q5. "I am comfortable learning a new technology even when I have little prior experience with it."

  • A) Disagree
  • B) Agree
  • C) Highly Agree
  • D) Highly Disagree
Answer & explanation

Answer: C) Highly Agree

Competency: Adaptability / learning. For a role where you are staffed onto whatever the client needs, this is close to the whole job description.

Collaboration

Q6. "When a teammate is struggling, I usually take over their task instead of discussing the problem with them."

  • A) Highly Agree
  • B) Disagree
  • C) Agree
  • D) Highly Disagree
Answer & explanation

Answer: B) Disagree

Competency: Collaboration. Reverse-scored, and the subtlest of the six.

Taking over a struggling teammate's work sounds helpful — that is exactly why it is a trap. It codes as rescuing instead of collaborating: it removes their learning opportunity and creates a single point of failure. The collaborative behaviour is to discuss the problem with them.

Generalise this one. Whenever a statement offers a helpful-sounding action that bypasses communication, the ideal response is to disagree. Accenture is a consulting and delivery organisation; communicating and escalating properly is the behaviour being selected for.

Motion — Shortest Path

Q8. A directed weighted network runs 0→5. Edges: 0→1 (4), 0→2 (2), 1→3 (5), 1→4 (10), 2→1 (1), 2→3 (8), 3→5 (3), 4→5 (1). What is the cheapest total cost from 0 to 5?

  • A) 12
  • B) 15
  • C) 13
  • D) 11
Answer & explanation

Answer: D) 11

✅ all five routes enumerated: costs 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. The cheapest is 0 → 2 → 1 → 3 → 5 = 2 + 1 + 5 + 3 = 11.

The trap, and the whole reason this game exists: the cheapest first step is not on the cheapest route. Taking 0→1 directly costs 4, but going the long way round via node 2 costs 2 + 1 = 3. ✅ verified. A greedy walk picks the wrong first edge.

Method — work backwards from the end, labelling each node with its cheapest cost to finish. Each node is computed once, and on a six-node graph it takes under a minute. For "how many routes", sum the path counts of each node's predecessors rather than listing routes by hand — you will miss one.

Motion — counting routes

Q9. On the same network, how many distinct routes run from 0 to 5?

  • A) 4
  • B) 3
  • C) 5
  • D) 6
Answer & explanation

Answer: C) 5

✅ enumerated exhaustively. The five routes cost 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15.

Method: count paths into the end node by summing the path counts of its predecessors, rather than tracing routes by eye. Hand-tracing this graph is exactly the sort of task where people confidently report 4.

Mental arithmetic — Select Bubbles

Q10. Bubbles show 7×7, 17×3, 54, 120÷2, 8². Selected in ascending order of value, which comes third?

  • A) 120÷2
  • B) 17×3
  • C) 8²
  • D) 54
Answer & explanation

Answer: D) 54

✅ computed. The order is 7×7 (49) → 17×3 (51) → 54 → 120÷2 (60) → 8² (64).

Method — order by magnitude, do not compute exactly. You need to know 17×3 sits between 50 and 55, not that it is 51. Compute precisely only the pair you cannot separate by size — here, 51 against 54.

At 15 seconds a question this is the difference between finishing and not.

45 questions in 45 minutes, with a cut-off on every sub-section

How much this topic is worth

Source Questions Note

Prep sites (legacy pattern) 12 of 45 Older 3-section split

Sub-topic weighting

From a prep site's published breakdown of the 12-question version — useful for proportions even though the total has changed:

Sub-topic Share Difficulty Priority
MS Office apps (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook) ~42% Medium 🔴 Highest
