What the questions actually look like

Analysing all 90 questions in your placement deck, they come in five shapes:

Shape Example Frequency
Direct recall "In MS Word, Ctrl+X is used to?" Most common
Multi-statement "Which are correct? 1, 2, 3" with combination options Very common
Scenario "Fastest way to find a large file in a 5000-email inbox?" Common
Output-based "Apply the formula in the formula bar — what is the result?" Common
Image-based "In the given image, which view is used?" ~30% of the deck

Two things follow from this. First, multi-statement questions are everywhere — you must evaluate each numbered statement independently, then pick the matching combination. Second, roughly a third of questions show a screenshot, so knowing what the Word ruler, the Gmail toolbar and the Excel ribbon look like is genuinely worth five minutes of looking at them.

MS Excel — the largest single sub-topic

1 Structure and limits

Item Value
Columns 16,384 (= 2¹⁴), last column XFD
Rows 1,048,576 (= 2²⁰)
Default sheets in a new workbook 1 (modern Excel; older versions 3)
File extension .xlsx (macro-enabled: .xlsm)

✅ Both limits verified as exact powers of two, and XFD confirmed as column 16,384.

Column lettering runs A…Z, AA…AZ, BA… — base-26. A = 1, Z = 26, AA = 27.

Parts of the window you must be able to name from a screenshot: Name Box (left of the formula bar — shows the active cell address) · Formula Bar · Active cell (bold border) · Fill Handle (small square at the bottom-right of the selection — drag to copy or continue a series) · Ribbon tabs · Sheet tabs · Status bar (shows Sum/Average/Count of the selection).

2 Cell references — the highest-frequency Excel question

$ locks whatever follows it.

Written Column Row When copied
A1 relative relative both shift
$A1 locked relative only the row shifts
A$1 relative locked only the column shifts
$A$1 locked locked never changes

F4 cycles a reference through all four while editing.

Worked example. C2 contains =A2*$B$1. Copy it down to C4:

  • A2 is relative → shifts down two rows → A4
  • $B$1 is absolute → does not move
  • Result: =A4*$B$1 ✅ computed

Why it exists: a tax rate or exchange rate parked in one cell gets locked as $B$1 so every row points at it. Forgetting the $ is why a filled-down column silently produces zeros — the reference walks off into empty cells.

Reference types across sheets and files: Sheet2!A1 (another sheet) · 'My Sheet'!A1 (sheet name with a space needs quotes) · [Book2.xlsx]Sheet1!A1 (another workbook).

3 Operators

Operator Does
+ - * / arithmetic
^ power — =2^10 is 1024
& concatenation — =A2&"@"&B2
% percent — 50% is 0.5
= <> > < >= <= comparison, returns TRUE/FALSE
: range — B8:B10 means all cells from B8 to B10
, union — =SUM(A1,B5,C9)

Precedence: () → ^ → * / → + - → & → comparisons.

🟢 Real deck question: "A2 is 'max', B2 is 'Yahoo.com'. Which returns 'max@yahoo.com' in C2?" → =A2&"@"&B2. & is the concatenation operator; + is arithmetic and errors on text. ✅ verified

🟡 Real PYQ: "The notation B8 : B10 indicates…" → all cells from B8 to B10. The colon is the range operator, not a product and not "only those two cells".

4 Functions — grouped by what gets asked

Aggregate

Function Returns
SUM(range) total
AVERAGE(range) mean of numeric cells
MAX / MIN largest / smallest
COUNT(range) count of numeric cells only
COUNTA(range) count of non-empty cells (text included)
COUNTBLANK(range) count of empty cells
MEDIAN / MODE middle value / most frequent

✅ Verified on [1, 2, "x", ""]: COUNT = 2, COUNTA = 3, COUNTBLANK = 1. That one example encodes the whole distinction — memorise it.

Conditional

Function Returns
COUNTIF(range,"crit") count matching one condition
COUNTIFS(...) count matching multiple conditions
SUMIF(range,"crit",[sum_range]) sum of matching cells
SUMIFS(...) sum matching multiple conditions
AVERAGEIF(...) mean of matching cells

Worked example. A1:A5 = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50:

  • =COUNTIF(A1:A5,">25") → 30, 40, 50 qualify → 3
  • =SUMIF(A1:A5,">25") → 30+40+50 → 120
  • =AVERAGEIF(A1:A5,">25") → 120/3 → 40 ✅ all computed

The four traps in this family, in order of how often they are set

  1. The criterion is a TEXT STRING — ">25", operator inside the quotes. =COUNTIF(A1:A5, >25) is a syntax error.
  2. SUMIF's optional third argument. SUMIF(A1:A5,">25") sums the same range it tested. SUMIF(A1:A5,">25",B1:B5) tests column A but sums column B.
  3. COUNT vs COUNTA — a column of names has COUNT = 0.
  4. Counting blanks — the dedicated function is COUNTBLANK, but COUNTIF(range,"") also works. COUNT can never count blanks.

Logical

IF(test, then, else) · AND(...) · OR(...) · NOT(...) · IFERROR(value, fallback) Nested: =IF(A1>=90,"A",IF(A1>=75,"B","C"))

Lookup

=VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index, FALSE)

VLOOKUP — three facts that are always tested

  1. It searches only the FIRST (leftmost) column of the table array.
  2. It can only return values to the RIGHT. To look leftward you need INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP.
  3. The 4th argument FALSE means EXACT match. Omitting it defaults to approximate, which silently returns wrong values on unsorted data.

HLOOKUP is the horizontal equivalent. INDEX(range, row, col) + MATCH(value, range, 0) is the flexible combination.

Text

Function Returns
LEN(text) length
LEFT(text,n) / RIGHT(text,n) first / last n characters
MID(text, start, n) n characters from position start (1-indexed)
UPPER / LOWER / PROPER ALL CAPS / all lower / Title Case
TRIM(text) strip extra spaces
CONCATENATE(...) or & join
EXACT(t1,t2) TRUE only if identical including case
FIND / SEARCH position of a substring (FIND is case-sensitive)
SUBSTITUTE / REPLACE replace text

✅ Verified on "ACCENTURE": LEN = 9, LEFT(3) = ACC, RIGHT(4) = TURE, MID(4,3) = ENT. Note MID is 1-indexed — position 4 is the 4th character.

🟢 Real deck question: "PROPER, LOWER and UPPER are used to…" → change the case of the text. They change the value, not the formatting — font and position are formatting, not functions.

🟢 Real deck question — EXACT: EXACT is case-sensitive, so "abc" and "ABC" are not the same. Any question asking which strings EXACT treats as identical is testing exactly that.

Date & time

Function Returns
NOW() current date AND time
TODAY() current date only
DAY / MONTH / YEAR components
DATEDIF(start,end,"Y") difference

🟢 Real deck question (Acc-2020): "NOW() returns: I. current time II. current date" → Both. TODAY() is date only. Both are volatile — they recalculate on every change.

Math

ROUND(x, n) · ROUNDUP / ROUNDDOWN · INT(x) (rounds down, so INT(-3.7) = −4) · ABS · MOD(a,b) (remainder) · POWER(a,b) · SQRT ✅ Verified: ROUND(2.567,2) = 2.57, MOD(10,3) = 1, POWER(2,10) = 1024.

Error values — know what each means

Error Cause
#DIV/0! division by zero
#VALUE! wrong data type (text where a number is expected)
#REF! reference to a deleted cell
#NAME? misspelled function name or unquoted text
#N/A lookup found nothing
#NUM! invalid numeric argument
##### column too narrow — not an error, just widen it

5 Features

Conditional formatting — applies formatting based on a rule. Highlight cells greater than 74, colour scales, data bars, icon sets, duplicate highlighting.

🟢 Real deck question (Acc-2021): "To highlight students who scored more than 74, which feature?" → Conditional formatting. Sort reorders rows, Filter hides rows, Cell style applies fixed formatting with no condition. The keyword is "highlight".

Sort reorders rows · Filter (Ctrl+Shift+L) hides non-matching rows · Freeze Panes keeps headers visible while scrolling · Data Validation restricts what can be typed · Pivot Table summarises large data by category · Text to Columns splits one column by a delimiter · Remove Duplicates · Goal Seek works backwards from a target result.

Charts: Column/Bar (compare categories) · Line (trend over time) · Pie (parts of a whole, one series) · Scatter (correlation between two numeric variables) · Area · Combo.

Cell formatting shortcuts (Ctrl+Shift+key):

Keys Format
Ctrl+Shift+~ General
Ctrl+Shift+$ Currency
Ctrl+Shift+% Percentage
Ctrl+Shift+^ Scientific
Ctrl+Shift+# Date
Ctrl+Shift+@ Time
Ctrl+Shift+! Number, 2 decimals

🟢 Real deck question (Acc-2021): "Which symbol with Ctrl+Shift changes the format to General?" → ~ (tilde).

6 How to attack the "formula bar" screenshot questions

Roughly six deck questions show a spreadsheet screenshot and ask "apply the formula in the formula bar — what is the result?" You cannot memorise these; you must be able to evaluate a formula quickly. The method:

  1. Read the formula inside-out, innermost parentheses first.
  2. Identify every reference and whether it is absolute — this decides what happens when it is dragged.
  3. If the question says "drag it down to C5", adjust each relative row by the number of rows moved, then re-evaluate.
  4. Check the option types. If options are 3105, 105, FZT, FZTA, the formula is a text function (concatenation or MID/LEFT), not arithmetic — that alone eliminates half the options.

7 From the real extracted paper — two Excel questions

INDEX + MATCH with MAX. Given Product / Category / Unit Price / … data, what does this return?

=INDEX(A2:A9, MATCH(MAX(C2:C9), C2:C9, 0))

→ the product name with the highest unit price. Read it inside-out: MAX(C2:C9) finds the largest price → MATCH(..., C2:C9, 0) finds its position (0 = exact) → INDEX(A2:A9, pos) returns the A-column value at that position. The captured options were products (Printer/Laptop/Mouse/Monitor) — evaluate, don't guess; the answer is whichever product carries the max price in the screenshot's column C.

FILTER — dynamic arrays (Excel 365). "Generate the list of employees from the South region dynamically" →

=FILTER(A2:D50, C2:C50="South")

FILTER returns every matching row and spills automatically — no helper columns, no copy-down. Distractors: QUERY (Sheets/SQL, not Excel), plain INDEX (needs explicit row numbers), UNIQUE(FILTER(...)) (deduplicates — only right if the question wants distinct values). 🟣 This confirms dynamic-array functions (FILTER/SORT/UNIQUE/ XLOOKUP) are now in scope for recent papers — older decks stopped at VLOOKUP.

MS Word

1 Essential shortcuts

Shortcut Action Shortcut Action
Ctrl+N / O / S New / Open / Save F12 Save As
Ctrl+P Print Ctrl+W Close document
Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y Undo / Redo Ctrl+C / X / V Copy / Cut / Paste
Ctrl+A Select all Ctrl+F / H Find / Replace
Ctrl+B / I / U Bold / Italic / Underline F7 Spelling & grammar
Ctrl+L / E / R / J Align left / centre / right / justify Ctrl+M Increase indent
Ctrl+Shift+M Decrease indent Ctrl+Home / End Doc start / end
Ctrl+Backspace Delete word to the LEFT Ctrl+Delete Delete word to the right
Page Down One screen down Ctrl+Page Down Next page
Ctrl+Enter Page break Ctrl+Shift+Enter Column break
Ctrl+= Subscript Ctrl+Shift+= Superscript
Shift+F3 Cycle case Ctrl+Space Clear character formatting

The three traps set most often

  1. Ctrl+Y is REDO. Ctrl+R is align RIGHT. Constantly confused.
  2. Ctrl+M is indent. Ctrl+I is italic. This exact question appears three times in your deck — it is guaranteed value.
  3. Ctrl means "word-level" — Ctrl+Backspace deletes a whole word, Ctrl+Arrow moves a whole word.

2 Features

Track Changes (Review tab) — records every edit for review; accept/reject individually. Comments are separate from tracked changes.

Mail Merge — one template + one data source (Excel/Access/Outlook contacts) → many personalised documents. Steps: start the merge → select recipients → insert merge fields → preview → finish.

Section break vs page break — a page break just starts a new page. A SECTION break is what lets orientation, margins, columns or page numbering change mid-document. That distinction is the question.

Views: Print Layout (default, shows the page as printed) · Read Mode · Web Layout · Outline · Draft.

3 From the real extracted paper — two Word questions

"Keep with next". Which paragraph setting keeps a title and its paragraph on the same page? → "Keep with next" (Paragraph dialog → Line and Page Breaks). The captured options were Wrap / Keep / Snap / Lock — the answer was "Keep", i.e. the "Keep with next" setting; Word has no Wrap/Snap/Lock paragraph option. Related settings worth knowing: "Keep lines together" (don't split a paragraph across pages) and "Widow/Orphan control" (no lone first/last line).

Insert today's date. "Insert today's date without typing it" → Alt+Shift+D (inserts a DATE field; Alt+Shift+T inserts TIME; Ctrl+; enters a static date in Excel). The captured distractors were Ctrl+Shift+I, Ctrl+Alt+D and Shift+F5 (which re-opens the Find/Replace Go To state, or starts a slideshow from the current slide in PowerPoint).

Other features: Styles (and the Table of Contents built from heading styles) · Headers/Footers · Page numbers (top, bottom, page margins, or current position — all four are valid) · Watermark (text or picture; you can set colour, size and layout) · Columns (the "Line between" checkbox draws the vertical divider) · AutoCorrect (fixes misspellings as you type) vs AutoText (stored blocks) vs AutoFormat.

3 Proofing marks

Mark Means
Red wavy underline spelling error
Green / blue wavy underline grammar or style
Double blue underline formatting inconsistency — typically a double space

🟢 Real deck question (Acc-2022): double blue lines → double space between words. The word double in the answer matches the double underline.

4 The ruler (for the image questions)

The horizontal ruler carries four markers you should be able to identify on sight:

   ▽  ← First Line Indent   (top triangle, points DOWN)
   △  ← Hanging Indent      (bottom triangle, points UP)
   ▭  ← Left Indent         (rectangle UNDER the bottom triangle — moves both)
                        ▲  ← Right Indent (on the right edge)

Top triangle = first line · bottom triangle = hanging · the small box below = left indent (drags both together). Two deck questions ask you to identify the first-line indent, which is the top, downward-pointing triangle.

MS PowerPoint

1 Shortcuts and keys

Key Action
F5 Start show from the beginning
Shift+F5 Start show from the current slide
Esc End the show
B or . (period) BLACK screen
W or , (comma) WHITE screen
Ctrl+M New slide
Ctrl+D Duplicate slide
Ctrl+P Pen tool during a show
Ctrl+L Laser pointer
N / P or arrows Next / previous slide

Mnemonic: W = White, B = Black.

🟢 Real deck question: "which key pauses the show and displays a WHITE screen?" → the comma key (or W).

2 Features

Slide Master — controls the look of all slides at once. Edit the master, not each slide, when a question asks how to change formatting globally.

Transitions vs Animations — a transition happens between slides; an animation happens within a slide (to an object).

Trigger — an object that starts an animation when clicked. It is not an action button, and not a motion-path name.

Action buttons — the Action Settings dialog has two tabs: Mouse Click and Mouse Over, so an action can fire on click or on hover. Both are valid.

Hyperlinks — Insert → Hyperlink offers four targets: Existing File or Web Page, Place in This Document, Create New Document, E-mail Address. So a link can navigate to a slide in the same deck or in a different presentation.

Views: Normal · Slide Sorter (thumbnails, for reordering) · Reading · Notes Page · Presenter View (speaker notes + next slide on your screen only).

Default pointer type: the Arrow. Pen, Highlighter and Laser are opt-in.

3 From the real extracted paper — bullet-by-bullet animation

A presenter wants key bullet points to appear one by one automatically, without manually animating each bullet — best feature? → the "By Paragraph" option (select the text's animation → Effect Options → By Paragraph): one animation applied once, PowerPoint sequences it paragraph by paragraph. Distractors: adding a delay per bullet (manual per-bullet work), a trigger (fires on click, which is what the question wants to avoid), or grouping bullets under one "Wipe" (animates them together, not one by one).

MS Outlook & Email

1 The fields — most-asked email fact

Field Visible to others?
To ✅ Yes
Cc (carbon copy) ✅ Yes — everyone sees these
Bcc (blind carbon copy) ❌ Hidden from ALL other recipients

Reply → sender only. Reply All → sender + everyone in To and Cc (never Bcc). Forward → send to new recipients, attachments included.

2 Outlook shortcuts

Shortcut Action
Ctrl+Shift+M New message
Ctrl+Shift+A New appointment
Ctrl+Shift+Q New meeting request
Ctrl+Shift+K New task
Ctrl+Shift+C New contact
Ctrl+R / Ctrl+Shift+R Reply / Reply All
Ctrl+F Forward
Ctrl+Enter Send
F9 Send/Receive all

3 Features

Search criteria — Outlook indexes body text, sender/recipient, subject and attachment names. Operators: from:, subject:, hasattachment:yes, attachment:filename.

Out-of-Office (OOF) / Automatic Replies — a server-side Exchange feature, so it replies even with Outlook closed. POP/IMAP accounts have no server to do this and need a client-side rule with Outlook left running.

Folders: Inbox · Drafts (unsent) · Sent · Deleted Items / Trash (recovery) · Junk/Spam · Outbox (queued). .pst is the Outlook data file.

Arrange by — From, Subject, Date, Size, Attachments, Categories, Importance.

🟢 Real deck question — a scenario worth studying: "Fastest way to find a large source-code file your senior sent, in an inbox of 5000+ emails where many are from that senior and many have attachments?" → Arrange by → Size.

The reasoning matters more than the answer. The question deliberately neutralises every other option: sorting by From still leaves many mails; by Attachments still leaves many; searching "Code" matches body text, not the file. The only distinguishing attribute given is "large" — so sort by the attribute that is unique.

Email risks: Forgery (SMTP has no built-in sender authentication — hence SPF, DKIM, DMARC) and Misdirection (autocomplete sending to the wrong person, a leading real-world data-leak cause).

MS Access & MS Publisher

PrepInsta's syllabus lists both. Low frequency — 10 minutes is enough.

MS Access (database): Tables (data) · Queries (retrieve/filter) · Forms (data entry UI) · Reports (formatted output) · Macros · Relationships. Creating a database: from a template, from scratch, by importing or linking external data. Extension .accdb.

MS Publisher (desktop publishing): publications from templates · text boxes that can be linked so text flows between them · building blocks · precise print layout. Extension .pub. Publisher is for layout-precise print work; Word is for documents.

MS Works is NOT part of the Microsoft Office suite — it was a separate, cheaper product. That appears as a real PYQ.

Browser & Internet fundamentals

1 URL anatomy — know every component by name

https:// mail . example . com / path ? q=1
  │        │       │        │
scheme  subdomain  SLD     TLD
Component Example Note
Scheme https The 's' indicates SSL/TLS is in use
Subdomain mail
Second-Level Domain (SLD) example the name you register
Top-Level Domain (TLD) com

🟢 Real deck question (asked twice, Acc-2021 and Acc-2022): "Which component indicates SSL is used?" → the Scheme.

TLD types: gTLD (generic, open) — .com, .org, .net, .info · sTLD (sponsored, restricted) — .gov, .edu, .mil, .int, .aero · ccTLD (country) — .in, .uk.

The sponsored-TLD question is pure recall: .gov and .edu are sponsored; .com, .org, .net are generic.

2 Browser shortcuts and concepts

Shortcut Action
Ctrl+T New tab
Ctrl+W Close tab
Ctrl+Shift+T Reopen last closed tab
Ctrl+Shift+N Incognito / private window
Ctrl+R or F5 Refresh
Ctrl+Shift+R Hard refresh (bypass cache)
Ctrl+D Bookmark
Ctrl+H / J History / Downloads
F11 Full screen

Cache stores page assets for speed. Cookies store site state and session data. Incognito does not save local history or cookies — it does not make you anonymous to the site, your employer, or your ISP.

Browsers: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari, Opera, Brave. Not browsers: NetBeans and Eclipse (IDEs), Norton (antivirus), Outlook (email client).

Command Prompt — rated HARD, and usually skipped

~17% of this section and the highest-difficulty sub-topic. Everyone memorises Word shortcuts and skips this. Learn it and take the marks.

1 File and directory commands

Command Does
dir list directory contents
cd folder / cd .. change directory / go up one level
cd \ go to the drive root
mkdir (md) make a directory
rmdir (rd) remove a directory
copy / xcopy copy files / copy with subdirectories
move move or rename
del (erase) delete a file
ren rename
type display a file's contents
cls clear the screen
tree show the directory structure graphically
attrib show or change file attributes

2 Network commands — the most-tested group

Command Does
ipconfig show IP configuration (/all for detail, /release, /renew, /flushdns)
ping host test reachability and latency (uses ICMP)
tracert host trace the route — every hop to the destination
netstat active connections and listening ports (-a, -n, -o)
nslookup name query DNS
arp -a show the ARP cache (IP ↔ MAC)
getmac show MAC addresses
telnet host port test whether a port is open
route print show the routing table

The diagnostic sequence that gets asked as a scenario: ping the gateway → ping an external IP (e.g. 8.8.8.8) → ping a domain name. If the IP works but the name fails, the problem is DNS. That single inference is the most likely scenario question in this sub-topic.

3 System commands

Command Does
tasklist / taskkill list / kill processes
systeminfo machine configuration
chkdsk check the disk
sfc /scannow System File Checker — repair system files
shutdown /s /r /t shut down / restart / with a timer
set environment variables
help / cmd /? list commands

Linux equivalents (occasionally contrasted): ls = dir · cd = cd · mkdir = mkdir · rm = del · cp = copy · mv = move · cat = type · clear = cls · ifconfig/ip addr = ipconfig · traceroute = tracert · man = help.

"Working flow of keys" — Alt key sequences

An unusual sub-topic name. It means the ribbon navigation sequences revealed when you press and release Alt, which shows a KeyTip letter over each tab.

The Alt tab letters in Office:

Key Tab
Alt+F File
Alt+H Home
Alt+N Insert
Alt+P Page Layout
Alt+M Formulas (Excel)
Alt+A Data (Excel)
Alt+R Review
Alt+W View

Sequences are typed one key after another, not held down together.

🟢 Real deck question: "To adjust a row's height, which key combination?" → Alt + H + O + H — Home tab → Format → row Height.

How to reason about these without memorising: the first letter is the tab, the rest walk the menu. Alt+H = Home is the anchor for most formatting actions. Any option starting Alt+N (Insert) or Alt+A (Data) is wrong for a formatting task.

Other common ones: Alt+H+O+I autofit column width · Alt+H+O+R rename sheet · Alt+= AutoSum · Alt+F4 close the application.

General computing

Windows: the taskbar shows open programs and windows; the system tray (notification area, right side) shows background services; the Start menu launches programs. Ctrl+R ≈ F5 (refresh). F2 rename · F3 search · Alt+Tab switch windows · Win+D show desktop · Win+L lock.

Operating systems: Linux is open source; Windows and macOS are proprietary. Siri = Apple · Cortana = Microsoft · Google Assistant = Google · Alexa = Amazon.

File extensions: .docx Word · .xlsx Excel · .pptx PowerPoint · .accdb Access · .pub Publisher · .pdf · .csv · .txt · .pst Outlook data · .zip · .exe

The .csv trap: a CSV holds no formatting, no formulas and no multiple sheets. Saving a workbook as CSV discards all of them. Frequently asked.

Hardware/cables: HDMI carries high-bandwidth audio + video together · Ethernet carries network data · USB general-purpose · PS/2 legacy keyboard/mouse · VGA video only, analogue.

Paint: rotates only in 90° increments and flips horizontally/vertically. Arbitrary angles like 45° are NOT supported.

Password policy questions: check each rule against each candidate mechanically — length, lowercase, uppercase, digit, special character. Each wrong option fails exactly one rule, which is how these are constructed.

AutoRecover: saves unsaved work after an abnormal shutdown, at a user-configurable interval whose default is 10 minutes. All three statements are true simultaneously — 10 minutes is the default of a configurable setting.

Question bank — all 62 questions, with derived answers

62 of these are REAL Accenture questions from your placement deck, year-tagged where the deck showed a year. The deck ships no answer key — every answer below is derived by me, with the reasoning shown so you can check it rather than trust it.

Work with the answers collapsed and a 60-second timer. That is the real budget. Open the solution only after you have committed to an answer.

Excel — operators

Q1. In Excel, if cell A2 is "max" and cell B2 is "Yahoo.com", which formula returns "max@yahoo.com" in C2?

  • A) =A2# "@" #B2
  • B) =A2$ "@" $B2
  • C) =A2+ "@" +B2
  • D) =A2& "@" &B2
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

D) =A2& "@" &B2

& is Excel's concatenation operator. =A2&"@"&B2 joins text. + is arithmetic and errors on text; # and $ are not concatenation ($ locks a reference). CONCATENATE(A2,"@",B2) and TEXTJOIN do the same job.

Excel — absolute reference

Q2. Which sign makes a cell reference absolute in MS Excel?

  • A) &
  • B) #
  • C) @
  • D) $
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

D) $

$ locks the part that follows it. $A$1 never moves when copied; $A1 locks the column only; A$1 locks the row only. F4 cycles through all four forms while editing.

Excel — text functions

Q3. PROPER, LOWER and UPPER functions in MS Excel are used to:

  • A) Change the font of the text
  • B) Change the cell reference
  • C) Change the position of the text
  • D) Change the case of the text
Answer — 🟢 REAL

D) Change the case of the text

All three change letter case. UPPER→ALL CAPS, LOWER→all lowercase, PROPER→Title Case Of Each Word. They change the value, not the formatting — font and position are formatting, not functions.

Excel — counting functions

Q4. Which function in MS Excel is used to count blank cells?

  1. COUNT() 2. COUNTIF() 3. COUNTIFS()
  • A) 2 and 3
  • B) 1 and 3
  • C) 1 and 2
  • D) 1, 2 and 3
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

A) 2 and 3

COUNTIF/COUNTIFS can count blanks using the criterion "" or "=", e.g. =COUNTIF(A1:A10,""). COUNT only counts numeric cells and can never count blanks. (The dedicated function is COUNTBLANK, but of the three offered, only 2 and 3 can do it.)

Excel — VLOOKUP

Q5. Which statement is correct for VLOOKUP?

  1. Looks for a value in the leftmost column of the selected table
  2. Looks for a value in the rightmost column
  3. Cannot find a value in a previous (left) column
  • A) 1 and 3
  • B) 2 and 3
  • C) Only 2
  • D) Only 1
Answer — 🟢 REAL

A) 1 and 3

VLOOKUP searches only the FIRST (leftmost) column of the table array, and can only return values to the right of it. So statement 1 is true and statement 3 is true; statement 2 is false. To look leftward you need INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP.

Excel — NOW()

Q6. If you use the NOW function in MS Excel, it returns:

I. Current time II. Current date

  • A) Only II
  • B) Both I and II
  • C) Only I
  • D) Neither I nor II
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2020

B) Both I and II

NOW() returns date AND time; TODAY() returns the date only. Both are volatile — they recalculate on every worksheet change.

Excel — conditional formatting

Q7. To highlight students who secured more than 74 marks, which feature should you use?

  • A) Sort
  • B) Filter
  • C) Conditional formatting
  • D) Cell style
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

C) Conditional formatting

Conditional formatting applies formatting based on a rule — highlight cells greater than 74. Sort reorders rows, Filter hides rows, Cell style applies fixed formatting with no condition. The keyword in the question is highlight.

Excel — Ctrl+Shift shortcuts

Q8. In MS Excel, which symbol with Ctrl+Shift changes the cell format to General?

  • A) ^
  • B) ~
  • C) #
  • D) @
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

B) ~

Ctrl+Shift+~ applies the General format. The family: ~ General · $ Currency · % Percentage · ^ Scientific · # Date · @ Time · ! Number with two decimals.

Excel — row height

Q9. To adjust a row's height in a spreadsheet, which key combination works?

  • A) Alt + H + O + H
  • B) Alt + N + O + H
  • C) Alt + A + O + H
  • D) Alt + M + O + H
Answer — 🟢 REAL

A) Alt + H + O + H

Alt+H opens the Home tab, O opens Format, H selects Row Height. Excel's Alt key-tips spell the ribbon path: H = Home, N = Insert, A = Data, M = Formulas.

Excel — autofit

Q10. What do you do to autofit the width of a column?

  • A) Click twice on the column header
  • B) Double-click the left edge of the column
  • C) Right-click twice on the column's edge
  • D) Both a and c
Answer — 🟢 REAL

B) Double-click the left edge of the column

Double-clicking the boundary of a column header autofits it to the widest entry. Right-clicking opens a context menu; clicking the header just selects the column. (Ribbon path: Home → Format → AutoFit Column Width.)

Excel — insert object

Q11. An attachment can be inserted into a worksheet by using:

  • A) Insert > Scatter
  • B) Insert > Smart Chart
  • C) Insert > Clipart
  • D) Insert > Object
Answer — 🟢 REAL

D) Insert > Object

Insert → Object embeds or links an external file (PDF, Word doc) into the worksheet. Scatter is a chart type and Clipart inserts images — neither attaches a file.

Word — shortcuts

Q12. In MS Word, Ctrl + X is used to:

  • A) Cut selected text
  • B) Close the current document
  • C) Undo last action
  • D) Redo the last action performed
Answer — 🟢 REAL

A) Cut selected text

Ctrl+X = Cut. Ctrl+C copy · Ctrl+V paste · Ctrl+Z undo · Ctrl+Y redo · Ctrl+W close document. The usual trap pairs Ctrl+Z with Ctrl+Y.

Word — indent

Q13. In MS Word, which shortcut key indents a paragraph?

  • A) Ctrl + I
  • B) Alt + I
  • C) Ctrl + M
  • D) Alt + M
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

C) Ctrl + M

Ctrl+M increases the indent; Ctrl+Shift+M decreases it. Ctrl+I is italic — that is the distractor. This question appears three separate times in the Accenture deck, so learn it.

Word — delete word

Q14. In MS Word, which modifier key with Backspace deletes the entire word to the left of the cursor?

  • A) Shift
  • B) Alt
  • C) TAB
  • D) Ctrl
Answer — 🟢 REAL

D) Ctrl

Ctrl+Backspace deletes the whole word to the left; Ctrl+Delete deletes the word to the right. Ctrl+Arrow moves the cursor a word at a time — the same 'Ctrl means word-level' rule.

Word — navigation

Q15. In MS Word, to move the cursor one screen down, which shortcut should you use?

  • A) Ctrl + Page Down
  • B) Ctrl + Down Arrow
  • C) Page Down
  • D) Ctrl + End
Answer — 🟢 REAL

C) Page Down

Page Down scrolls one screen down. Ctrl+End jumps to the end of the document, Ctrl+Down moves one paragraph, Ctrl+Page Down jumps to the next page/browse object.

Word — Save As

Q16. To make a copy of a Word document with a new name, which action should you use?

  • A) Drag and Drop
  • B) Cut-Paste
  • C) Save As
  • D) Save
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

C) Save As

Save As writes a new file under a new name, leaving the original untouched. Save overwrites the original. The keyboard shortcut is F12.

Word — spelling

Q17. In MS Word, which feature reduces spelling errors as you type?

  • A) Auto Format
  • B) Smart Tags
  • C) Auto Text
  • D) Auto Correct
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

D) Auto Correct

AutoCorrect fixes common misspellings automatically as you type (teh → the). AutoText inserts stored blocks of text, AutoFormat applies formatting rules.

Word — spell check key

Q18. Which function key runs the spelling check?

  • A) F2
  • B) F4
  • C) F7
  • D) F9
Answer — 🟢 REAL

C) F7

F7 = Spelling & Grammar in Office. Also worth knowing: F12 Save As, F5 Go To (Find & Replace dialog in Word), F4 repeat last action.

Word — grammar marks

Q19. In a Word document, a double blue underline under a word indicates:

  1. Spelling error 2. Double space between words 3. Wrong letter case
  • A) 1 and 3
  • B) Only 3
  • C) Only 2
  • D) Only 1
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

C) Only 2

A double blue underline flags a spacing/formatting inconsistency — typically a double space. A red wavy underline is a spelling error; a blue/green wavy underline is grammar or style. The word double in the answer matches the double underline.

Word — centring

Q20. The title of a document can be placed in the centre of a page in MS Word using:

  • A) Alignment feature
  • B) Tab key
  • C) Spacing
  • D) Font style
Answer — 🟢 REAL

A) Alignment feature

Centre alignment (Ctrl+E) is the correct feature. Using the Tab key or spaces to push text to the middle looks similar but breaks the moment the font or margins change — a point these questions like to test.

Word — translate

Q21. Which option is used to translate selected content in MS Word?

  • A) Translate to Language
  • B) Translate the Content
  • C) Translate Selected Text
  • D) Translate Selection
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2020

C) Translate Selected Text

Under Review → Translate, the options are Translate Selected Text and Translate Document. Exact menu wording is what is being tested.

Word — hyperlinks

Q22. Pasted web addresses appear in blue with an underline in Word. How do you remove that formatting?

  • A) By removing hyperlink
  • B) All of the mentioned options
  • C) By using Text formatting options
  • D) By using conditional formatting
Answer — 🟢 REAL

A) By removing hyperlink

Right-click → Remove Hyperlink (or Ctrl+Shift+F9) strips the link and its automatic blue-underline style. Manually recolouring the text leaves the hyperlink live, so 'text formatting options' is an incomplete fix. Conditional formatting is Excel, not Word — that option does not exist here.

Word — watermark

Q23. To add a watermark in a Word document, which of these can you select?

  1. Colour 2. Size 3. Layout
  • A) 1 and 2
  • B) 2 and 3
  • C) 1, 2 and 3
  • D) 1 and 3
Answer — 🟢 REAL

C) 1, 2 and 3

The Custom Watermark dialog exposes all three. For a text watermark you set the font, size, colour and layout (diagonal or horizontal); for a picture watermark you set scale and washout.

Word — page numbers

Q24. In MS Word, page numbers can be added at:

  1. Top of the page 2. Bottom of the page 3. The page margins
  • A) 2 and 3
  • B) 1 and 2
  • C) 1 and 3
  • D) 1, 2 and 3
Answer — 🟢 REAL

D) 1, 2 and 3

Insert → Page Number offers Top of Page, Bottom of Page, Page Margins and Current Position. All three listed options are genuine positions.

Word — selection info

Q25. When you select text in MS Word, which information is provided?

  1. Formatting used 2. Number of words 3. Language
  • A) 1, 2 and 3
  • B) 1 and 2
  • C) 1 and 3
  • D) 2 and 3
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

A) 1, 2 and 3

The status bar and ribbon together surface all three: the word count of the selection, the proofing language, and the applied formatting (visible in the Font/Paragraph groups and the Reveal Formatting pane).

Word — columns

Q26. Which of the following can create a vertical division between columns?

  • A) Margin
  • B) Header
  • C) None of the mentioned options
  • D) Orientation

C) None of the mentioned options

A vertical line between columns is added by the 'Line between' checkbox in Layout → Columns → More Columns — none of the listed items. Margins set page edges, headers sit at the top, orientation is portrait/landscape.

PowerPoint — presenter view

Q27. To start the presenter view from the CURRENT slide in PowerPoint, which key do you press?

  • A) Shift + F5
  • B) F5
  • C) Ctrl + F5
  • D) Alt + F5
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

A) Shift + F5

Shift+F5 starts the show from the current slide; F5 starts from the beginning. (Alt+F5 opens Presenter View from the current slide in newer builds, but the standard answer tested here is Shift+F5.)

PowerPoint — blank screen

Q28. In PowerPoint, which key pauses the slideshow and displays a WHITE screen?

  • A) Period key
  • B) Backspace key
  • C) Comma key
  • D) Esc key
Answer — 🟢 REAL

C) Comma key

Comma (,) or W → white screen. Period (.) or B → black screen. Mnemonic: White/Black. Esc ends the show entirely.

PowerPoint — pointer

Q29. In MS PowerPoint, which is the default pointer type?

  • A) Arrow
  • B) Laser Pointer
  • C) Pen
  • D) Highlighter
Answer — 🟢 REAL

A) Arrow

The default is the standard Arrow pointer. Pen, Highlighter and Laser Pointer are opt-in annotation tools during a slideshow (Ctrl+P pen, Ctrl+L laser).

Q30. In PowerPoint, an action button can perform its assigned action:

  • A) Both 1 and 2
  • B) Only 2
  • C) Only 1
  • D) Neither 1 nor 2
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

A) Both 1 and 2

The Action Settings dialog has two tabs: 'Mouse Click' and 'Mouse Over'. So an action can fire either on click or on hover — both statements are true.

PowerPoint — triggers

Q31. In the context of animation, what is a trigger?

  • A) The name of a motion path
  • B) An action button that advances to the next slide
  • C) All of the above
  • D) An item on the slide that performs an action when clicked
Answer — 🟢 REAL

D) An item on the slide that performs an action when clicked

A trigger is an object that starts an animation when clicked. It is not the same as an action button (which navigates) and has nothing to do with motion-path names.

Q32. Which linking operations can be performed in PowerPoint?

  • A) Only 1 and 3
  • B) Only 2 and 3
  • C) Only 1 and 2
  • D) All 1, 2 and 3
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

D) All 1, 2 and 3

The Insert Hyperlink dialog offers exactly four targets: Existing File or Web Page, Place in This Document, Create New Document, and E-mail Address. All three listed options are supported.

Q33. Which type of connection lets you navigate from one slide to another in the same presentation, and to a slide in another presentation?

  • C) Attachment
  • D) Hyperlink
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

D) Hyperlink

A hyperlink can target a slide in the same deck or a slide in a different file. Headers and footers are static page furniture; PowerPoint has no 'attachment' navigation.

Outlook — reply all

Q35. Which option should you choose to mail every person present on a received email?

  • A) Reply all
  • B) New mail
  • C) Reply
  • D) Forward
Answer — 🟢 REAL

A) Reply all

Reply All sends to the sender plus everyone in To and Cc. Reply goes only to the sender; Forward sends to new recipients. Bcc recipients are never included — they are hidden from everyone.

Q36. In MS Outlook, which criteria can you use to search an old mail?

  • B) 1 and 2 Only
  • C) 2 and 3 Only
  • D) All 1, 2 and 3
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

D) All 1, 2 and 3

Outlook indexes body text, sender/recipient fields and attachment names. Search operators: from:, subject:, hasattachment:yes, attachment:filename.

Outlook — auto reply

Q37. In which type of account can you set an automatic Reply / Out-of-Office Assistant (OOF)?

  • A) Microsoft Exchange account
  • B) Checking account
  • C) Windows Manage account
  • D) None of the mentioned options
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

A) Microsoft Exchange account

Out-of-Office is a server-side Exchange feature — the server replies even when Outlook is closed. POP/IMAP accounts have no such server, so they need a client-side rule with Outlook left running.

Email — recovery

Q38. If a mail is deleted by accident, which folder can be used to recover it?

  • B) Trash
  • C) Inbox
  • D) Draft
Answer — 🟢 REAL

B) Trash

Deleted mail goes to Trash / Deleted Items and is recoverable until purged (Gmail keeps it 30 days). Spam holds filtered mail, Drafts holds unsent messages.

Email — disadvantages

Q39. Which are possible disadvantages of e-mail?

  1. Forgery 2. Misdirection
  • A) Only 2
  • B) Only 1
  • C) Neither 1 nor 2
  • D) Both 1 and 2
Answer — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

D) Both 1 and 2

Both are genuine risks. Forgery — SMTP has no built-in sender authentication, so headers can be spoofed (hence SPF, DKIM and DMARC). Misdirection — autocomplete sends mail to the wrong recipient, one of the most common real-world data-leak causes.

Email — searching a large inbox

Q40. What is the fastest way to find a large file containing source code that your senior sent, in an inbox of 5000+ emails where many are from that senior and contain attachments?

  • A) Search the word "Code"
  • B) Arrange by → From
  • C) Arrange by → Size
  • D) Arrange by → Attachments
Answer — 🟢 REAL

C) Arrange by → Size

Sorting by size surfaces the largest attachment immediately. The question deliberately removes the other options' usefulness: From still leaves many mails, Attachments still leaves many, and searching "Code" matches body text, not the file. The distinguishing attribute given is large file — so sort by the attribute that is unique: size.

The scheme is the https:// prefix — the 's' signals TLS/SSL. In https://mail.example.com: scheme = https, subdomain = mail, second-level domain = example, top-level domain = com.

Q52. Which cable would you prefer for transmitting high-quality, high-bandwidth audio AND video between devices?

Check each rule against each candidate:

Password ≥8 lower UPPER digit special
Bat@123 ✗ (7) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
wonder@123 ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✓
IronMan@123# ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓
Super@Man ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✓

Only IronMan@123# satisfies all five. Check rules mechanically — each wrong option fails exactly one, which is how these are built.
