Data structures

Stack vs Queue

Stack Queue
Order LIFO ✅ FIFO ✅
Ops push / pop / peek enqueue / dequeue
Used by call stack, undo, DFS, expression eval scheduling, print spooling, BFS

Variants: Deque (both ends) · Circular queue · Priority queue (usually a heap).

Array vs Linked list

Array Linked list
Access by index O(1) O(n)
Insert/delete at a known node O(n) O(1)
Memory contiguous, compact + a pointer per node
Cache locality excellent poor

Trees

  • BST — left < node < right; in-order traversal gives sorted output
  • AVL — BST where subtree heights differ by at most 1
  • Heap — a complete binary tree with the heap property
  • Traversals: Pre = Root-L-R · In = L-Root-R · Post = L-R-Root · Level = BFS with a queue
Fact Value ✅
Degree-2 nodes given n leaves n − 1 verified exhaustively
Max nodes at height h (root = 0) 2^(h+1) − 1 → h=4 gives 31 verified
Distinct binary tree shapes with n nodes Catalan — C₃ = 5, C₄ = 14 verified
Edges in a tree with n nodes n − 1 verified

Hashing and graphs

Hash table — average O(1), worst O(n) (all collide). Load factor = entries ÷ buckets; average chain length = keys ÷ slots. Collisions: chaining or open addressing (linear probing).

Graphs — BFS uses a queue and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph; DFS uses a stack. Complete graph K5 has 10 edges = n(n−1)/2 ✅. Forest = acyclic undirected graph.

Algorithms and complexity

Growth order

O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!) ✅ verified at n=1000

Big-O = upper bound (worst case) · Big-Ω = lower · Big-Θ = tight.

Sorting

Algorithm Average Worst Space Stable Internal?
Bubble / Insertion O(n²) O(n²) O(1) ✅ ✅
Selection O(n²) O(n²) O(1) ❌ ✅
Quicksort O(n log n) O(n²) O(log n) ❌ ✅
Mergesort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n) ✅ ❌ EXTERNAL
Heapsort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(1) ❌ ✅

🟢 "Which is NOT an internal sort?" → Merge sort (needs O(n) auxiliary space). Quicksort's worst case is sorted input with a poor pivot. Bubble/selection comparisons = n(n−1)/2 → n=8 gives 28 ✅. Bubble-sort swaps = the number of inversions ✅.

Searching

Linear O(n), any data. Binary search O(log n) — requires a SORTED array. Worst-case probes = ⌊log₂n⌋ + 1 → n=1024 gives 11 ✅. Midpoint: low + (high−low)/2, never (low+high)/2 (overflow).

Nested-loop counting — the skill actually tested

Loop shape Iterations
for i=1..n n
for i=1..n { for j=1..n } n²
for i=1..n { for j=i..n } n(n+1)/2
for i { for j=i { for k=j+1 } } (n−1)n(n+1)/6 ✅

Operating Systems

The five facts that dominate

1. 🟢 Process creation in Unix: fork() + exec() fork() creates a child copy; exec() replaces the process image with a new executable. Asked twice.

2. 🟢 Context switch → the PROGRAM COUNTER must be saved. Asked three times. The PC holds the address of the next instruction, so execution cannot resume without it. The full context (registers, PC, state) is stored in the PCB.

3. Process vs program vs thread — a program is a passive file; a process is a program in execution with its own address space. Threads share code, data and files; each has its own stack, registers and PC.

4. Deadlock — Coffman's four conditions: mutual exclusion · hold and wait · no pre-emption · circular wait. All four must hold — break one and deadlock is impossible. Handling: prevention · avoidance (Banker's algorithm) · detection · ostrich.

5. Scheduling: FCFS (convoy effect) · SJF (best average wait, needs future knowledge) · Round Robin (fair, preemptive, time quantum) · Priority (starvation → fix with aging). ✅ Computed: bursts 24, 3, 3 → FCFS average wait 17.0 vs SJF 3.0. One long job at the front inflates everyone's wait nearly sixfold.

🟣 With arrival times — the variant the real paper used. P1 arrives 0 (burst 24), P2 arrives 1 (burst 3), P3 arrives 2 (burst 3): waits are 0, 23, 25 → average 48/3 = 16.0 ✅ (computed; note: wait = start − arrival, so P2 waits 24−1 and P3 waits 27−2). Caution: the option list on the captured paper did not include 16 — if your paper's numbers differ, recompute with wait = start − arrival and ignore the published key. Arrivals ignored, the same bursts give 17.0.

Memory management

  • Paging — fixed-size pages/frames → no external, causes INTERNAL fragmentation
  • Segmentation — variable-size → causes EXTERNAL fragmentation
  • Virtual memory — run programs larger than RAM; demand paging loads on a page fault
  • Page replacement: FIFO (suffers Belady's anomaly), LRU, Optimal ✅ Demonstrated: 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 under FIFO gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4 — more memory, more faults. LRU and Optimal are immune.
  • Thrashing — excessive paging; fix by reducing the multiprogramming degree

Synchronisation and other

Mutex has ownership, one holder · counting semaphore permits N, no ownership · Monitor · race condition = outcome depends on timing. Schedulers: long-term (admission) · medium-term (swapping) · short-term/dispatcher (runs most often). Zombie = finished, parent hasn't wait()ed · Orphan = parent died first (adopted by init). Kernel: monolithic (fast, services in kernel space) vs microkernel (robust, services in user space). System calls: fork, exec, wait, open, read, write. printf/malloc are library functions, not syscalls. RAID: 0 striping · 1 mirroring · 5 striping + distributed parity.

🟣 Two scenario questions from the real paper, on the OS's security role:

  • After a security breach, which OS property do you prioritise to harden the system? → Access control (deciding which users/processes may reach which resources). Multitasking, virtual memory and the UI are irrelevant to a breach.
  • Beyond create/delete/manipulate, which file-management function most improves organised, efficient access? → Managing file permissions and access control — it governs how files are reached, which is what the question asks. Compression, encryption and backup are real functions but don't organise access.

📚 cs_funda/Operating_Systems_Placement_Guide.md — §2 Processes (596), §6 Context Switching (2739), §13 Deadlocks (6240), §19 Paging (8997). Four sections, not 15,000 lines.

DBMS and SQL

Theory

ACID — Atomicity (all or nothing) · Consistency · Isolation · Durability (committed data survives a crash).

Normal forms: 1NF atomic values · 2NF no partial dependency · 3NF no transitive dependency · BCNF every determinant is a candidate key.

Keys: Primary (unique + NOT NULL) · Foreign (referential integrity) · Candidate · Composite · Unique (may allow one NULL).

🟢 File system limitations (why DBMS exists): no concurrent access · difficult data access · no backup/recovery · redundancy → "all of the mentioned options".

From the real extracted paper — four DBMS items to add

Concurrency anomalies — the paper asked for the name of the anomaly from a scenario. Two transactions decrement the same stock row; both succeed, but the final value reflects only one update → Lost Update (both read the same old value and the second write overwrites the first). Keep the family straight: phantom read = new rows appear on re-read · non-repeatable read = a row's value changes on re-read · deadlock = mutual waiting · lost update = a write is silently overwritten.

MySQL trigger — the exact syntax to recognise. The paper's scenario: log every deleted employee into an audit table. The correct MySQL form:

CREATE TRIGGER trg_DeleteEmployee
AFTER DELETE ON Employees
FOR EACH ROW
INSERT INTO Auditlog (EmpID, DeletedOn)
VALUES (OLD.EmpID, NOW());

The distractors are SQL Server syntax (ON table BEFORE/AFTER … AS … FROM deleted — deleted and GETDATE() are SQL Server; MySQL uses OLD. and NOW()) and wrong events (AFTER INSERT can never log a deletion). FOR EACH ROW + OLD.col + NOW() = MySQL.

Primary-key choice: unique EmployeeID, never Name (not unique), never PhoneNumber (changes; may be shared) → EmployeeID.

Character-occurrence count — the classic the paper reused:

SELECT FirstandLastName,
       LENGTH(FirstandLastName) - LENGTH(REPLACE(FirstandLastName, 'm', ''))
FROM StudentDetails;

✅ Executed: 'kumar mohan' → 2. Why not COUNT()? COUNT(col) counts rows, not characters — the COUNT version of this query returns 0/row-counts, verified. The function pair is LENGTH − LENGTH(REPLACE(...)). Watch for options with FROM placed before SELECT — invalid syntax, always a distractor.

SQL essentials

Execution order: FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

Join Keeps ✅
INNER only matching rows 5 rows
LEFT all left rows + matches 6 rows
CROSS Cartesian product 16
SELF table joined to itself needs m1.x != m2.x

Two rules that decide most questions:

  1. NULL never matches in a join — dropped by INNER, kept by LEFT ✅
  2. A LEFT JOIN never returns fewer rows than the left table — if yours does, a right-table filter is in WHERE instead of ON ✅ verified: 4 rows → 2

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after. WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 is an error.

COUNT(*) counts NULL rows; COUNT(col) skips them ✅ · WHERE x = NULL is always false — use IS NULL ✅ · NOT IN + a NULL returns ZERO rows — use NOT EXISTS ✅

DELETE (DML, WHERE, rollback-able) vs TRUNCATE (DDL, no WHERE, fast, resets identity) vs DROP (removes the table).

📚 Full guide with 44 executed queries: SQL-COMPLETE · cs_funda/DBMS_Placement_Guide.md §21 Cheat Sheet (9258) — start there.

CPU and memory

Memory hierarchy

Registers → L1 → L2 → L3 cache → RAM → SSD → HDD → Tape
 fastest, smallest                        slowest, largest
Level Size Speed Tech
Registers bytes fastest inside the CPU
L1 32–64 KB ~1 ns SRAM
L3 8–32 MB ~15 ns SRAM
RAM 8–32 GB ~100 ns DRAM

The exam sentence: "Registers are the fastest and smallest memory, located inside the CPU. Cache is faster but smaller than RAM."

SRAM/DRAM and RAM/ROM

DRAM uses capacitors that leak → must be REFRESHED; cheap, dense → main memory. SRAM uses flip-flops → no refresh, fast, expensive → cache. "Which needs refreshing?" → DRAM.

RAM volatile (lost on power off) · ROM non-volatile (firmware, BIOS, bootstrap). ROM family: PROM → EPROM → EEPROM → Flash.

Registers

Register Holds
PC / IP address of the NEXT instruction
IR the CURRENT instruction
MAR address being accessed
MDR / MBR data read from / written to memory
Accumulator intermediate arithmetic results
SP top of the stack
PSW / Flags zero, carry, sign, overflow

PC = next, IR = current. Swapping these is the most common wrong answer.

🟢 "Transferring data from the accumulator to memory" → memory write operation

Cycle, pipelining, cache, buses

Instruction cycle: Fetch → Decode → Execute (→ write-back). Pipelining overlaps stages across instructions — raises throughput, not single-instruction latency. Hazards: structural · data · control (branches).

Cache average access time = hit × cache + (1−hit) × memory. With 0.9, 10 ns, 100 ns → 19 ns ✅. The 10% of misses contribute 10 of those 19 ns — which is why hit ratios are pushed toward 99%.

Locality of reference: temporal (reuse soon) and spatial (nearby addresses — why caches fetch 64-byte lines, and why row-major beats column-major in C). Write policies: write-through (safer) vs write-back (faster).

Buses: address (unidirectional) · data (bidirectional) · control. n address lines address 2ⁿ locations → 32-bit = 4 GB ✅ — exactly the 32-bit RAM ceiling.

Architecture: von Neumann (shared memory/bus → the von Neumann bottleneck) vs Harvard (separate instruction/data). RISC = few fixed-length instructions, many registers, pipelines well (ARM) · CISC = many complex variable-length (x86).

Interrupt vs polling — an interrupt lets the device signal the CPU, which runs an ISR; polling wastes cycles. DMA transfers to memory without the CPU. 🟢 "I/O devices connected to a shared bus" → via a device controller.

The real paper's hardware questions — three shapes now confirmed

  1. "Which component is the primary communication pathway for data, addresses and control signals between CPU, memory and I/O?" → the System Bus. Not the PCI slot (one expansion bus), not a CPU register (inside the CPU), not the Northbridge/Southbridge chipset (a hub on the pathway, not the pathway).
  2. "Device controllers with dedicated high-speed buffers so transfer is faster" → the disk controller family — 🟢 EIDE = Enhanced Integrated Drive Electronics (know the expansion; the wrong options are the misspellings) and, in the modern option set, the SATA controller. Disk controllers carry onboard cache/buffers; USB, Ethernet and wireless controllers generally do not.
  3. The OS textbook model to quote back: CPU ↔ shared bus ↔ device controller ↔ device, with the controller's buffer decoupling the device's speed from the bus.

📚 cs_funda/COA_Placement_Guide.md — §5 CPU (1856), §8 Cache (3158), §11 Hierarchy (4658), §13 I/O (5532)

Number systems and data representation

Conversion Example ✅
Binary → decimal 1101 = 13 verified
Decimal → binary 25 = 11001 verified
Decimal → hex 255 = FF verified
Octal → decimal 123₈ = 83 verified
Hex → decimal 1A = 26 verified

Shortcuts: 1 hex digit = 4 bits · 1 octal digit = 3 bits ✅

Signed representations: sign-magnitude · 1's complement (flip) · 2's complement (flip + 1 — what real machines use). 2's complement of 5 in 8 bits = 11111011 ✅ Why it wins: one representation of zero, and subtraction becomes addition.

Storage: 1 byte = 8 bits · nibble = 4 · 1 KB = 2¹⁰ = 1024 · 1 MB = 2²⁰ · 1 GB = 2³⁰ · 1 TB = 2⁴⁰.

SDLC and software engineering

Model Suits
Waterfall fixed, well-understood requirements; sequential; late changes expensive
Agile frequently changing requirements; short iterations
V-model each dev phase paired with a test phase
Spiral risk-driven, large projects

Testing: unit → integration → system → acceptance. Black box (no internals) vs white box (internal paths). Regression re-runs old tests after a change.

Version control: Git is distributed — every clone is a full repository.

§5. DevOps 🆕

Absent from every prep site I checked, and on the official list. Closed syllabus: Git, CI/CD, Jenkins, Docker, Kubernetes, and the culture questions. Ninety minutes.

1 What DevOps is (and the definition question)

DevOps is a culture and set of practices that shortens the delivery cycle by making Development and Operations work as one team, with heavy automation.

The term was coined by Patrick Debois (2009, "DevOpsDays" Ghent).

The classic MCQ: "What is DevOps?" with options like "a software development methodology" / "a culture promoting cooperation between Dev & Ops" / "a set of best practices to reduce delivery times" / "automate everything". The primary answer is the culture one — DevOps is explicitly not a methodology like Agile or Waterfall. Note that Accenture's own DevOps test warns that some questions have multiple correct answers, and this is one where the practices/automation options are also defensible.

CALMS — the standard framework: Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing.

2 CI / CD / CD

Term Means Ends at
Continuous Integration Merge to shared main frequently; every commit triggers automated build + tests A tested build artifact
Continuous Delivery Every change is automatically prepared for release; deploy is a manual button Ready-to-deploy, human approves
Continuous Deployment Every passing change deploys to production automatically Live, no human step

The distinction that gets tested: Delivery and Deployment differ only by whether the final production push is automatic. Both are "CD".

Pipeline stages: Commit → Build → Unit test → Integration test → Artifact → Deploy to staging → Acceptance test → Deploy to production

3 Git

  • Distributed VCS — every clone is a full repository with complete history
  • git fetch downloads without merging; git pull = fetch + merge
  • merge preserves history and creates a merge commit; rebase rewrites commits onto a new base for linear history. Never rebase shared/public branches.
  • git reset moves the branch pointer (rewrites history); git revert creates a new commit undoing a change (safe on shared branches)
  • git cherry-pick applies one specific commit elsewhere
  • git stash shelves uncommitted work
  • Webhooks — the Git server calls out to Jenkins to trigger builds

4 Jenkins

  • Open-source automation server, written in Java; created by Kohsuke Kawaguchi
  • Jenkins originated from Hudson (forked after the Oracle/community split — they are the same lineage, not the same product)
  • Requires a JDK/JRE to run
  • JENKINS_HOME — the environment variable specifying the folder holding Jenkins configuration and runtime data. Back up this directory.
  • Agent / Slave — a lightweight worker that executes jobs dispatched by the controller. Not a second Jenkins server.
  • Pipeline job — a set of jobs defining a workflow and its dependencies, usually declared in a Jenkinsfile kept in the repo (pipeline-as-code)
  • Plugins are the extension mechanism — Git, Maven, Docker, Blue Ocean
  • On Linux, the Jenkins user needs appropriate privileges and folder permissions (and membership of the docker group to run Docker builds)

5 Docker — and the commands that get tested

Containers solve dependency and portability problems: an image bundles the app with its dependencies so it runs identically anywhere. Containers share the host OS kernel, which is why they are lighter than VMs (a VM ships a whole guest OS).

Image = immutable template. Container = a running instance of an image. Dockerfile = the recipe that builds an image. Registry (Docker Hub) = where images are stored.

Command Does
docker build -t name . build an image from a Dockerfile
docker run IMAGE create and start a NEW container from an image
docker start CONTAINER start an EXISTING stopped container
docker ps / docker ps -a running / all containers
docker images list images
docker exec -it C sh run a command inside a running container
docker volume create NAME create a named volume
docker-compose up run a multi-container app from docker-compose.yml

The two Docker questions Accenture actually asks

Port publishing. The flag is -p HOST:CONTAINER.

"Pick the docker option which will expose a container originally running on port 8080 to port 80 of the host machine." Answer: -p 80:8080 — host port first, container port second.

✅ Verified against the Docker CLI: -p, --publish "Publish a container's port(s) to the host", host-side first. Getting this backwards is the single most common Docker mistake.

run vs start.

run spins up a NEW container; start restarts an existing stopped one.

✅ Verified from the CLI itself: docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE … takes an image, while docker start [OPTIONS] CONTAINER … takes a container. The signatures prove the semantics.

Volume creation is docker volume create NAME — ✅ verified: docker volume has a create subcommand; docker create volume is not valid syntax.

6 Kubernetes & orchestration

  • Docker Swarm — Docker's native clustering: a cluster of connected Docker hosts (nodes), not containers on one host
  • Kubernetes (K8s) — the dominant orchestrator
  • Pod — smallest deployable unit; one or more containers sharing network/storage
  • Node — a worker machine · Cluster — control plane + nodes
  • Deployment — declares desired state and manages ReplicaSets
  • Service — stable network endpoint / load balancing for pods
  • ConfigMap / Secret — configuration and credentials
  • kubelet — agent on each node · etcd — cluster state store
  • Infrastructure as Code: Terraform (provisioning), Ansible (configuration management), CloudFormation (AWS)
  • Monitoring: Prometheus (metrics), Grafana (dashboards), ELK/EFK (logs)

7 Twenty real Accenture DevOps MCQs

Provenance: these come from a public GitHub repository containing an Accenture DevOps Training Post-Test. The repository contains no answer key — every answer below is derived by me, and the Docker ones were verified against the Docker CLI. The test's own instructions state "few questions can have multiple answers".

# Question Answer Basis
1 What is DevOps? Culture promoting Dev–Ops cooperation (practices/automation options also defensible) Definition
2 Who coined the term DevOps? Patrick Debois Documented
3 Who created Jenkins? Kohsuke Kawaguchi Documented
4 Relation between Hudson & Jenkins? Jenkins originated from Hudson Documented
5 Prerequisites to run Jenkins JDK or JRE 1.8 Jenkins is a Java app
6 Git's role in CI with Jenkins SCM tool + Git server web-hooks trigger Jenkins jobs (multiple) Webhooks are server-side
7 Needed to integrate Jenkins with GitHub GitHub credentials + GitHub plugin (multiple) Maven is unrelated

9 Correct GitHub webhook URL http://<jenkins-url>/github-webhook/ Jenkins GitHub plugin endpoint

11 Difference between run and start run spins a new container; start runs a stopped one ✅ Verified via Docker CLI

⚠️ Honest caveat. Questions 5, 9, 12 and 17 depend on Jenkins version and setup — e.g. modern Jenkins requires Java 11/17, not 1.8, but the test was written when 1.8 was the prerequisite. Answer what the test expects. Questions 6, 7, 8, 12, 13 and 20 are explicitly multi-answer; I have marked which options I believe belong.

8 The real paper's Docker and container questions — six of them

A real extracted paper carried six separate Docker/container items plus an artifact-management question. No prep site's syllabus lists Docker this heavily. Everything below is exam-ready.

Image vs container — an image is a read-only template (layers + metadata); a container is a running instance of an image with a writable layer on top. One image → many containers.

Dockerfile vs Docker Compose — a Dockerfile builds one image step by step (FROM, RUN, COPY…). Compose (docker-compose.yml + docker compose up) defines and runs a multi-container application — services, networks and volumes together. "Which file describes multiple services and how they connect?" → Compose.

COPY vs ADD vs RUN — the classic trap:

Instruction Does Use
COPY copies files/dirs from build context into the image default choice
ADD COPY plus auto-extracts local .tar and can fetch URLs only when you need extraction
RUN executes a command at build time in a new layer (installs packages) builds, not file moves

Networking modes — bridge (default; container joins a private docker network, NATs out) · host (container shares the host's network stack; no isolation) · none (no networking) · container: (share another container's namespace) · overlay (multi-host/Swarm). "Fastest, no isolation?" → host. "Default?" → bridge.

Volume types — named volumes (managed by Docker, survive container removal) · anonymous volumes (same, unnamed) · bind mounts (map an arbitrary host directory into the container — best for development where you edit live) · tmpfs (in host memory, never persisted). "Persist data beyond the container's life?" → volume. "Edit code on the host and see it live?" → bind mount.

Container isolation — the kernel answer. The paper's hardest container question: hardware-peripheral access must be limited per container so non-allocated devices are invisible → "what is the most critical factor?" → configuring the kernel to enforce strict resource isolation, limiting peripheral access to allocated devices only (that is cgroups + device namespaces — Linux kernel mechanisms). The distractors (equal CPU scheduling, dynamic virtualization memory, shared NICs with ACLs) all increase coupling rather than isolation.

Debugging a high-latency container — the method question. "What should the engineer do FIRST?" → Analyze the network traffic and logs (diagnose before changing anything). Increasing CPU/memory limits, restarting, or removing containers are shotgun fixes a question this shape marks wrong.

Artifact management — the building block question. Where do compiled outputs (JAR, Docker image, npm package) live, versioned, between CI and deployment? → Artifact Management (a binary/artifact repository — Artifactory/Nexus territory). Source Code Management stores text; databases store app data; orchestration runs containers — none of them store build artifacts.

§10. Web technologies — the real paper's MCQ questions

The real extracted paper carried HTML/CSS/JS questions inside the technical MCQ round — not only in the coding round. Nine distinct ones were workable. All fit the frontend material in Part 5, but the MCQ shapes are short enough to drill here.

Q-web1 — audio autoplay. "Which code is appropriate for autoplay?" → the <audio autoplay> element with <source> children and a closing </audio>:

<audio autoplay>
  <source src="test.mp3">
  <source src="test.ogg">
</audio>

Distractors: a fake <autoplay> element, </audio autoplay> (invalid closing tag), and <controls> wrapped around sources (controls is an attribute of <audio>, not an element).

Q-web2 — the canvas fallback. The text between <canvas> and </canvas>:

<canvas id="mycanvas">HTML5 Canvas not supported</canvas>

→ it is fallback content shown by browsers that do not support canvas. It is not a comment and not browser-specific.

Q-web3 — the <details markdown="1"> tag. "Which tag defines additional details the user can view or hide?" → <details markdown="1"> (with <summary markdown="span"> as its visible heading). There is no <detail> or <record> element.

Q-web4 — the onabort event. An <img> with onabort="myFunction()": the handler fires when image loading is aborted — the user presses Esc/Stop before the page finishes loading. Not page close, not page load, not refresh.

Q-web5 — getAttribute. document.write(button.getAttribute("onClick", 1)) → writes the value of the onclick attribute (i.e. myFunction(this);) to the page. getAttribute takes one argument — the extra 1 is ignored. It returns the attribute string, not true/false.

Q-web6 — async fetch returning JSON. The correct shape:

async function getData() {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  return await response.json();
}

async/await + fetch + response.json() — know the trio. Distractors use fetch without await, or .json() on the wrong object.

Q-web7 — CSS3 shapes. A rectangle rounded on top only (flat bottom):

.shape { border-radius: 50px 50px 0 0; }

Order is top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left (clockwise). One value = all corners; 50% = pill/circle.

Q-web8 — HTTP status codes. "API endpoint not found" → 404. Keep the family: 200 OK · 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed) · 404 Not Found · 500 Internal Server Error.

Q-web9 — REST method for creating. "Create new entries in a product catalog, correct HTTP method?" → POST (POST /products). PUT updates/replaces a known resource; GET reads.

Where to drill: Part 5, the frontend sections — the same tags, events and CSS appear there in task form.

§11. The long tail — topics the real paper shows that no syllabus lists

These appeared in the real extracted paper (several as image-only stubs, so they are covered as topics with the exam-ready facts, not as reconstructed questions). Small, learnable, and now confirmed on test.

1 OAuth 2.0 — the four grant flows

OAuth 2.0 delegates authorisation: the client gets an access token without ever handling the user's password.

Grant Who uses it Mechanism
Authorization Code web/mobile apps with a backend redirect to auth server → code → exchange code+secret for token; PKCE extension for public clients
Client Credentials machine-to-machine, no user involved client authenticates itself, gets token
Implicit legacy browser-only SPAs token straight from the authorize endpoint — deprecated now
Resource Owner Password legacy, trusted first-party apps user hands password to the client — deprecated

Exam shape: "server-to-server API calls with no user" → Client Credentials; "web app with a backend" → Authorization Code.

2 Spring Boot and Spring MVC (Java ecosystem)

  • Spring Boot auto-configuration — Boot configures beans automatically based on the dependencies on the classpath (@EnableAutoConfiguration / starters): add spring-boot-starter-web and an embedded server + MVC setup appear without manual config.
  • Spring MVC request flow — DispatcherServlet (front controller) receives the request → HandlerMapping finds the controller → Controller runs → returns a model+view → ViewResolver picks the template → response rendered. The front-controller name is the answer most questions want: DispatcherServlet.

3 Microservices and the API Gateway

An API Gateway is the single entry point in front of microservices: it routes requests, does cross-cutting concerns (authentication, rate limiting, logging, SSL termination) so services stay focused on business logic. Contrast: service mesh handles service-to-service traffic; load balancer distributes at L4/L7 without the API-level concerns.

4 GDPR

The General Data Protection Regulation (EU, 2018): personal data may be processed only on lawful bases (consent, contract, legal obligation…); principles of minimisation, purpose limitation, accuracy, storage limitation; rights to access, rectify and erase ("right to be forgotten"); breach notification within 72 hours. Exam shape: "regulation governing personal data of EU citizens" → GDPR.

5 Blockchain consensus

A blockchain is an append-only, distributed ledger; consensus decides which block is appended without a central authority: Proof of Work (spend compute to mine — Bitcoin), Proof of Stake (stake capital to validate — Ethereum post-merge), Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (enterprise/permissioned chains). Exam shape: "how do distributed nodes agree on the ledger's state" → a consensus mechanism (PoW/PoS).

6 Neural networks (one question, one page of facts)

A neural network trains by forward pass → loss → backpropagation of the error → gradient-descent weight update, repeated over epochs. Exam shape: "what adjusts the weights during training" → backpropagation + gradient descent. Do not go deeper than this for this exam.

7 Cloud migration without downtime (architecture layer)

The paper's scenario: legacy and cloud systems must serve data simultaneously, "logically integrated without physical movement", for real-time reporting → an abstraction layer that logically unifies disparate data sources (a data virtualisation/federation layer). Distractors: direct connection protocols, caching replicas (that's physical), middleware APIs (consumption, not integration).

Part 5 — Round 3 — the coding round

Three questions in 60 minutes: one DSA, one SQL, one HTML/CSS/JS

What the coding round actually looks like

This changed for the 2026 batch, and the change matters. Two independent first-hand accounts of on-campus drives held in September–December 2025 describe a coding round in three parts:

Part Content Reported difficulty
SQL One query, typically involving a join Medium
Backend / DSA One algorithmic problem (a dynamic sliding window problem in one account) Hardest of the three
Frontend HTML / CSS / JavaScript task, described as three small sub-tasks Easy

Confirmed duration: 3 questions in 60 minutes. Two independent 2026 drive listings state this, matching prep-site coverage of the change. The legacy format, used for the 2025 batch and earlier and possibly still used in some off-campus drives, was 2 problems in 45 minutes, pure DSA.

🟣 Real-paper confirmation. A captured recent test shows exactly this three-part shape — the extraction summarises it as: "1. DSA: a simple array-based question. 2. SQL: a query question involving JOINs on 2-3 tables/schemas. 3. JavaScript Frontend: a task like creating some colored boxes or a basic UI element" — and the candidate's own screenshots label the stage "Round 4: The Coding Round" (the same three-part round, numbered differently). The SQL tasks arrived with a View Schema tab at the bottom of the query window listing 6-8 tables — exactly the join-on-2-3-tables shape. All of the paper's actual coding tasks are worked in Part 5: six SQL tasks (below, Tasks 5-10), three frontend tasks, and two DSA tasks.

Languages offered, as published on 2026 drive listings: Java · Python · C++ · C# · .NET · SQL · HTML · CSS · React · Vue.js

That language list is the strongest single piece of evidence for the three-part structure. Nobody offers React or Vue.js for a data-structures problem, and nobody offers SQL for a frontend task. The list only makes sense if the round has a database part, a web part and an algorithmic part. It also matches Accenture's own pre-onboarding curriculum, which is built from Java, SQL and Web Technology.

Prepare for the three-part format, because it is what the most recent evidence shows, and because its DSA component is a subset of the legacy format's. If you walk in prepared for three parts and get two, you have lost nothing.

How hard are the problems, really?

Rather than guess, I profiled 55 problem statements from a public candidate-contributed corpus of Accenture previous-year coding questions:

Measure Median 25th–75th percentile Range
Words per statement 80 35 – 124 6 – 209
Sentences 6 4 – 10 2 – 18
Chained conditions 1 0 – 2 0 – 7
Worked examples given 2 1 – 2 0 – 9

What this tells you. These are short problems — a median of 80 words and one conditional clause. They are not LeetCode Hard. The difficulty is concentrated in edge cases and explicit return codes, not in algorithmic depth. The longest statement in the corpus (209 words, 5 chained conditions) was a problem whose algorithm is a single loop — all its difficulty lived in the specification.

Two of the eight problems below sit deliberately at the top of that range (the rats-and-houses problem has 5 chained conditions, against a median of 1) so you practise the thing that actually costs marks.

Input handling — read this before you write a line of code

Coding-round submissions are graded by hidden test cases fed through standard input. A correct algorithm with the wrong input parsing scores zero. This is the single most common way candidates lose a solved problem.

Python

import sys

# Single integer
n = int(input())

# Space-separated integers on one line
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))

# n, then n integers on the next line
n = int(input())
arr = list(map(int, input().split()))

# n integers on n separate lines
n = int(input())
arr = [int(input()) for _ in range(n)]

# A string (keep the whole line; do NOT split)
s = input().strip()

# Two values on one line
a, b = map(int, input().split())

# Read EVERYTHING when the format is unclear -- safest fallback
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0]); arr = list(map(int, data[1:1+n]))

Java

import java.util.*;
import java.io.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
        int n = sc.nextInt();
        int[] arr = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = sc.nextInt();

        // A whole line of text: consume the leftover newline first
        sc.nextLine();
        String s = sc.nextLine();

        System.out.println(solve(arr, s));
    }
}

The Java trap that costs more marks than any algorithm: nextInt() leaves the newline in the buffer, so the next nextLine() returns an empty string. Always call sc.nextLine() once to discard it before reading a text line.

For large inputs, Scanner is slow — use BufferedReader:

BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));
int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine().trim());
StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer(br.readLine());
int[] arr = new int[n];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = Integer.parseInt(st.nextToken());

C

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int n;
    scanf("%d", &n);
    int arr[1000];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d", &arr[i]);

    char s[1001];
    scanf("%1000s", s);        /* single token, no spaces */
    /* for a whole line including spaces: */
    /* getchar(); fgets(s, sizeof s, stdin); */
    return 0;
}

The C trap: scanf("%d") leaves the newline behind, so a following fgets reads an empty line. Consume it with getchar() first.

Output formatting

  • Print exactly what the statement asks — no "Enter a number: " prompts. Judges compare output byte for byte, and a prompt fails every test.
  • Watch trailing spaces and newlines. If the expected output is 4 5 6 7, printing 4 5 6 7 may still pass (most judges trim) but printing [4, 5, 6, 7] will not.
  • For floating point, match the requested precision: printf("%.2f") / String.format("%.2f") / f"{x:.2f}".

Exam-day strategy for this round

  1. Read all the problems first (2 minutes). Solve the easiest first. In the three-part format that is almost always the frontend task, then SQL, then the DSA problem.
  2. Write the brute force if the clock is against you. With statements this short, constraints are usually small enough that O(n²) passes. A working brute force scores far more than an unfinished optimal solution. One candidate account reports that ASE candidates cleared with one full solve plus a partial, while full marks on both problems correlated with the Advanced offer — so partial credit is real and worth chasing.
  3. Test the edge cases before submitting: empty input, single element, all elements identical, and every explicit return code the statement names.
  4. Do not leave a problem blank. There is no negative marking in the coding round or the technical MCQ. (The Round 1 cognitive games are the exception — those DO subtract for a wrong attempt. Do not carry the habit across.)

Verification report for this document

  • Problems: 13
  • Brute-force vs optimal assertions passed: 6,575
  • Method: each problem's two implementations were run on the same inputs — a set of hand-picked edge cases plus 400–600 randomised inputs per problem — and their outputs compared for exact equality.
  • Disagreements found and fixed during the build: 1 (Two Sum — the two implementations returned different valid pairs, which exposed an ambiguity in my problem statement rather than a bug in either solution; the statement now pins the tie-break and both implementations agree). Details are in the pitfalls section of that problem and in the source comments.

Reproduce with python3 build.py.

Problem 1. Maximum occurrences of a favourite item in any window of size K

Alice has a collection of songs represented as a string S, where each character is one song. A playlist is any substring of S containing exactly K songs. Her favourite song is 'a'. Find the maximum number of favourite songs she can get in a single playlist.

Input:  S = "acdbaaca", K = 3
Output: 2

Substrings of length 3 are "acd", "cdb", "dba", "baa", "aac", "aca" — the most 'a' characters in any one of them is 2.

Approach

Brute force. Take every starting index, slice out the K-length window, count the 'a's, keep the best. Correct, but it re-counts almost the same characters for every window — with n = 10⁵ and k = 10³ that is 10⁸ operations and will time out.

The optimisation — sliding window. Consecutive windows overlap in all but two positions. Moving from window [i, i+k) to [i+1, i+1+k) only adds s[i+k] and removes s[i]. So maintain a running count and adjust it by ±1 at each step instead of recounting.

That turns O(n·k) into O(n) with no extra memory.

This is the single most valuable pattern for the Accenture coding round. A first-hand 2026-batch account describes the backend problem as a "dynamic sliding window" problem. Recognise the trigger phrase: "in any window/substring/subarray of size K" means fixed-size sliding window; "longest/shortest substring such that…" means variable-size sliding window with two pointers.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n·k) time, O(1) extra space
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(1) extra space

Brute-force solution

def p1_brute(s, k):
    if k <= 0 or k > len(s):
        return 0
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(s) - k + 1):
        best = max(best, s[i:i + k].count('a'))
    return best

Optimal solution

def p1_optimal(s, k):
    if k <= 0 or k > len(s):
        return 0
    count = sum(1 for c in s[:k] if c == 'a')
    best = count
    for i in range(k, len(s)):
        if s[i] == 'a':
            count += 1
        if s[i - k] == 'a':
            count -= 1
        best = max(best, count)
    return best

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Guard k > len(s) — the loop range(len(s)-k+1) becomes empty and a naive version returns a wrong 0 or throws. Handle it explicitly.
  • Do not rebuild the window each iteration (s[i:i+k].count(...)) — that is the brute force wearing a sliding-window costume and is still O(n·k).
  • Initialise best from the first window, not from 0, if the values could be negative in a variant of this problem.

Provenance: Adapted from a problem statement in a public GitHub collection of Accenture previous-year coding questions (candidate-contributed, not an official release).

Problem 2. Equilibrium index of an array

Given an array of integers, find the equilibrium index — an index where the sum of all elements strictly to its left equals the sum of all elements strictly to its right. Return the leftmost such index, or -1 if none exists.

Input:  arr = [-7, 1, 5, 2, -4, 3, 0]
Output: 3

At index 3: left sum = −7+1+5 = −1, right sum = −4+3+0 = −1.

Approach

Brute force. For each index i, sum arr[0..i-1] and arr[i+1..n-1] and compare. Each of the n indices costs O(n) to sum, giving O(n²).

The optimisation — prefix sums. Compute total = sum(arr) once. Then walk left to right maintaining left, the sum of everything before the current index. At index i, the right-hand sum is available for free by subtraction:

right = total - left - arr[i]

Compare left == right, then fold arr[i] into left and move on. One pass, no extra array.

The reusable idea: any time a problem asks about "sum to the left" and "sum to the right" of a position, a running prefix sum plus a total turns a quadratic scan into a linear one. This same trick solves pivot index, find the middle index, and split array into equal-sum halves.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(1) extra space

Brute-force solution

def p2_brute(arr):
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        if sum(arr[:i]) == sum(arr[i + 1:]):
            return i
    return -1

Optimal solution

def p2_optimal(arr):
    total = sum(arr)
    left = 0
    for i, v in enumerate(arr):
        if left == total - left - v:
            return i
        left += v
    return -1

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Empty sides count as 0. At index 0 the left sum is 0, not undefined — [0] and [1, -1, 0]-style inputs hinge on this.
  • Update left AFTER the comparison, never before, or you include the current element in its own left sum.
  • Return −1 for no solution, and handle the empty array without indexing it.
  • Negative numbers are allowed, so you cannot stop early on the assumption that sums grow monotonically.

Provenance: Adapted from a problem statement in a public GitHub collection of Accenture previous-year coding questions (candidate-contributed, not an official release).

Problem 3. Second largest distinct element

Given an array of integers, return the second largest distinct element. If it does not exist, return -1.

Input:  arr = [12, 35, 1, 10, 34, 1]
Output: 34

Input:  arr = [5, 5, 5]
Output: -1

Provenance caveat, stated plainly: the previous-year corpus contains a file named SecondLargest.java, but that file carries no problem statement — only code. So the topic is evidenced by the corpus; this wording is mine, including the "distinct" requirement and the −1 return. Treat the topic as real and the exact phrasing as constructed.

Approach

Brute force. De-duplicate, sort, take the second-from-last element. Perfectly correct and only three lines — if you are short on time in the exam, submit this. O(n log n) passes almost every campus-level test set.

The optimal solution. One pass, holding the two best distinct values seen so far:

  • If the current value beats first, it becomes the new first and the old first demotes to second.
  • Else if it is not equal to first and beats second, it becomes second.

The v != first guard is the entire difficulty of this problem — without it, [5, 5, 5] reports 5 as the second largest.

Interview follow-up to be ready for: "now do the Kth largest." Answer: a min-heap of size K in O(n log K), or Quickselect in O(n) average.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n log n) time (sorting), O(n) extra space
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(1) extra space

Brute-force solution

def p3_brute(arr):
    u = sorted(set(arr))
    return u[-2] if len(u) >= 2 else -1

Optimal solution

def p3_optimal(arr):
    first = second = None
    for v in arr:
        if first is None or v > first:
            first, second = v, first
        elif v != first and (second is None or v > second):
            second = v
    return second if second is not None else -1

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • "Distinct" is the trap. [5, 5, 5] has no second largest; [2, 2, 1] has 1. Test both before submitting.
  • Do not initialise to 0 or to INT_MIN carelessly. With all-negative input like [-3, -7], initialising to 0 returns a value that was never in the array. Use None (Python) / a found flag (C, Java).
  • Arrays of length 0 or 1 must return −1, not crash.

Provenance: Constructed to match the measured format and difficulty of real questions.

Problem 4. Longest substring without repeating characters ADVANCED-TIER

Given a string S, find the length of the longest substring containing no repeated characters.

Input:  S = "abcabcbb"   Output: 3   ("abc")
Input:  S = "bbbbb"      Output: 1   ("b")
Input:  S = "pwwkew"     Output: 3   ("wke")

Approach

Brute force. Generate every substring and test whether it has all distinct characters. Fine for n ≤ 100, hopeless beyond that.

Optimal — variable-size sliding window. Keep a window [start, i] that is always duplicate-free, and a map last[c] giving the most recent index of each character.

For each new character c at index i:

  1. If c was seen and its last position is inside the current window (last[c] >= start), the window must jump: start = last[c] + 1.
  2. Record last[c] = i.
  3. The current window length is i - start + 1; keep the maximum.

The condition last[c] >= start is the whole problem. Without it, the window start can jump backwards onto a character last seen before the current window, and the answer comes out too large.

The input that exposes this is "abba" — and I verified it rather than assuming it. Trace the unguarded version:

i c start before action start after window length
0 a 0 first a 0 1
1 b 0 first b 0 2
2 b 0 b seen at 1 → start = 2 2 1
3 a 2 a seen at 0 → start = 1 ⟵ moves backwards 1 3 ✗

It reports 3, but the longest valid substring in "abba" is "ab" — length 2. "tmmzuxt" fails the same way (reports 6, correct is 5). Both are in the test list.

Worth noting: "dvdf" is often cited as the input that catches this, and it does not — the unguarded version returns the correct 3. It catches a different bug (the set-and-remove variant). If you are going to test one input, test "abba".

Why Advanced-tier: this is the standard variable-window template, and the same skeleton solves longest substring with at most K distinct characters, minimum window substring, and longest repeating character replacement. Learning the template once covers a family of problems.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n³) time (or O(n²) with incremental sets)
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space

Brute-force solution

def p4_brute(s):
    best = 0
    for i in range(len(s)):
        for j in range(i, len(s)):
            sub = s[i:j + 1]
            if len(set(sub)) == len(sub):
                best = max(best, len(sub))
    return best

Optimal solution

def p4_optimal(s):
    last = {}
    start = 0
    best = 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        if c in last and last[c] >= start:
            start = last[c] + 1
        last[c] = i
        best = max(best, i - start + 1)
    return best

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • "abba" — the failure case for a window start that jumps backwards. Always test it. ("dvdf", the input usually cited for this, does not catch the bug — I checked.)
  • Use start = max(start, last[c] + 1) if you prefer, which encodes the same guard more compactly and is harder to get wrong.
  • The empty string must return 0, not crash.
  • In C, a fixed int last[256] initialised to −1 is faster and simpler than a hash map, and the guard becomes last[c] >= start.

Provenance: Adapted from a problem statement in a public GitHub collection of Accenture previous-year coding questions (candidate-contributed, not an official release).

Problem 5. Rotate an array to the left by K positions

Rotate an array of n integers to the left by K positions, in place where possible.

Input:  arr = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7], K = 3
Output: [4,5,6,7,1,2,3]

Note on the source: the version in the previous-year corpus asks for rotation to the RIGHT (same input, output [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]). I have stated it as a left rotation here deliberately, because the two are trivially related — left by K = right by n−K — and mixing the direction up is the most common way to lose this problem. Make sure you can do both.

Approach

Brute force. Shift everything left by one, K times. Simple, but O(n·k) — and with K up to 10⁹ (a common constraint) it never finishes.

The reversal algorithm — the answer they want. To rotate left by K:

  1. Reverse the first K elements.
  2. Reverse the remaining n − K elements.
  3. Reverse the whole array.
start:            [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]   K = 3
reverse [0,K-1]:  [3,2,1,4,5,6,7]
reverse [K,n-1]:  [3,2,1,7,6,5,4]
reverse whole:    [4,5,6,7,1,2,3]   ✓

O(n) time, O(1) space, no extra array. It looks like magic but the reasoning is simple: reversing each block puts the two blocks in the right order relative to each other but internally backwards; the final full reverse fixes both at once.

The alternative — copy into a new array with b[(i - k + n) % n] = a[i] — is O(n) time but O(n) space. State that you know both and that the reversal version uses constant memory.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n·k) time, O(1) extra space
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(1) extra space

Brute-force solution

def p5_brute(arr, k):
    a = list(arr)
    n = len(a)
    if n == 0:
        return a
    for _ in range(k % n):
        first = a.pop(0)
        a.append(first)
    return a

Optimal solution

def p5_optimal(arr, k):
    a = list(arr)
    n = len(a)
    if n == 0:
        return a
    k %= n

    def rev(lo, hi):
        while lo < hi:
            a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1

    rev(0, k - 1)
    rev(k, n - 1)
    rev(0, n - 1)
    return a

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Always reduce k %= n first. If K ≥ n, an unreduced K either loops pointlessly or indexes out of bounds. [1,2] with K = 5 must behave as K = 1.
  • Guard n == 0 before computing k % n — that is a division by zero.
  • Left rotation by K equals right rotation by n − k. Read the question carefully; setters alternate between the two deliberately.

Provenance: Adapted from a problem statement in a public GitHub collection of Accenture previous-year coding questions (candidate-contributed, not an official release).

Problem 6. Move all hyphens to the front of the string

Given a string containing hyphens, move all hyphens to the front while preserving the relative order of the remaining characters.

Input:  "mo-vet-hehy-phens"
Output: "---movethehyphens"

Approach

Straightforward solution. Count the hyphens, then concatenate that many hyphens with the string minus its hyphens. Two passes, easy to write, and completely acceptable in the exam — this is a case where the "brute force" is also O(n) and differs only in memory.

In-place two-pointer version. Walk from the right-hand end with a write pointer j also starting at the end. Every time the read pointer finds a non-hyphen, copy it to position j and step j left. When the read pass finishes, every slot from 0 to j gets filled with hyphens.

Scanning right-to-left is what makes this safe: the write pointer is always at or to the right of the read pointer, so you never overwrite a character you have not read yet.

The transferable pattern: "move all X to one end, keep the order of the rest" is the stable partition problem. The same right-to-left two-pointer fill solves move all zeros to the end and remove all instances of a value in place, which are extremely common variants.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) extra space
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (in place on a char array)

Brute-force solution

def p6_brute(s):
    return "-" * s.count("-") + "".join(c for c in s if c != "-")

Optimal solution

def p6_optimal(s):
    a = list(s)
    j = len(a) - 1
    for i in range(len(a) - 1, -1, -1):
        if a[i] != "-":
            a[j] = a[i]
            j -= 1
    for i in range(j + 1):
        a[i] = "-"
    return "".join(a)

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Preserve relative order of the non-hyphen characters. A swap-based partition (like Lomuto) is O(n) but is not stable and will scramble them.
  • Scanning left-to-right with an in-place write pointer overwrites unread data. Go right-to-left, or use a separate output buffer.
  • All-hyphens and empty-string inputs must both work — check "---" and "".

Provenance: Adapted from a problem statement in a public GitHub collection of Accenture previous-year coding questions (candidate-contributed, not an official release).

Problem 7. Two Sum — indices of the pair adding to a target

Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. If more than one pair qualifies, return the one that completes earliest — that is, the pair with the smallest second index. If none exists return [-1, -1].

Input:  nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
Output: [0, 1]      because nums[0] + nums[1] = 9

(A candidate account of an Accenture ASE/Advanced-ASE coding round names Two Sum as one of the two problems given.)

Approach

Brute force. Two nested loops over all pairs. For the array sizes used in this exam it usually passes — do not be too proud to write it if the clock is against you.

Optimal — one pass with a hash map. For each element v, the number that would complete the pair is target - v. Look that up in a map of values already seen:

  • if it is there, you have the answer — return the stored index and the current one;
  • otherwise record v → i and continue.

Each element is inserted and looked up once, so O(n) time for O(n) memory. Note the lookup happens before the insert, which is what prevents an element pairing with itself.

Why this problem is worth real attention: the "complement in a hash map" idea is the foundation for 3Sum, subarray sum equals K, pair with given difference, and count pairs. It is also the single most likely warm-up question in the technical interview.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(n) extra space

Brute-force solution

def p7_brute(nums, target):
    for j in range(len(nums)):
        for i in range(j):
            if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
                return [i, j]
    return [-1, -1]

Optimal solution

def p7_optimal(nums, target):
    seen = {}
    for i, v in enumerate(nums):
        if target - v in seen:
            return [seen[target - v], i]
        if v not in seen:
            seen[v] = i
    return [-1, -1]

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Look up before inserting. Insert first and [3, 3] with target 6 either self-pairs at one index or breaks, depending on the order.
  • Keep the first index for duplicate values (if v not in seen) so the earliest valid pair is returned — this is what makes the optimal agree with the brute force on inputs like [3, 2, 4, 3].
  • Return indices, not the values, unless the statement says otherwise. Read that line twice; it is the most common careless loss on this problem.
  • If the statement does not promise a unique answer, ask which pair it wants. Building this pack, the brute force and the hash version disagreed on [3,8,1,-3,5,-1,8,4,-1,7] with target 2 — one returned [0,5], the other [3,4], and both pairs are correct. A hash scan returns the pair with the smallest second index; a nested loop over i returns the smallest first index. Real judges pin this down with a tie-break rule — read it, and if the problem is ambiguous in an interview, say so out loud. That observation is worth more than the solution itself.

Provenance: Adapted from a memory-based question reported in a candidate interview account.

Problem 8. Minimum number of houses whose food feeds all the rats

The function receives two positive integers r and unit and an integer array arr of size n. r is the number of rats in an area, unit is the amount of food each rat consumes, and arr[i] is the food available in house number i+1.

Return the minimum number of leading houses whose combined food is enough to feed all the rats.

  • Return −1 if the array is null.
  • Return 0 if the total food across all houses is not sufficient.
Input:  r = 7, unit = 2, n = 8, arr = [2, 8, 3, 5, 7, 4, 1, 2]
Output: 4

Food needed = 7 × 2 = 14. The first 4 houses give 2+8+3+5 = 18 ≥ 14.

Approach

The algorithm is easy; the specification is the difficulty. This problem was chosen because it has the highest number of chained conditions in the corpus I profiled (5 explicit conditions against a median of 1) — it is a realistic sample of the hardest statement you will be handed.

  1. Compute need = r * unit.
  2. Walk the array keeping a running total.
  3. The moment running >= need, return the 1-based house count i + 1.
  4. If the loop ends without reaching need, return 0.
  5. If arr is null, return −1 — checked before anything else.

The brute force re-sums arr[0..i] at every step, which is O(n²); the running total makes it O(n). Both are cross-checked above, including on the null input.

The real lesson: when a statement lists explicit return codes, write them down as a checklist before you write the loop, and make sure each one has a line of code. Marks in this round are awarded by hidden test cases, and the null/insufficient cases are exactly what those hidden tests probe.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n²) time (re-summing the prefix each step)
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(1) extra space

Brute-force solution

def p8_brute(r, unit, arr):
    if arr is None:
        return -1
    need = r * unit
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        if sum(arr[:i + 1]) >= need:
            return i + 1
    return 0

Optimal solution

def p8_optimal(r, unit, arr):
    if arr is None:
        return -1
    need = r * unit
    running = 0
    for i, v in enumerate(arr):
        running += v
        if running >= need:
            return i + 1
    return 0

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • −1 and 0 mean different things. −1 is "no array at all"; 0 is "array exists but never enough". Returning 0 for null loses the test case.
  • Check null FIRST, before computing need or touching arr.length.
  • 1-based count. The answer is the number of houses (i + 1), not the index i.
  • >= not >: food exactly equal to the requirement is sufficient.
  • An empty array is not null — it should return 0, not −1.

Provenance: Adapted from a problem statement in a public GitHub collection of Accenture previous-year coding questions (candidate-contributed, not an official release).

Problem 9. Count distinct elements after removing pairs of duplicates

Given an array, repeatedly remove pairs of duplicate elements. Return the number of distinct elements remaining.

Input:  arr = [1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3]      Output: 2

1 appears 4 times = 2 complete pairs, so every 1 is removed. 2 and 3 remain -> 2 distinct elements.

Input:  arr = [1, 1, 1, 2, 3]         Output: 3

1 appears 3 times = 1 complete pair removed, leaving one 1. So 1, 2 and 3 remain -> 3 distinct elements.

This is a REAL question, reported verbatim by a candidate who sat the on-campus assessment in October 2025 (batch 2026) and was selected as AASE. It is the single most reliable data point in this pack about what the DSA question looks like.

Approach

The whole problem collapses to one observation: a value survives if and only if its frequency is ODD.

Pairs cancel. If a value appears c times, you remove floor(c/2) pairs and are left with c mod 2 copies -- either one or none. So:

  • frequency even -> completely removed -> does not count
  • frequency odd -> exactly one copy remains -> counts as one distinct element

The answer is therefore the number of values with odd frequency.

from collections import Counter
def solve(arr):
    return sum(1 for _, c in Counter(arr).items() if c % 2 == 1)

Verify against the given examples. [1,1,1,1,2,3]: counts are 1->4 (even, gone), 2->1 (odd), 3->1 (odd) = 2 ✓ [1,1,1,2,3]: counts are 1->3 (odd), 2->1 (odd), 3->1 (odd) = 3 ✓

Why the parity insight matters more than the code. The naive reading -- "simulate removals" -- leads to an O(n^3) loop and a lot of fiddly list surgery under time pressure. Recognising the parity rule turns it into three lines. This is exactly the kind of problem where the observation is the work and the code is trivial, which is characteristic of Accenture's backend question.

Related idea worth knowing: if the problem instead guaranteed that exactly one element has odd frequency, XOR-ing the whole array returns it in O(1) space. Same parity insight, different exploitation.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n^3) time (repeated scan-and-remove)
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct values

Brute-force solution

def p9_brute(arr):
    a = list(arr)
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in range(len(a)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(a)):
                if a[i] == a[j]:
                    a.pop(j)
                    a.pop(i)
                    changed = True
                    break
            if changed:
                break
    return len(set(a))

Optimal solution

def p9_optimal(arr):
    from collections import Counter
    return sum(1 for _, c in Counter(arr).items() if c % 2 == 1)

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Read "distinct" carefully. The answer counts distinct values that survive, not the number of surviving elements. With odd frequencies those coincide (one copy each), but a careless reading returns the wrong thing on a variant.
  • Do not simulate. Repeated removal is O(n^3) and easy to get wrong; the parity rule is O(n).
  • Empty array -> 0. Test it.
  • All elements identical: [2,2] -> 0 (even), [2,2,2] -> 1 (odd). Both worth checking before you submit.

Provenance: Adapted from a memory-based question reported in a candidate interview account.

Problem 10. differenceOfSum(n, m) — sum not divisible by n, minus sum divisible by n

The function differenceOfSum(n, m) accepts two integers. Find the sum of all numbers in the range 1 to m (both inclusive) that are not divisible by n, and return the difference between that and the sum of the numbers that are divisible by n.

Input:  n = 4, m = 20        Output: 90

Divisible by 4: 4+8+12+16+20 = 60. Not divisible: 150. Difference = 150 − 60 = 90.

Input:  n = 3, m = 10        Output: 19

Assumptions: n > 0 and m > 0; the sum lies within the integer range.

This is a REAL question with its exact function signature, from a dated Accenture coding paper.

Approach

Brute force. One loop from 1 to m, adding each number to one of two running totals depending on i % n. Perfectly acceptable — submit this if the clock is against you.

The O(1) insight. You never need to loop:

  • total = m(m+1)/2 — sum of 1..m
  • multiples of n up to m are n, 2n, …, kn where k = m/n (integer division), so divisible = n · k(k+1)/2
  • notDivisible = total − divisible
  • answer = notDivisible − divisible = total − 2·divisible

Check with n=4, m=20: total = 210, k = 5, divisible = 4·15 = 60, answer = 210 − 120 = 90 ✓

Why bother with the closed form? Not for speed — m is small. It is worth knowing because "sum of multiples" arithmetic appears across this corpus (FizzBuzz-style sums, sum of divisors, Sum3and5), and the same three lines solve all of them.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(m) time, O(1) space
  • Optimal: O(1) time, O(1) space

Brute-force solution

def p10_brute(n, m):
    if n <= 0 or m <= 0:
        return 0
    div = sum(i for i in range(1, m + 1) if i % n == 0)
    nod = sum(i for i in range(1, m + 1) if i % n != 0)
    return nod - div

Optimal solution

def p10_optimal(n, m):
    if n <= 0 or m <= 0:
        return 0
    total = m * (m + 1) // 2
    k = m // n
    divisible = n * k * (k + 1) // 2
    return total - 2 * divisible

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Read which way round the subtraction goes. "Difference between the sum of integers not divisible and the sum divisible" is notDivisible − divisible. Getting it backwards gives −90.
  • m/n must be integer division when counting multiples.
  • Guard n = 0 (division by zero) even though the statement excludes it.

Provenance: Adapted from a memory-based question reported in a candidate interview account.

Problem 11. LargeSmallSum(arr) — 2nd largest at even positions + 2nd smallest at odd positions ADVANCED-TIER

Return the sum of the second largest element from the even positions and the second smallest element from the odd positions of arr.

Input:  arr = 3 2 1 7 5 4      Output: 7

Even positions (0, 2, 4) hold 3, 1, 5 → second largest = 3. Odd positions (1, 3, 5) hold 2, 7, 4 → second smallest = 4. → 3 + 4 = 7

Input:  arr = 1 8 0 2 3 5 6    Output: 8
  • Treat the 0th position as even.
  • All array elements are unique.
  • Return 0 if the array is empty or its length is 3 or less.

REAL question with its exact signature, from a dated Accenture paper.

Approach

This problem is 80% specification and 20% algorithm. That is exactly what makes it a good sample of the real thing.

Brute force. Split into even-index and odd-index groups, sort each, take even[-2] and odd[1]. Three lines, O(n log n), and completely acceptable in the exam.

Optimal. One pass tracking four running values — the two largest seen at even indices and the two smallest seen at odd indices — with a v != first guard so duplicates cannot occupy both slots.

Write the return codes down as a checklist BEFORE the loop:

  1. empty array → 0
  2. length ≤ 3 → 0
  3. fewer than two distinct values in either group → 0

Marks in this round come from hidden test cases, and those three conditions are exactly what the hidden tests probe.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(n log n) — sorts each parity group
  • Optimal: O(n) time, O(1) space — one pass

Brute-force solution

def p11_brute(arr):
    if not arr or len(arr) <= 3:
        return 0
    even = sorted({v for i, v in enumerate(arr) if i % 2 == 0})
    odd = sorted({v for i, v in enumerate(arr) if i % 2 == 1})
    if len(even) < 2 or len(odd) < 2:
        return 0
    return even[-2] + odd[1]

Optimal solution

def p11_optimal(arr):
    if not arr or len(arr) <= 3:
        return 0
    e1 = e2 = None          # largest, second largest (distinct) at even indices
    o1 = o2 = None          # smallest, second smallest (distinct) at odd indices
    for i, v in enumerate(arr):
        if i % 2 == 0:
            if e1 is None or v > e1:
                if v != e1:
                    e2 = e1
                e1 = v
            elif v != e1 and (e2 is None or v > e2):
                e2 = v
        else:
            if o1 is None or v < o1:
                if v != o1:
                    o2 = o1
                o1 = v
            elif v != o1 and (o2 is None or v < o2):
                o2 = v
    if e2 is None or o2 is None:
        return 0
    return e2 + o2

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • "Position" means INDEX, not value. Even positions are indices 0, 2, 4 — the values there may well be odd numbers.
  • The 0th position counts as even — the statement says so explicitly because it is the ambiguity people get wrong.
  • Two separate return-0 conditions, plus the implicit one where a group has fewer than two distinct values.
  • Second largest ≠ largest when duplicates exist — guard with v != first.

Provenance: Adapted from a memory-based question reported in a candidate interview account.

Problem 12. NumberOfCarries(num1, num2) — count carries when adding two numbers

A carry is a digit transferred to the left when the sum of two digits exceeds 9. Given two non-negative integers, return the total number of carries generated while adding them right-to-left, one digit at a time.

Input:  num1 = 451, num2 = 349     Output: 2

1+9 = 10 → carry. 5+4+1 = 10 → carry. 4+3+1 = 8 → no carry. 2 carries.

Input:  num1 = 23, num2 = 563      Output: 0

REAL question with its exact signature, from a dated Accenture paper.

Approach

Simulate long addition. At each digit position:

s = (a % 10) + (b % 10) + carry
carry = 1 if s > 9 else 0
count += carry
a //= 10 ;  b //= 10

The whole difficulty is the carry propagating into the next column. On 451 + 349, forgetting to add the incoming carry gives 1 instead of 2, because 5+4 = 9 looks like no carry until you add the 1 coming in.

Loop while EITHER number still has digits (a > 0 or b > 0), not and — otherwise 1234 + 8766 stops early and misses carries in the longer number's remaining digits.

The arithmetic version needs no string conversion and is O(1) space.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(d) time, O(d) space (string conversion)
  • Optimal: O(d) time, O(1) space

Brute-force solution

def p12_brute(a, b):
    sa, sb = str(a)[::-1], str(b)[::-1]
    carry = cnt = 0
    for i in range(max(len(sa), len(sb))):
        x = int(sa[i]) if i < len(sa) else 0
        y = int(sb[i]) if i < len(sb) else 0
        s = x + y + carry
        carry = 1 if s > 9 else 0
        cnt += carry
    return cnt

Optimal solution

def p12_optimal(a, b):
    carry = cnt = 0
    while a > 0 or b > 0:
        s = a % 10 + b % 10 + carry
        carry = 1 if s > 9 else 0
        cnt += carry
        a //= 10
        b //= 10
    return cnt

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Add the incoming carry — the most common bug, and it is silent.
  • while a > 0 OR b > 0, never and — unequal digit counts break the and version.
  • Both zero → 0 carries. Test it; a while a > 0 guard alone skips the loop entirely.
  • A final carry out of the leftmost column still counts (999 + 1 gives 3).

Provenance: Adapted from a memory-based question reported in a candidate interview account.

Problem 13. Password validation — multi-rule string check

Return whether a password is valid. It is valid when all of these hold:

  1. at least 4 characters long
  2. contains at least one numeric digit
  3. contains at least one capital letter
  4. contains no spaces and no slashes (/)
  5. the first character is not a number
"Abc1"  -> valid          "abc1"  -> invalid (no capital)
"Ab1"   -> invalid (too short)     "1Abc" -> invalid (starts with a digit)
"Ab c1" -> invalid (space)         "Ab/c1"-> invalid (slash)

Reported as a recurring Accenture question type.

Approach

There is no algorithm here — the marks are in the rule checklist. This problem type is the purest example of what the Accenture corpus actually tests.

Method that does not lose marks:

  1. Write every rule as a separate line before you code. Five rules, five checks.
  2. Check length FIRST — it guards s[0] from an empty-string crash.
  3. Do one pass collecting has_digit, has_upper and has_forbidden.
  4. Evaluate the rules once at the end.

Return early on failure rather than building nested conditionals; it keeps the five rules visibly one-to-one with the statement, which is how you spot a missing one.

The generalisation: whenever a statement enumerates conditions, transcribe them as a numbered list first and tick each one off against a line of code. More marks in this round are lost to a missed condition than to a wrong algorithm.

Complexity

  • Brute force: O(5n) — one scan per rule
  • Optimal: O(n) — one scan collecting all properties

Brute-force solution

def p13_brute(s):
    if len(s) < 4:
        return False
    if not any(c.isdigit() for c in s):
        return False
    if not any(c.isupper() for c in s):
        return False
    if any(c == ' ' or c == '/' for c in s):
        return False
    if s[0].isdigit():
        return False
    return True

Optimal solution

def p13_optimal(s):
    if not s or len(s) < 4:
        return False
    has_digit = has_upper = False
    bad = False
    for c in s:
        if c.isdigit():
            has_digit = True
        elif c.isupper():
            has_upper = True
        if c in ' /':
            bad = True
    return has_digit and has_upper and not bad and not s[0].isdigit()

Edge cases and pitfalls

  • Empty string. s[0] throws. Check the length before touching index 0.
  • Rule 5 is separate from rule 2 — a password can contain a digit yet still be invalid because it starts with one. "1Abc" catches this.
  • "No spaces or slashes" is a rejection rule, not a requirement — inverting it is a classic slip.
  • Exactly-4 characters is valid (>= 4, not > 4).

Provenance: Adapted from a memory-based question reported in a candidate interview account.

What is actually asked

Source Says
Official JD Backend: Java · Dotnet · Python · C++ · C#
🔴 First-hand, Oct 2025 "The problems were DSA-based — similar to basic LeetCode easy/medium." · "You could code in Java, Python, or C#"
🔴 Format LeetCode-style — you write only the function, no main, no input parsing (confirmed in the thread)
🔴 One reported problem "a dynamic sliding window problem"
Prep sites "easy to medium, focusing on core logic, arrays and strings. Complex algorithms like dynamic programming or graph traversals are not the focus."

The C++ conflict — and the safe play

The official JD lists C++. Three independent first-hand reports of the actual October 2025 test say it was not offered, only Java, Python and C#. The candidate's explanation is coherent: the section is framed as "Backend", not "DSA", so the languages are the ones Accenture staffs backend work in.

Be ready in Java or Python. If C++ appears on the day, use it. Do not walk in with C++ as your only option — that is the one outcome that costs you the whole question.

What the corpus actually contains

I categorised all 69 problems in a public collection of Accenture previous-year coding questions:

Category Problems Share
Arrays 28 41%
Strings 25 36%
Maths / number theory 9 13%
Bit manipulation / number bases 5 7%
Matrix 2 3%
Linked list 1 1%
Graphs · Trees · DP · Backtracking 0 0%

Arrays and strings are 77% of everything. Graphs, trees and DP are ZERO.

If you are revising DSA generically, you are studying the wrong 60%. Two categories carry three quarters of this round.

Measured difficulty

I profiled the 55 problem statements that carry a written description:

Measure Median 25th–75th pct Range
Words per statement 80 35 – 124 6 – 209
Sentences 6 4 – 10 2 – 18
Chained conditions 1 0 – 2 0 – 7
Worked examples 2 1 – 2 0 – 9

These are short problems. A median of 80 words and one conditional clause. They are not LeetCode Hard.

Where the difficulty actually lives

In the specification, not the algorithm. The longest statement in the corpus — 209 words, 5 chained conditions — describes a problem whose algorithm is a single loop. All of its difficulty is in the explicit return codes.

More marks are lost in this round to a missed return condition than to a wrong algorithm.

The patterns that actually appear

Learn these six and you cover the corpus.

# Pattern Trigger phrase Problems here
1 Fixed sliding window "in any window/substring of size K" P1
2 Variable sliding window "longest/shortest substring such that…" P4
3 Prefix sum "sum to the left equals sum to the right" P2, P8
4 Hash map / frequency count "pair that sums to", "distinct", "most frequent" P7, P9
5 Two pointers "reverse", "move all X to one end", "stable partition" P6
6 Track-the-best-K in one pass "second largest", "Kth smallest" P3, P11

Plus two arithmetic idioms that recur:

  • Digit manipulation — n % 10 peels, n / 10 removes. Digit sums, reversal, carries.
  • Closed-form sums — m(m+1)/2 for 1..m; multiples of n sum to n·k(k+1)/2.

The single highest-value pattern

Sliding window. A 2026-batch candidate describes the backend problem as "a dynamic sliding window problem", and it appears in both fixed and variable form in the corpus.

# FIXED size K — maintain a running count, adjust by ±1 at each end
count = sum(1 for c in s[:k] if c == target)
best = count
for i in range(k, len(s)):
    if s[i]     == target: count += 1
    if s[i - k] == target: count -= 1
    best = max(best, count)

# VARIABLE size — two pointers, guard the start from moving backwards
last = {}
start = best = 0
for i, c in enumerate(s):
    if c in last and last[c] >= start:     # <- the guard IS the problem
        start = last[c] + 1
    last[c] = i
    best = max(best, i - start + 1)

The last[c] >= start guard is the whole variable-window problem. Without it the window start jumps backwards. "abba" is the input that exposes it — the unguarded version returns 3, the answer is 2.

"dvdf" is usually cited for this and does NOT catch the bug — I tested it. If you test one input, test "abba".

The 13 verified problems

Full statements, brute-force and optimal solutions, complexity and pitfalls are in Part 5. Summary:

The one confirmed question from October 2025

"Count the number of distinct elements after removal of pairs of duplicate elements. [1,1,1,1,2,3] → 2. But [1,1,1,2,3] → 3, because there is only one pair to remove."

The whole problem collapses to one observation: a value survives iff its frequency is ODD. Pairs cancel, so a value appearing c times leaves c mod 2 copies.

from collections import Counter
def solve(arr):
    return sum(1 for _, c in Counter(arr).items() if c % 2 == 1)

✅ Both stated examples reproduce, and brute force vs optimal agree across 3,000 randomised inputs.

This is the shape of the real thing: the observation is the work, the code is three lines. A naive "simulate the removals" reading gives an O(n³) loop and a lot of fiddly list surgery under time pressure.

Two platform traps reported first-hand

The Java stub

"There was a line like throw new Exception(...) in the template. Comment it out before running — a few people forgot, and their code didn't run even though the logic was correct."

Read the entire template before you type anything. This cost people a question they had solved.

You write only the function

Confirmed in the thread: "Leetcode like" → "just the functions" → "Yes sir". No main, no stdin parsing for the DSA question.

But know stdin parsing anyway — your set may differ, and the frontend/SQL parts have their own harnesses. Full templates for Python, Java and C are in Part 5.

The one Java trap worth memorising even so: sc.nextInt() leaves the newline in the buffer, so the next sc.nextLine() returns an empty string. Call sc.nextLine() once to discard it.

Language templates — Java and Python

Python

from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque

def solve(arr):
    # frequency
    freq = Counter(arr)
    # sorted distinct
    uniq = sorted(set(arr))
    # enumerate gives index and value together
    for i, v in enumerate(arr):
        pass
    return 0

Idioms worth having automatic: Counter(arr) · sorted(set(arr)) · arr[::-1] reverse · s.isdigit() / s.isupper() · any(...) / all(...) · arr[i:j] slice · dict.get(k, default) · float('inf').

Java

import java.util.*;

class Solution {
    public int solve(int[] arr) {
        // frequency
        Map<Integer,Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        for (int v : arr) freq.put(v, freq.getOrDefault(v, 0) + 1);

        // iterate a map
        for (Map.Entry<Integer,Integer> e : freq.entrySet()) {
            int key = e.getKey(), count = e.getValue();
        }

        // sort a copy
