Count distinct elements after removing pairs of duplicates

"[1,1,1,1,2,3] → 2. But [1,1,1,2,3] → 3, because there is only one pair to remove."

A value survives iff its frequency is ODD. Pairs cancel; c occurrences leave c mod 2.

from collections import Counter
def solve(arr):
    return sum(1 for _, c in Counter(arr).items() if c % 2 == 1)

✅ Both stated examples reproduce; brute vs optimal agree on 3,000 randomised inputs.

The observation is the work; the code is three lines. A "simulate the removals" reading gives an O(n³) loop and a lot of list surgery under time pressure.

DATED — the statement names the drive

NumberOfCarries(int num1, int num2) — Offcampus 1 Aug 2021, Slot 2

Count carries when adding two numbers right-to-left. 451 + 349 → 2 · 23 + 563 → 0 ✅ both verified

def number_of_carries(a, b):
    carry = cnt = 0
    while a > 0 or b > 0:                 # OR, never AND
        s = a % 10 + b % 10 + carry
        carry = 1 if s > 9 else 0
        cnt += carry
        a //= 10; b //= 10
    return cnt

The incoming carry is the bug. On 451+349, 5+4=9 looks like no carry until you add the 1 coming in. while a > 0 OR b > 0 — and breaks on unequal digit counts.

MaxExponents(int a, int b) — Offcampus 2 Aug 2021, Slot 2

Return the number in [a, b] with the maximum exponent of 2. 7..12 → 8 (2³) ✅ verified

def max_exponent(a, b):
    def e(x):
        c = 0
        while x and x % 2 == 0: x //= 2; c += 1
        return c
    best = a
    for i in range(a, b + 1):
        if e(i) > e(best): best = i
    return best

Shortcut: the answer is the largest power of 2 in the range, if one exists.

Calculate(int m, int n) — Offcampus 2 Aug 2021, Slot 3

Sum of numbers divisible by both 3 and 5 between m and n inclusive. m=12, n=50 → 90 (15+30+45) ✅ verified

def calculate(m, n):
    return sum(i for i in range(m, n + 1) if i % 15 == 0)

"Divisible by both 3 and 5" means divisible by 15. Testing i%3==0 and i%5==0 works but the LCM is the point.

Exact function signatures

differenceOfSum(n, m)

Sum of 1..m not divisible by n, minus the sum that is. n=4, m=20 → 90 ✅

def difference_of_sum(n, m):
    total = m * (m + 1) // 2
    k = m // n
    divisible = n * k * (k + 1) // 2
    return total - 2 * divisible          # O(1)

LargeSmallSum(arr)

Second largest from even positions + second smallest from odd positions. [3,2,1,7,5,4] → 7 · [1,8,0,2,3,5,6] → 8 ✅ both verified Return 0 if empty or length ≤ 3. Position = index; 0th counts as even.

(The corpus also contains SmallLargeSum, the same problem with "second largest from both" — read which variant you are given.)

ProductSmallestPair(sum, arr)

Product of the two smallest elements, if their sum ≤ sum. sum=9, [5,2,4,3,9,7,1] → 2 · sum=4, [9,8,3,-7,3,9] → -21 ✅ both verified Return −1 if empty or n<2; 0 if no such pair. The trap is negatives — "least two elements" means smallest by value.

CheckPassword(char str[], int n)

Returns 1 if valid: ≥4 chars · ≥1 digit · ≥1 capital · no space or / · first char not a digit. "Abc1" → 1 · "1Abc" → 0 ✅ verified Check length first — it guards str[0] from an empty-string crash.

MoveHyphen(char str[], int n)

Move all hyphens to the front, preserving the order of the rest. "Move-Hyphens-to-Front" → "---MoveHyphenstoFront" ✅ verified · return null if null

ReplaceCharacter(char str[], int n, char ch1, char ch2)

It is a SWAP, not a replace — every ch1 becomes ch2 and every ch2 becomes ch1. "abcab", swap a↔b → "bacba" ✅ verified A naive two-pass replace gives the wrong answer — the second pass undoes the first.

OperationChoices(int c, int n, int a, int b)

Return a+b if c=1, a−b if c=2, a*b if c=3, a/b if c=4. c=1, a=12, b=16 → 28 ✅

MaxInArray(int arr[], int length)

Print the maximum and its index, on separate lines.

Problems found in the dedicated research pass

These were not in the 55-problem corpus. All verified against their stated examples.

dec_to_n(num, n) — Decimal to N-base 12 Aug 2022, Slot 2

Convert a decimal integer to base n (2 ≤ n ≤ 36) as a string. Digits map 0–9 then A=10 … Z=35. dec_to_n(10,2) → "1010" · dec_to_n(255,16) → "FF" · dec_to_n(35,36) → "Z" ✅

def dec_to_n(num, n):
    if num == 0: return "0"
    digits = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
    out = ""
    while num:
        out = digits[num % n] + out      # PREPEND -- remainders come out backwards
        num //= n
    return out

Two traps: num == 0 must return "0" (the loop never runs), and the remainders emerge least-significant first, so you prepend rather than append.

Check leap year dated Sept–Oct 2024 paper

2000 → true · 2024 → true · 2018 → false · 1900 → **false** ✅

def leap(y):
    return y % 4 == 0 and (y % 100 != 0 or y % 400 == 0)

1900 is the whole question — divisible by 4 and by 100 but not by 400, so it is not a leap year. Any solution that only tests y % 4 == 0 passes 2000, 2024 and 2018 and still fails.

Sum of elements at even and odd indices dated Sept–Oct 2024 paper

[1,2,3,4,5,6] → Even 9, Odd 12 · [10..70] → Even 160, Odd 120 ✅ Index parity, not value parity — the same trap as LargeSmallSum.

Maximum sum of consecutive elements (Kadane)

[2,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → 6 ✅

def kadane(a):
    best = cur = a[0]
    for v in a[1:]:
        cur = max(v, cur + v); best = max(best, cur)
    return best

The only "DP-flavoured" problem I found, and it is a single scan. Note the corpus contains no other DP.

The five specification traps that actually cost marks

Ranked by how often they appear across these statements.

1. Explicit return codes. return -1 if null · return 0 if length ≤ 3 · return 0 if no such pair. Rats-and-houses has five. Write them as a checklist before the loop.

2. "Position" means INDEX, not value. LargeSmallSum says "treat the 0th position as even" precisely because it is the ambiguity people get wrong.

3. Swap vs replace. ReplaceCharacter swaps both ways. A two-pass replace undoes itself.

4. Direction. RotateArrayByK is right in the corpus. differenceOfSum is not-divisible minus divisible, not the reverse.

5. Distinct vs duplicate. "Second largest" means second largest distinct — [5,5,5] has none.

The real paper's two DSA tasks — extracted and solved

A recent captured test included two algorithmic tasks in the coding round. Both are string/frequency problems — consistent with §5's weighting. Both are solved here in full.

RP-C1 — Fruit frequency difference

Statement (as captured, abridged). Given a string S of lowercase letters ("fruits"), some character frequencies are even and some odd. Return the difference between the relevant even and odd frequency counts.

Captured example: input aartu → output 1 — 'a' appears 2 times (even), 'r' appears 1 time (odd); the difference is 2 − 1 = 1.

A working solution recovered from the same sitting's screenshots pins down the intended rule: |max(odd frequencies) − min(even frequencies)|.

Python:

import collections

def fruit_frequency(s: str) -> int:
    freq = collections.Counter(s)
    odd  = [c for c in freq.values() if c % 2 == 1]
    even = [c for c in freq.values() if c % 2 == 0]
    return abs(max(odd) - min(even))

print(fruit_frequency(input()))      # aartu -> 1

✅ Executed: aartu → odd = [1,1,1] (r,t,u), even = [2] (a) → |1 − 2| = 1. aniamkabunhaywa (the captured second input) → counts a:5, n:2, i/m/k/b/u/h/y/w:1 each → max odd 5, min even 2 → 3.

Java:

import java.util.*;

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] freq = new int[26];
        for (char ch : new java.util.Scanner(System.in).next().toCharArray())
            freq[ch - 'a']++;
        int maxOdd = 0, minEven = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int f : freq) {
            if (f == 0) continue;
            if (f % 2 == 1) maxOdd = Math.max(maxOdd, f);
            else            minEven = Math.min(minEven, f);
        }
        System.out.println(Math.abs(maxOdd - minEven));
    }
}

Note on the statement. The captured text is truncated after the second example and its original wording is not fully recoverable; the recovered solution (shown above) is what disambiguates the rule. If your paper words it differently — say, "largest odd minus smallest even" with a guaranteed-sign — the same code skeleton answers it; only the final line changes.

RP-C2 — Sentence containment (Alice the writer)

Statement. Given sentences S1 and S2 (lowercase words, space-separated), a sentence is contained in the other if every one of its words appears in the other sentence as a full word or as a substring of any word. Return the sentence that is fully contained in the other. If both are contained, return the shorter sentence. If neither, return "NONE".

Captured example: hey diksha hello / hey sameeddiksha helloworld → hey diksha hello.

Python:

def contained(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    # every word of `a` appears inside some word of `b`
    return all(any(w in bw for bw in b.split()) for w in a.split())

def solve(s1: str, s2: str) -> str:
    c1, c2 = contained(s1, s2), contained(s2, s1)
    if c1 and c2:
        return s1 if len(s1) <= len(s2) else s2
    if c1: return s1
    if c2: return s2
    return "NONE"

print(solve(input(), input()))   # hey diksha hello / hey sameeddiksha helloworld

Java:

static boolean contained(String a, String b) {
    for (String w : a.split(" ")) {
        boolean found = false;
        for (String bw : b.split(" "))
            if (bw.contains(w)) { found = true; break; }
        if (!found) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
public static void main(String[] args) {
    String s1 = "hey diksha hello", s2 = "hey sameeddiksha helloworld";
    boolean c1 = contained(s1, s2), c2 = contained(s2, s1);
    if (c1 && c2) System.out.println(s1.length() <= s2.length() ? s1 : s2);
    else if (c1)  System.out.println(s1);
    else if (c2)  System.out.println(s2);
    else          System.out.println("NONE");
}

✅ Executed on the example: words of S1 — hey is a word of S2, diksha is a substring of sameeddiksha, hello of helloworld → S1 contained, return hey diksha hello. S2 is not contained in S1 (sameeddiksha appears nowhere). Complexity: O(|S1|·|S2|) worst case — trivially fast at these input sizes; the brute force is the intended solution.

Why this problem is instructive. The entire difficulty is specification reading, which is exactly §10's finding: "'contained' means substring-of-any-word; 'both' means shorter; 'neither' means NONE" — three return rules in one statement. Underline every return rule before writing a line.

OSI — router layer

Q1. At which OSI layer does a ROUTER primarily operate, and which PDU does it forward?

  • A) Layer 2 (Data Link) — frames
  • B) Layer 1 (Physical) — bits
  • C) Layer 3 (Network) — packets
  • D) Layer 4 (Transport) — segments
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: C) Layer 3 (Network) — packets

A router forwards on IP addresses, which live in the Layer 3 header.

L Name PDU Device
7 Application Data HTTP, DNS
6 Presentation Data encryption, JPEG
5 Session Data session control
4 Transport Segment TCP/UDP, ports
3 Network Packet Router, IP
2 Data Link Frame Switch, MAC
1 Physical Bits cable, hub

All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

OSI — switch vs router (scenario)

Q2. A company connects 20 PCs in one office so they can share files locally, with no internet. Which device is sufficient, and at which layer does it work?

  • A) A firewall, Layer 4
  • B) A hub, Layer 3
  • C) A router, Layer 3
  • D) A switch, Layer 2
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: D) A switch, Layer 2

Within a single LAN, a switch is enough — it forwards frames using MAC addresses at Layer 2 and learns which port each MAC sits on.

A router is only needed to move traffic between different networks (e.g. LAN → internet). A hub is Layer 1 and repeats to every port (collisions, no learning).

This is the scenario style the Oct-2025 candidate reported — you must map a situation to a layer, not just recite the table.

Provenance: Question type reported first-hand for the Oct-2025 assessment.

OSI — encryption layers

Q3. Match the encryption to its OSI layer: TLS, IPsec, WPA2.

  • A) TLS = L7, IPsec = L4, WPA2 = L1
  • B) All three operate at Layer 7
  • C) TLS ≈ L6, IPsec = L3, WPA2 = L2
  • D) TLS = L4, IPsec = L2, WPA2 = L3
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) TLS ≈ L6, IPsec = L3, WPA2 = L2

Encryption exists at several layers, and which one is a classic exam question.

  • TLS/SSL straddles L5/L6 — usually answered as Presentation (6), running above TCP
  • IPsec encrypts at the Network layer (3) — hence VPNs that protect all IP traffic
  • WPA2 encrypts the wireless link at the Data Link layer (2)

If asked 'at which layer does encryption happen?', the correct answer is it depends on which encryption.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

TCP vs UDP

Q4. Which correctly describes the difference between TCP and UDP?

  • A) TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery; UDP is connectionless and does not
  • B) TCP is faster because it does not perform error checking
  • C) Both guarantee delivery, but UDP is encrypted
  • D) UDP is connection-oriented and guarantees delivery; TCP is connectionless
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery; UDP is connectionless and does not

TCP UDP
Connection 3-way handshake none
Reliability guaranteed, retransmits best-effort
Ordering preserved not preserved
Header 20 bytes 8 bytes
Used by HTTP, FTP, SMTP, SSH DNS, DHCP, VoIP, streaming

Neither protocol encrypts — that is TLS's job, one layer up. And TCP is slower because it does more checking, not less.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

TCP — handshake

Q5. What is the correct sequence of the TCP three-way handshake?

  • A) SYN-ACK → SYN → ACK
  • B) SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK
  • C) SYN → ACK → SYN-ACK
  • D) ACK → SYN → SYN-ACK
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK

Client sends SYN (synchronise, with its initial sequence number) → server replies SYN-ACK (acknowledges and sends its own sequence number) → client sends ACK. The connection is then established.

Teardown uses a four-way exchange: FIN → ACK → FIN → ACK. A SYN flood attack exploits step 2 by never sending the final ACK, exhausting the server's half-open connection table.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Ports — well known

Q6. Which port pair is correct?

  • A) HTTPS = 8080, SSH = 21
  • B) HTTPS = 443, SSH = 25
  • C) HTTPS = 443, SSH = 22
  • D) HTTPS = 80, SSH = 23
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) HTTPS = 443, SSH = 22

20/21 FTP · 22 SSH · 23 Telnet · 25 SMTP · 53 DNS · 80 HTTP · 110 POP3 · 143 IMAP · 443 HTTPS · 3306 MySQL · 1433 MS SQL · 5432 PostgreSQL · 3389 RDP · 8080 HTTP-alt.

Trap pair: 22 (SSH, encrypted) vs 23 (Telnet, plaintext). Telnet should never be used on an untrusted network.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DNS

Q7. What is the primary function of DNS?

  • A) Encrypt web traffic
  • B) Route packets between networks
  • C) Translate domain names into IP addresses
  • D) Assign IP addresses dynamically
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Translate domain names into IP addresses

DNS resolves names to IPs (example.com → 93.184.216.34). It runs mainly on UDP port 53 (TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses).

Do not confuse with DHCP, which assigns IP addresses to clients (UDP 67/68). Record types worth knowing: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (nameserver), TXT (SPF/DKIM).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DHCP

Q8. Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses to devices joining a network?

  • A) DHCP
  • B) ICMP
  • C) DNS
  • D) ARP
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) DHCP

DHCP hands out IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers.

Its four-step exchange is DORA: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge.

Neighbours: ARP maps IP → MAC within a LAN; ICMP carries diagnostics (ping, traceroute); DNS maps names → IP.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

ARP

Q9. What does ARP do?

  • A) Encrypts link-layer traffic
  • B) Resolves an IP address to a MAC address
  • C) Resolves a domain name to an IP address
  • D) Assigns IP addresses
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Resolves an IP address to a MAC address

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) finds the MAC address for a known IP on the local network — necessary because Layer 2 delivery needs a MAC, not an IP.

ARP spoofing lets an attacker associate their MAC with another host's IP and become a man-in-the-middle. This is exactly why HTTPS matters on public Wi-Fi: the attacker can intercept at Layer 2, but TLS makes the intercepted traffic useless.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Subnetting — usable hosts

Q10. How many usable host addresses does 192.168.10.0/26 provide, and what is its broadcast address?

  • A) 62 hosts, broadcast 192.168.10.63
  • B) 30 hosts, broadcast 192.168.10.31
  • C) 64 hosts, broadcast 192.168.10.63
  • D) 62 hosts, broadcast 192.168.10.64
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) 62 hosts, broadcast 192.168.10.63

Formula: usable hosts = 2^(32 − prefix) − 2.

/26 leaves 32−26 = 6 host bits → 2⁶ = 64 addresses → 64 − 2 = 62 usable (network + broadcast are not assignable). The block spans .0–.63, so broadcast = .63.

/24 /25 /26 /27 /28 /30
254 126 62 30 14 2

Trap: .64 is the next subnet's network address, not this one's broadcast.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Subnetting — why cloud providers subnet (scenario)

Q11. Why do major cloud providers require you to divide a VPC into subnets?

  • A) To make DNS resolution faster
  • B) Because IPv4 requires at least four subnets
  • C) To increase the total number of IP addresses available
  • D) To isolate resources, control routing, and apply security boundaries per tier
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: D) To isolate resources, control routing, and apply security boundaries per tier

Subnetting a VPC is about ISOLATION and CONTROL, not address count — splitting a block gives you fewer usable addresses, because each subnet loses a network and a broadcast address.

Real reasons:

  • Public vs private tiers — a public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; a private one does not, so databases stay unreachable from the internet
  • Availability zones — one subnet per AZ for fault tolerance
  • Security and routing — separate route tables and network ACLs per subnet
  • Blast-radius containment

🔴 The Oct-2025 candidate reported being asked exactly this — 'why subnetting is done in major cloud providers'.

Provenance: Question type reported first-hand for the Oct-2025 assessment.

Subnetting — private ranges

Q12. Which of these is NOT a private IP address range?

  • A) 10.0.0.0/8
  • B) 172.16.0.0/12
  • C) 172.32.0.0/12
  • D) 192.168.0.0/16
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) 172.32.0.0/12

The three private ranges (RFC 1918) are:

  • 10.0.0.0/8 → 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255
  • 172.16.0.0/12 → 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255
  • 192.168.0.0/16 → 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255

172.32.x.x falls outside the 16–31 window, so it is public. That boundary is the trap.

Also reserved: 127.0.0.0/8 loopback · 169.254.0.0/16 APIPA (link-local, which is what you get when DHCP fails).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Subnetting — mask

Q13. What is the subnet mask for a /27 network?

  • A) 255.255.255.224
  • B) 255.255.255.240
  • C) 255.255.255.128
  • D) 255.255.255.192
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) 255.255.255.224

/27 = 27 network bits = 11111111.11111111.11111111.11100000 → the last octet is 128+64+32 = 224.

Prefix Last octet Block Usable
/24 0 256 254
/25 128 128 126
/26 192 64 62
/27 224 32 30
/28 240 16 14
/30 252 4 2

Shortcut: last octet = 256 − block size. Block for /27 is 32, so 256−32 = 224.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

IPv4 vs IPv6

Q14. What is the address size of IPv6?

  • A) 128 bits
  • B) 64 bits
  • C) 32 bits
  • D) 256 bits
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) 128 bits

IPv4 = 32 bits (~4.3 billion addresses) · IPv6 = 128 bits (3.4×10³⁸).

IPv6 also removes the need for NAT, has built-in IPsec support, uses no broadcast (multicast/anycast instead), and does not fragment in routers.

Written as eight hex groups: 2001:0db8:0000:... — :: compresses one run of zero groups.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

NAT

Q15. What is the primary purpose of NAT?

  • A) Resolve hostnames to addresses
  • B) Assign IP addresses to hosts
  • C) Allow multiple private IPs to share one public IP
  • D) Encrypt traffic leaving the network
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Allow multiple private IPs to share one public IP

NAT (Network Address Translation) rewrites private source addresses to a public one, letting a whole home or office network share a single public IP. It was the main stopgap for IPv4 exhaustion.

Side effect often tested: NAT gives a degree of inbound protection because unsolicited traffic has no translation entry to match — but NAT is not a firewall and provides no encryption.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Wi-Fi — protocol strength

Q16. Which Wi-Fi security protocol is the strongest?

  • A) WPA2
  • B) WPA3
  • C) WPA
  • D) WEP
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) WPA3

Strongest → weakest: WPA3 > WPA2 > WPA > WEP.

Protocol Year Encryption Key mechanism
WEP 1999 RC4 static key, 24-bit IV — broken
WPA 2003 RC4 + TKIP per-packet keys — deprecated
WPA2 2004 AES-CCMP 4-way handshake — KRACK vuln
WPA3 2018 AES-GCMP SAE (Dragonfly)

If WPA3 is not offered, the answer is WPA2 — never WPA, which was only an interim patch for WEP.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Wi-Fi — TKIP vs AES

Q17. Which encryption standard is associated with WPA2?

  • A) DES
  • B) TKIP
  • C) RC4
  • D) AES
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) AES

WPA2 mandates AES-CCMP. TKIP belongs to WPA (an RC4-based stopgap) and is now deprecated.

The trap: TKIP sounds newer because it arrived with 'WPA', but AES is strictly stronger. If a router offers 'WPA2 with TKIP' for compatibility, that is a downgrade.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Wi-Fi — WPA3 feature

Q18. Which feature defines WPA3 and prevents offline dictionary attacks?

  • A) SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)
  • B) WPS
  • C) TKIP
  • D) MAC filtering
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)

SAE (Dragonfly) replaces the WPA2 pre-shared-key handshake. Under WPA2, an attacker who captures the 4-way handshake can guess passwords offline, forever. SAE makes every guess require a fresh live interaction with the access point, and adds forward secrecy — traffic captured today stays unreadable even if the password leaks later.

WPA3 also adds OWE, which encrypts open networks (café Wi-Fi with no password).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Wi-Fi — weak measures

Q19. Which of these is NOT a genuine security measure on a wireless network?

  • A) Using WPA2-Enterprise with RADIUS
  • B) Using WPA3 encryption
  • C) Disabling WPS
  • D) Hiding the SSID broadcast
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) Hiding the SSID broadcast

SSID hiding is obscurity, not security — the SSID still appears in client probe requests and is trivially captured. The same applies to MAC filtering: MAC addresses are easily spoofed.

The other three are real: WPA3 encryption, WPA2/3-Enterprise with per-user 802.1X/RADIUS credentials, and disabling WPS (its 8-digit PIN is brute-forcible).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Wi-Fi — KRACK

Q20. The KRACK attack targets which mechanism?

  • A) The WPA2 4-way handshake
  • B) The DNS resolution process
  • C) The WPA3 SAE exchange
  • D) The WEP initialisation vector
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) The WPA2 4-way handshake

KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack, 2017) manipulates the WPA2 4-way handshake to force nonce reuse, which lets an attacker decrypt traffic. It is a protocol-level flaw, not a password weakness — a strong passphrase does not help.

Mitigation: patch clients and access points, or move to WPA3, whose SAE handshake is not vulnerable.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — SQL injection

Q21. An attacker enters ' OR '1'='1 into a login form and gains access. Which attack is this, and what is the PRIMARY defence?

  • A) MITM — enforce TLS
  • B) XSS — escape HTML output
  • C) DoS — rate-limit requests
  • D) SQL injection — parameterised queries / prepared statements
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: D) SQL injection — parameterised queries / prepared statements

The payload turns the WHERE clause always-true:

SELECT * FROM users
WHERE username = '' OR '1'='1' AND password = '';

Parameterised queries send SQL structure and data SEPARATELY, so input can only ever be a value, never executable syntax.

'Sanitise the input' is the tempting wrong answer — blacklists get bypassed. Parameterisation removes the possibility structurally.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Security — XSS

Q22. Which attack injects malicious JavaScript that executes in another user's browser?

  • A) Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
  • B) Phishing
  • C) SQL injection
  • D) CSRF
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

XSS injects script into a page that other users then load. Types: stored (saved in the database), reflected (echoed from the request), DOM-based (client-side only).

Defences: output encoding, a Content-Security-Policy header, and HttpOnly cookies so stolen scripts cannot read the session token.

In JavaScript this is why you prefer textContent over innerHTML.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — CSRF

Q23. Which attack tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted authenticated request?

  • A) CSRF
  • B) SQL injection
  • C) Brute force
  • D) XSS
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) CSRF

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) abuses the fact that browsers attach cookies automatically. A malicious page triggers a request to a site where the victim is already logged in, and the server cannot tell it was not intended.

Defences: anti-CSRF tokens (unpredictable per-session value the attacker cannot guess), SameSite cookies, and re-authentication for sensitive actions.

XSS vs CSRF: XSS steals or acts inside the site's context; CSRF acts from outside using the victim's session.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — MITM

Q24. An attacker intercepts and possibly alters traffic between two parties. What is this, and the defence?

  • A) Phishing — user training
  • B) DDoS — rate limiting
  • C) Man-in-the-Middle — TLS with certificate validation
  • D) Ransomware — offline backups
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Man-in-the-Middle — TLS with certificate validation

MITM sits between two endpoints, reading or modifying traffic. Enablers: ARP spoofing, rogue Wi-Fi access points, DNS poisoning.

TLS defeats it — but only with certificate validation. Encryption alone is not enough; if the client accepts any certificate, the attacker simply presents their own. That is why certificate-pinning and CA validation matter.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — DDoS

Q25. What distinguishes a DDoS attack from a DoS attack?

  • A) There is no difference
  • B) DDoS uses many distributed sources; DoS comes from one
  • C) DDoS is encrypted; DoS is not
  • D) DDoS targets databases; DoS targets web servers
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) DDoS uses many distributed sources; DoS comes from one

The extra D is 'Distributed' — traffic arrives from many compromised machines (a botnet), which makes blocking by source IP ineffective and amplifies the volume.

Defences: rate limiting, CDN/scrubbing services, anycast distribution, and autoscaling. Types include volumetric (bandwidth), protocol (SYN flood) and application-layer (HTTP flood).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — phishing

Q26. An employee receives an email that appears to be from their bank asking them to confirm credentials via a link. This is:

  • A) Phishing
  • B) A SQL injection attempt
  • C) Spoofing at the network layer
  • D) A brute-force attack
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Phishing

Phishing is social engineering — deceiving a person into surrendering credentials. Variants: spear phishing (targeted at one person), whaling (executives), vishing (voice), smishing (SMS).

Defences are mostly human plus MFA, which limits the damage even when credentials are given away. Technical controls: SPF, DKIM and DMARC to make sender forgery harder.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — symmetric vs asymmetric

Q27. Which is an ASYMMETRIC (public-key) encryption algorithm?

  • A) DES
  • B) RSA
  • C) AES
  • D) Blowfish
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: B) RSA

Memorise the SHORT list — asymmetric: RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman, DSA. Everything else is symmetric (AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish, RC4).

Symmetric Asymmetric
Keys one shared public + private
Speed fast slow
Used for bulk data key exchange, signatures

MD5/SHA are hashing, not encryption — one-way and irreversible. If a question offers SHA-256 as an 'encryption algorithm', that is the wrong answer.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Security — AES key sizes

Q28. Which key sizes does AES support?

  • A) 128, 192 and 256 bits
  • B) Only 128 bits
  • C) 56 and 112 bits
  • D) 512 and 1024 bits
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) 128, 192 and 256 bits

AES supports 128, 192 and 256-bit keys, with 10, 12 and 14 rounds respectively. It is a block cipher with a fixed 128-bit block size.

DES used a 56-bit key — far too small today, brute-forcible in hours. 3DES applies DES three times (~112-bit effective strength) and is also deprecated.

✅ This exact question appears in a mined Accenture paper.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Security — hashing

Q29. Which statement about hashing is TRUE?

  • A) It is used to keep data confidential in transit
  • B) It is one-way and cannot be reversed to recover the input
  • C) It always produces output the same length as the input
  • D) It is a form of encryption that can be decrypted with a key
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) It is one-way and cannot be reversed to recover the input

A hash is a one-way function producing a FIXED-length digest regardless of input size. It provides integrity, not confidentiality.

Uses: password storage (with a salt, using bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2 — not raw MD5/SHA), checksums, digital signatures.

MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for collision resistance; use SHA-256 or better.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — firewall types

Q30. Which firewall type inspects the actual content of application traffic?

  • A) Packet-filtering firewall
  • B) Stateful inspection firewall
  • C) Application-layer (proxy) firewall
  • D) NAT gateway
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Application-layer (proxy) firewall

Evolution of firewalls:

  1. Packet-filtering — L3/L4, stateless: checks IP and port only
  2. Stateful inspection — tracks connection state, so it knows a reply belongs to an outbound request
  3. Application/proxy (L7) — understands HTTP, FTP and so on, and can inspect and filter content

A WAF is a Layer-7 firewall specialised for web attacks like SQLi and XSS.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — IDS vs IPS

Q31. What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?

  • A) IDS works at Layer 2; IPS at Layer 7
  • B) IDS blocks; IPS only logs
  • C) They are the same thing
  • D) IDS detects and alerts; IPS detects and blocks
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) IDS detects and alerts; IPS detects and blocks

IDS = Intrusion DETECTION System — passive, sits out-of-band, raises alerts. IPS = Intrusion PREVENTION System — inline, so it can drop malicious traffic.

The trade-off: an IPS can stop an attack in real time, but a false positive blocks legitimate traffic. An IDS is safer but requires someone to act on the alert.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — VPN purpose

Q32. What is the primary purpose of a VPN?

  • A) Cache web content closer to users
  • B) Create an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network
  • C) Increase internet bandwidth
  • D) Assign public IP addresses
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: B) Create an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network

A VPN encrypts traffic between endpoints across a public network, giving confidentiality and integrity, plus access to private resources as if you were on the LAN.

🔴 The Oct-2025 candidate reported being asked 'VPN questions and types of VPN' — so know the types in the next question too.

A VPN is not anonymity — the provider can still see your traffic.

Provenance: Question type reported first-hand for the Oct-2025 assessment.

Security — VPN types

Q33. Which pair correctly names the two main VPN deployment types?

  • A) Inbound and outbound
  • B) Public and private
  • C) Symmetric and asymmetric
  • D) Site-to-site and remote-access
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: D) Site-to-site and remote-access

Site-to-site connects two whole networks (branch office ↔ head office) — the tunnel runs between gateways and users need no client software. Remote-access connects a single user's device to the corporate network — this is the 'work from home' VPN.

Protocols: IPsec (L3), SSL/TLS VPN (often browser-based), WireGuard, OpenVPN, and the legacy PPTP/L2TP.

🔴 Reported as directly asked in the Oct-2025 technical round.

Provenance: Question type reported first-hand for the Oct-2025 assessment.

Cloud — service models

Q34. A provider supplies the OS, runtime and middleware; you are responsible only for your application code and data. Which service model is this?

  • A) IaaS
  • B) On-premises
  • C) PaaS
  • D) SaaS
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: C) PaaS

Decide by where YOUR responsibility starts:

Model You manage Examples
IaaS OS, runtime, app, data EC2, Azure VMs, Compute Engine
PaaS app code + data only Elastic Beanstalk, App Service, Heroku
SaaS nothing but your data Gmail, Salesforce, Office 365

One-line test: patch the OS → IaaS · only push code → PaaS · just log in → SaaS.

Cloud — SaaS example

Q35. Gmail is an example of which cloud service model?

  • A) SaaS
  • B) IaaS
  • C) PaaS
  • D) FaaS
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) SaaS

You just log in and use it — Google manages hardware, OS, runtime and the application itself. You control only your data and settings.

Other SaaS: Salesforce, Office 365, Dropbox, Zoom. FaaS (Functions-as-a-Service, e.g. AWS Lambda) is a serverless subset of PaaS where you deploy individual functions and pay per invocation.

Cloud — deployment models

Q36. Which is a cloud DEPLOYMENT model (not a service model)?

  • A) IaaS
  • B) Hybrid cloud
  • C) PaaS
  • D) SaaS
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Hybrid cloud

Two independent axes, and questions mix them deliberately.

Deployment models: Public · Private · Hybrid · Community Service models: IaaS · PaaS · SaaS

'A private cloud running PaaS' is perfectly coherent — the axes are orthogonal.

Hybrid combines public and private, typically keeping regulated data private while bursting compute to the public cloud.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Cloud — NIST characteristics

Q37. Which is NOT one of the five essential characteristics of cloud computing (NIST)?

  • A) Permanent local storage
  • B) Rapid elasticity
  • C) On-demand self-service
  • D) Measured service
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Permanent local storage

The five NIST characteristics:

  1. On-demand self-service — provision without human interaction
  2. Broad network access — reachable over the network on standard devices
  3. Resource pooling — multi-tenant, dynamically assigned
  4. Rapid elasticity — scale out and in quickly
  5. Measured service — metered, pay-per-use

Permanent local storage is the opposite of the cloud model — resources are pooled and ephemeral.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Cloud — scaling

Q38. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?

  • A) Vertical adds machines; horizontal adds power to one machine
  • B) They are the same
  • C) Vertical adds power to one machine; horizontal adds more machines
  • D) Vertical applies only to databases
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Vertical adds power to one machine; horizontal adds more machines

Vertical (scale UP) — bigger CPU/RAM on one server. Simple, but has a hard ceiling and usually requires downtime; it remains a single point of failure. Horizontal (scale OUT) — more servers behind a load balancer. Effectively unlimited and fault-tolerant, but the application must be stateless to benefit.

Cloud architecture is built around horizontal scaling — that is what auto-scaling groups do.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Cloud — region vs AZ

Q39. In cloud terminology, what is an Availability Zone?

  • A) An isolated datacentre location within a region
  • B) A billing category
  • C) A network security boundary
  • D) A geographic area containing multiple regions
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) An isolated datacentre location within a region

A region is a geographic area (e.g. ap-south-1, Mumbai). Each region contains multiple Availability Zones — physically separate datacentres with independent power, cooling and networking, linked by low-latency connections.

Deploying across two or more AZs is the standard high-availability pattern: one AZ can fail without taking your application down. Deploying across regions addresses geographic latency and disaster recovery.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Cloud — containers vs VMs

Q40. What is the key difference between a container and a virtual machine?

  • A) VMs share the host kernel; containers do not
  • B) Containers cannot be networked
  • C) Containers are always slower than VMs
  • D) Containers share the host OS kernel; VMs each run a full guest OS
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: D) Containers share the host OS kernel; VMs each run a full guest OS

A VM virtualises hardware — hypervisor plus a complete guest OS per VM (GBs, boots in minutes, strong isolation). A container virtualises the OS — shares the host kernel, packaging only the app and its dependencies (MBs, starts in seconds, weaker isolation).

🔴 The Oct-2025 candidate reported being asked 'containerisation concepts and why we use them' — the answer is portability and dependency isolation with far less overhead.

Provenance: Question type reported first-hand for the Oct-2025 assessment.

DevOps — definition

Q41. What best describes DevOps?

  • A) A culture and set of practices that unites Development and Operations to shorten delivery cycles
  • B) A specific tool made by Jenkins
  • C) A programming language for automation
  • D) A testing framework
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) A culture and set of practices that unites Development and Operations to shorten delivery cycles

DevOps is a culture, not a tool or a methodology. It is explicitly not an SDLC model like Agile or Waterfall.

CALMS framework: Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing.

The term was coined by Patrick Debois (DevOpsDays, Ghent, 2009).

DevOps — CI vs CD

Q42. What distinguishes Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment?

  • A) They are identical
  • B) Delivery prepares every change for release but a human approves the production push; Deployment pushes automatically
  • C) Delivery deploys automatically; Deployment requires approval
  • D) Delivery applies only to databases
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Delivery prepares every change for release but a human approves the production push; Deployment pushes automatically

Term Ends at
Continuous Integration merge frequently; every commit triggers automated build + tests → a tested artifact
Continuous Delivery every change is release-ready; a human clicks deploy
Continuous Deployment every passing change goes live automatically

Both are 'CD' — they differ ONLY by whether the final production step is automatic. That is the whole question.

DevOps — Docker port mapping

Q43. Which Docker option exposes a container running on port 8080 to port 80 of the host?

  • A) -p 8080:80
  • B) -p 80:8080
  • C) -p 8080:8080
  • D) -p 80:80
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: B) -p 80:8080

The format is -p HOST:CONTAINER — host port FIRST.

The container listens on 8080 and you want it reachable on host port 80, so -p 80:8080.

✅ Verified against the Docker CLI: -p, --publish Publish a container's port(s) to the host. Getting the order backwards is the single most common Docker mistake, and this exact question appears in Accenture's own DevOps training test.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — run vs start

Q44. What is the difference between docker run and docker start?

  • A) There is no difference
  • B) run only works on Linux
  • C) start creates a new container; run restarts a stopped one
  • D) run creates and starts a NEW container from an image; start restarts an existing stopped container
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: D) run creates and starts a NEW container from an image; start restarts an existing stopped container

The command signatures prove it:

docker run   [OPTIONS] IMAGE  [COMMAND]
docker start [OPTIONS] CONTAINER

run takes an image; start takes a container. ✅ Verified from the Docker CLI.

docker run is effectively docker create + docker start.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — volumes

Q45. Which command creates a Docker volume?

  • A) docker create volume myvol
  • B) docker make volume myvol
  • C) docker new volume myvol
  • D) docker volume create myvol
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: D) docker volume create myvol

Docker's CLI groups object commands as docker <object> <verb> — hence docker volume create, docker network create, docker image ls.

✅ Verified: docker volume exposes a create subcommand; docker create volume is not valid syntax.

Volumes persist data beyond a container's lifetime — without one, everything written inside a container is lost when it is removed.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — Jenkins home

Q46. Which environment variable specifies the folder containing Jenkins configuration and runtime data?

  • A) M2_HOME
  • B) JENKINS_ROOT
  • C) JAVA_HOME
  • D) JENKINS_HOME
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: D) JENKINS_HOME

JENKINS_HOME holds all jobs, plugins, build history and configuration — it is therefore the directory you back up.

The others: JAVA_HOME points at the JDK, M2_HOME at Maven. Jenkins is a Java application, so a JDK/JRE is a prerequisite.

Backup best practice: run as few jobs as possible during the backup, or shut Jenkins down, so the snapshot is consistent.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — Jenkins agent

Q47. What is a Jenkins Agent (formerly Slave)?

  • A) A type of pipeline script
  • B) A lightweight worker that executes jobs dispatched by the controller
  • C) A plugin for source control
  • D) A second full Jenkins server
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: B) A lightweight worker that executes jobs dispatched by the controller

The controller schedules and coordinates; agents do the actual building. This lets you distribute load and build on different platforms (a Windows agent, a Linux agent) from one controller.

An agent is not another Jenkins server — it runs a small agent process, not the full web application.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — pipeline

Q48. What best defines a Pipeline job in Jenkins?

  • A) Jobs that listen to the same message queue
  • B) A series of jobs owned by the same user
  • C) Jenkins has no pipeline jobs
  • D) A set of jobs defining a workflow and its dependencies
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: D) A set of jobs defining a workflow and its dependencies

A pipeline models the whole path from commit to production as code, usually in a Jenkinsfile kept in the repository (pipeline-as-code), with stages such as Build, Test and Deploy.

Benefits: versioned with the source, reviewable, survives Jenkins reinstalls, and supports pause/resume and parallel stages.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — Git webhook

Q49. What role do Git webhooks play in Continuous Integration with Jenkins?

  • A) The Git server calls Jenkins to trigger a build when code is pushed
  • B) They merge branches automatically
  • C) Jenkins polls Git every minute
  • D) They encrypt the repository
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) The Git server calls Jenkins to trigger a build when code is pushed

A webhook is a push notification from the Git SERVER to Jenkins, so a build starts immediately on commit.

The alternative — SCM polling — has Jenkins ask Git repeatedly on a schedule. Webhooks are more efficient and lower-latency; polling wastes cycles and delays feedback.

The Jenkins GitHub plugin endpoint is http://<jenkins-url>/github-webhook/.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — Docker Swarm

Q50. What is Docker Swarm?

  • A) A cluster of connected Docker hosts (nodes) managed as one
  • B) Several containers running on one powerful host
  • C) A list of all containers in an organisation
  • D) A container image registry
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) A cluster of connected Docker hosts (nodes) managed as one

Swarm is Docker's native clustering and orchestration mode — multiple Docker hosts joined into a single virtual host, with scheduling, scaling and service discovery.

The trap is 'containers on one host' — Swarm is about clustering hosts, not containers. Kubernetes is the dominant alternative and has largely displaced it.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

DevOps — Kubernetes pod

Q51. What is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes?

  • A) Cluster
  • B) Node
  • C) Pod
  • D) Container
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: C) Pod

A Pod wraps one or more containers that share a network namespace and storage — Kubernetes schedules Pods, not bare containers.

Hierarchy: Cluster → Node → Pod → Container.

Other objects: Deployment (declares desired state, manages ReplicaSets and rollouts) · Service (stable endpoint and load balancing) · ConfigMap/Secret (configuration) · kubelet (node agent) · etcd (cluster state store).

🔴 Kubernetes questions were explicitly reported in the Oct-2025 technical round.

DevOps — infrastructure as code

Q52. Which tool is primarily used for infrastructure provisioning as code?

  • A) Terraform
  • B) Prometheus
  • C) Git
  • D) Jenkins
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Terraform

Terraform provisions infrastructure declaratively — you describe the desired cloud resources and it creates them.

The neighbouring tools: Ansible = configuration management (configure existing machines) · Jenkins = CI/CD automation · Prometheus = metrics/monitoring · Git = version control.

IaC benefits: repeatability, version control, and no manual console clicking.

DevOps — Git merge vs rebase

Q53. What is the key difference between git merge and git rebase?

  • A) Rebase deletes branches
  • B) Merge preserves history and adds a merge commit; rebase rewrites commits onto a new base for linear history
  • C) They produce identical results
  • D) Rebase preserves history; merge rewrites it
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Merge preserves history and adds a merge commit; rebase rewrites commits onto a new base for linear history

Merge keeps the true history including the branch point, at the cost of a merge commit and a non-linear graph. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a clean linear history — but it creates new commit hashes.

The golden rule: never rebase a branch other people have pulled. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else into a painful recovery.

Related: git revert (safe, adds an undo commit) vs git reset (rewrites history).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — CIA triad

Q54. Which trio forms the CIA triad in information security?

  • A) Control, Isolation, Authentication
  • B) Compliance, Integrity, Auditing
  • C) Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
  • D) Cryptography, Identity, Access
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability

The three goals every security control serves:

  • Confidentiality — only authorised parties can read the data (encryption, access control)
  • Integrity — data is not altered undetectably (hashing, digital signatures)
  • Availability — the system is reachable when needed (redundancy, DDoS protection, backups)

Mapping an attack to the property it violates is a common question form: a DDoS attacks availability; tampering attacks integrity; eavesdropping attacks confidentiality.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — authentication vs authorisation

Q55. What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?

  • A) They are synonyms
  • B) Authentication determines what you may do; authorisation verifies who you are
  • C) Authentication applies only to APIs
  • D) Authentication verifies WHO you are; authorisation determines WHAT you may do
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) Authentication verifies WHO you are; authorisation determines WHAT you may do

AuthN comes first, AuthZ second. Logging in with a password proves identity (authentication); whether you may then delete a record is authorisation.

MFA strengthens authentication by combining factors: something you know (password), have (phone/token), are (biometric). RBAC implements authorisation through roles.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — ransomware

Q56. Which defence is most effective against ransomware?

  • A) Regular offline/immutable backups
  • B) Using HTTP instead of HTTPS
  • C) A stronger Wi-Fi password
  • D) Disabling the SSID broadcast
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Regular offline/immutable backups

Ransomware encrypts your data and demands payment for the key. The only defence that reliably restores you without paying is a backup the malware cannot reach — offline, or immutable/versioned storage.

Backups that stay mounted get encrypted too, which is why 'offline' matters. Supporting controls: patching, least privilege, email filtering and user awareness.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Networking — protocol layer mapping

Q57. At which OSI layer does HTTP operate?

  • A) Layer 4 (Transport)
  • B) Layer 7 (Application)
  • C) Layer 6 (Presentation)
  • D) Layer 3 (Network)
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Layer 7 (Application)

HTTP is an Application-layer protocol (L7), alongside FTP, SMTP, DNS and DHCP.

Common layer placements worth memorising: TCP/UDP → L4 · IP/ICMP → L3 · Ethernet/ARP/MAC → L2 · cables and hubs → L1.

Nuance: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, and TLS is usually placed at L6 — so 'HTTPS' can legitimately be described as spanning layers.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Networking — troubleshooting tools

Q58. Which command traces the path packets take to a destination host?

  • A) nslookup
  • B) ping
  • C) netstat
  • D) tracert / traceroute
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) tracert / traceroute

tracert (Windows) / traceroute (Linux) shows every hop by sending packets with increasing TTL values and recording which router replies.

The toolkit: ping tests reachability and latency (ICMP) · netstat lists connections and listening ports · nslookup/dig query DNS · ipconfig/ifconfig show local configuration.

Diagnostic order: ping the gateway → ping an external IP → ping a domain name. If IP works but the name fails, the problem is DNS.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Networking — LAN/WAN/MAN

Q59. Which network type spans a city or metropolitan area?

  • A) MAN
  • B) PAN
  • C) WAN
  • D) LAN
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) MAN

By geographic scope:

  • PAN — Personal, a few metres (Bluetooth)
  • LAN — Local, one building or campus (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
  • MAN — Metropolitan, a city (metro Ethernet, fibre)
  • WAN — Wide, country or global (the internet, MPLS, leased lines)

LANs are the fastest and cheapest per bit; WANs the slowest and most expensive — a direct consequence of distance.
