OS — process vs program

Q60. What is the difference between a program and a process?

  • A) A program has its own address space; a process does not
  • B) A process is stored on disk; a program runs in memory
  • C) A program is a passive file on disk; a process is a program in execution
  • D) They are the same thing
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) A program is a passive file on disk; a process is a program in execution

A program is passive — bytes in a file. A process is active — a program loaded into memory with its own address space, program counter, registers, stack and PCB.

One program can spawn many processes (several browser tabs from one binary).

The PCB (Process Control Block) holds the process's ID, state, registers, memory limits and open files — it is what the OS saves and restores on a context switch.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — process vs thread

Q61. Which resource is NOT shared between threads of the same process?

  • A) Code section
  • B) The stack
  • C) Open files
  • D) Data section
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) The stack

Threads share code, data, heap and open files. Each thread has its OWN stack, registers and program counter.

That is exactly why threads are cheap to create and switch (no address-space change) but dangerous: shared data means race conditions, requiring mutexes or semaphores.

Each thread needs its own stack because each has its own chain of function calls and local variables.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — process states

Q62. Which sequence correctly shows the main process states?

  • A) New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated
  • B) New → Waiting → Ready → Running → Terminated
  • C) Ready → New → Waiting → Running → Terminated
  • D) New → Running → Ready → Waiting → Terminated
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated

New (being created) → Ready (waiting for CPU) → Running (executing) → Waiting/Blocked (waiting for I/O) → Terminated.

Key transitions: Running → Ready is preemption (time slice expired); Running → Waiting is an I/O request; Waiting → Ready is I/O completion.

A blocked process never goes straight back to Running — it must pass through Ready and be scheduled again.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — deadlock conditions

Q63. Which are the four Coffman conditions necessary for deadlock?

  • A) Mutual exclusion, Starvation, Pre-emption, Circular wait
  • B) Deadlock, Livelock, Starvation, Thrashing
  • C) Mutual exclusion, Hold and wait, No pre-emption, Circular wait
  • D) Hold and wait, Aging, No pre-emption, Race condition
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: C) Mutual exclusion, Hold and wait, No pre-emption, Circular wait

All FOUR must hold simultaneously — break any one and deadlock becomes impossible.

  1. Mutual exclusion — a resource is non-shareable
  2. Hold and wait — a process holds one resource while waiting for another
  3. No pre-emption — resources cannot be forcibly taken
  4. Circular wait — a closed chain of processes each waiting on the next

Asked by name constantly. Prevention attacks one condition; avoidance uses the Banker's algorithm; detection-and-recovery lets it happen and then kills a process.

Provenance: Question type reported first-hand for the Oct-2025 assessment.

OS — scheduling algorithms

Q64. Which CPU scheduling algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time?

  • A) Round Robin
  • B) Shortest Job First (SJF)
  • C) First Come First Served (FCFS)
  • D) Priority scheduling
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Shortest Job First (SJF)

SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time — running short jobs first minimises cumulative waiting. Its catch: it requires knowing burst times in advance, which is impossible in practice, so real schedulers estimate.

  • FCFS — simple, suffers the convoy effect (a long job blocks everyone)
  • Round Robin — fair, preemptive, uses a time quantum; good response time
  • Priority — can cause starvation, fixed by aging

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — scheduler types

Q65. Which scheduler decides which process gets the CPU next, and runs most frequently?

  • A) Long-term scheduler
  • B) I/O scheduler
  • C) Medium-term scheduler
  • D) Short-term scheduler (dispatcher)
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) Short-term scheduler (dispatcher)

Short-term (CPU scheduler / dispatcher) — picks from the Ready queue, runs milliseconds apart, so it must be fast. Long-term (job scheduler) — decides which jobs enter the system at all, controlling the degree of multiprogramming. Runs rarely. Medium-term — handles swapping processes out of memory and back in.

This exact three-way distinction appears in a mined Accenture interview paper.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — paging vs segmentation

Q66. Which type of fragmentation does paging eliminate, and which does it cause?

  • A) Eliminates both
  • B) Causes both
  • C) Eliminates internal, causes external
  • D) Eliminates external, causes internal
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) Eliminates external, causes internal

Paging uses FIXED-size pages and frames. Because every block is the same size, free memory is never left in unusable odd-sized gaps → no external fragmentation. But the last page of a process is usually partly empty → internal fragmentation.

Segmentation is the reverse: variable-size logical units match the program's structure, so no internal waste, but free memory becomes scattered → external fragmentation.

Internal = waste inside an allocated block · External = free space scattered in unusable gaps.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — virtual memory

Q67. What is the purpose of virtual memory?

  • A) Allow programs larger than physical RAM to run, using disk as backing store
  • B) Increase the CPU clock speed
  • C) Encrypt memory contents
  • D) Replace the need for a hard disk
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Allow programs larger than physical RAM to run, using disk as backing store

Virtual memory gives each process the illusion of a large contiguous address space, with only the actively used pages held in RAM and the rest on disk.

Demand paging loads a page only when a page fault occurs. Too many page faults leads to thrashing — the CPU spends more time swapping than executing. The fix is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming (the working-set model).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — page replacement

Q68. Which page-replacement algorithm can suffer Belady's anomaly?

  • A) None of them
  • B) FIFO
  • C) Optimal
  • D) LRU
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) FIFO

Belady's anomaly: giving FIFO MORE frames can produce MORE page faults — the opposite of what you would expect.

FIFO is vulnerable. LRU and Optimal are not, because they are stack algorithms — the set of pages held with n frames is always a subset of the set held with n+1.

Optimal (evict the page used furthest in the future) is the theoretical best but unimplementable; LRU approximates it using the past.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — zombie vs orphan

Q69. What is a zombie process?

  • A) A process with no memory allocated
  • B) A process that has terminated but whose parent has not yet read its exit status
  • C) A process whose parent died before it
  • D) A process stuck in an infinite loop
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) A process that has terminated but whose parent has not yet read its exit status

Zombie — finished execution, but its entry stays in the process table because the parent has not called wait(). It holds no memory or CPU, only a table entry, but too many exhaust the table.

Orphan — the parent died first; the process is adopted by init/systemd (PID 1), which reaps it properly.

The distinction: zombie = child finished, parent negligent. Orphan = parent finished first.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — mutex vs semaphore

Q70. What is the key difference between a mutex and a semaphore?

  • A) They are identical
  • B) A semaphore allows only one holder; a mutex allows many
  • C) A mutex works only between processes
  • D) A mutex has ownership and allows one holder; a counting semaphore permits N concurrent holders
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) A mutex has ownership and allows one holder; a counting semaphore permits N concurrent holders

Mutex — mutual exclusion lock with ownership: only the thread that locked it may unlock it. Binary by nature. Semaphore — a counter permitting up to N concurrent accesses, with no ownership — any thread may signal it.

Use a mutex to protect a critical section; a counting semaphore to manage a pool of N identical resources.

A binary semaphore resembles a mutex but still lacks ownership, which matters for priority inheritance.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — system call

Q71. Which of the following is a system call?

  • A) strlen()
  • B) printf()
  • C) fork()
  • D) malloc()
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) fork()

fork() crosses the user→kernel boundary to create a new process — a true system call.

The others are library functions: printf formats text and eventually calls the write syscall; malloc manages a user-space heap and only occasionally calls brk/mmap; strlen is pure computation with no kernel involvement.

Common syscalls: fork, exec, wait, exit, open, read, write, close, kill.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — kernel types

Q72. What distinguishes a microkernel from a monolithic kernel?

  • A) A microkernel keeps most services in user space; a monolithic kernel runs them in kernel space
  • B) A monolithic kernel has no device drivers
  • C) A microkernel cannot support multitasking
  • D) A microkernel is always faster
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) A microkernel keeps most services in user space; a monolithic kernel runs them in kernel space

Monolithic (Linux) — file systems, drivers and networking all run in kernel space. Fast (no message passing) but a driver bug can crash the whole system. Microkernel (QNX, Minix) — the kernel provides only IPC, scheduling and basic memory management; services run as user processes. More robust and modular, but slower due to message-passing overhead.

The trade-off is performance vs isolation — that is the whole comparison.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — thrashing

Q73. What is thrashing in an operating system?

  • A) A process being starved of CPU time
  • B) Two processes deadlocked on each other
  • C) Excessive paging where the CPU spends more time swapping than executing
  • D) Memory being fragmented into small gaps
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Excessive paging where the CPU spends more time swapping than executing

Thrashing happens when processes collectively need more pages than RAM holds, so every page brought in evicts one that is needed immediately. CPU utilisation collapses.

The dangerous feedback loop: the OS sees low CPU utilisation and admits more processes, making it worse.

Fix: reduce the degree of multiprogramming, use the working-set model, or add RAM.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OS — RAID

Q74. Which RAID level provides striping with distributed parity?

  • A) RAID 0
  • B) RAID 10
  • C) RAID 5
  • D) RAID 1
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) RAID 5

  • RAID 0 — striping only: fast, no redundancy (one disk fails, all data lost)
  • RAID 1 — mirroring: full redundancy, 50% capacity
  • RAID 5 — striping + distributed parity: survives one disk failure, needs ≥3 disks
  • RAID 6 — dual parity, survives two failures
  • RAID 10 — mirrored stripes: best performance + redundancy, 50% capacity

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

SQL — joins with NULL

Q75. employees has 6 rows, one with dept_id = NULL. departments has 4 rows, one with no employees. What do INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN counts return?

  • A) 5 and 5
  • B) 5 and 6
  • C) 6 and 7
  • D) 6 and 6
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: B) 5 and 6

NULL never matches in a join — not even another NULL. NULL = anything evaluates to unknown, never true.

  • INNER JOIN drops the NULL-dept employee → 5
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every left row, padding with NULLs → 6

✅ Verified by executing both queries against a real SQLite database.

A LEFT JOIN can never return fewer rows than the left table. If yours does, you put a right-table condition in WHERE instead of ON.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

SQL — WHERE vs HAVING

Q76. Which statement is TRUE about WHERE and HAVING?

  • A) WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping
  • B) They are interchangeable
  • C) Both can use aggregate functions
  • D) HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters groups
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping

Logical execution order:

FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
Filters Runs Aggregates?
WHERE rows before grouping ❌
HAVING groups after grouping ✅

WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 is an error — no groups exist yet when WHERE runs. This execution order also explains why you cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

SQL — second highest

Q77. Which query correctly returns the second-highest salary?

  • A) SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)
  • B) SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)
  • C) SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 2
  • D) SELECT MIN(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM emp)
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: B) SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)

Read inside-out: the inner query finds the top salary; the outer takes the maximum of everything strictly below it.

Option 3 fails — it returns two rows, not the second-highest value, and breaks with duplicate top salaries. Option 4 returns the second lowest.

Generalises to Nth: ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 (with DISTINCT), or DENSE_RANK() — not RANK(), which skips numbers after ties.

✅ This exact pattern appears in Accenture's own pre-onboarding curriculum.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

SQL — COUNT and NULL

Q78. Given a column with values 1, 2 and NULL, what do COUNT(*) and COUNT(col) return?

  • A) 3 and 3
  • B) 2 and 3
  • C) 3 and 2
  • D) 2 and 2
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: C) 3 and 2

COUNT(*) counts ROWS, including those with NULLs → 3. COUNT(col) counts NON-NULL values in that column → 2.

✅ Verified in SQLite.

The same rule applies to other aggregates: AVG ignores NULLs, so AVG of (1, 2, NULL) is 1.5, not 1.0 — it divides by 2, not 3. That difference is a favourite trap.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

SQL — NULL comparison

Q79. Which condition correctly finds rows where email has no value?

  • A) WHERE email = NULL
  • B) WHERE email = ''
  • C) WHERE email IS NULL
  • D) WHERE email == NULL
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: C) WHERE email IS NULL

= NULL is ALWAYS false — comparing anything to NULL yields unknown, and WHERE only keeps rows evaluating to true. You must use the IS NULL operator.

✅ Verified: WHERE x = NULL returned 0 rows; WHERE x IS NULL returned 1.

= '' is different — an empty string is a value, not the absence of one. A column can hold '' and NULL as distinct states.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

SQL — DELETE vs TRUNCATE

Q80. Which statement about DELETE and TRUNCATE is TRUE?

  • A) DELETE removes rows one at a time and can use WHERE; TRUNCATE removes all rows and cannot
  • B) Both are DDL commands
  • C) DELETE is faster than TRUNCATE on large tables
  • D) TRUNCATE can use a WHERE clause; DELETE cannot
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) DELETE removes rows one at a time and can use WHERE; TRUNCATE removes all rows and cannot

DELETE TRUNCATE DROP
Type DML DDL DDL
WHERE ✅ ❌ ❌
Speed slow (row by row, logged) fast (deallocates pages) fast
Rollback ✅ usually ❌ (auto-commits) ❌
Structure kept kept removed

TRUNCATE also resets identity/auto-increment counters; DELETE does not.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

SQL — normalisation

Q81. A table is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and:

  • A) Every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole key
  • B) Every determinant is a candidate key
  • C) It has no repeating groups
  • D) No non-key attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) No non-key attribute is transitively dependent on the primary key

The normal forms in one line each:

  • 1NF — atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF — 1NF + no partial dependency (every non-key attribute depends on the whole composite key)
  • 3NF — 2NF + no transitive dependency (a non-key attribute must not depend on another non-key attribute)
  • BCNF — stricter 3NF: every determinant is a candidate key

Purpose: eliminate redundancy and the insert/update/delete anomalies it causes.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

SQL — ACID

Q82. In ACID, what does 'Durability' guarantee?

  • A) The database moves from one valid state to another
  • B) A transaction completes fully or not at all
  • C) Transactions do not interfere with each other
  • D) Once committed, changes survive a system crash
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) Once committed, changes survive a system crash

A — Atomicity: all or nothing C — Consistency: only valid states, constraints preserved I — Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere D — Durability: committed data survives crashes (via write-ahead logging)

Atomicity vs Durability is the pair most often confused: atomicity is about partial completion being impossible; durability is about committed work being permanent.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

SQL — keys

Q83. What is a foreign key?

  • A) A column that references the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity
  • B) An index used to speed up joins
  • C) Any column with a UNIQUE constraint
  • D) A key that uniquely identifies each row in its own table
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) A column that references the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity

A foreign key links two tables and enforces referential integrity — you cannot insert a value that does not exist in the referenced table, nor delete a parent row that children still point at (unless ON DELETE CASCADE).

The key family: Primary (unique + NOT NULL, one per table) · Candidate (any column set that could be primary) · Composite (multiple columns) · Unique (unique but may allow one NULL) · Foreign.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

SQL — UNION vs UNION ALL

Q84. What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?

  • A) UNION ALL removes duplicates; UNION keeps them
  • B) They are identical
  • C) UNION works only on two tables
  • D) UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them and is faster
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them and is faster

UNION de-duplicates, which requires a sort or hash — real cost on large sets. UNION ALL simply concatenates and is therefore faster.

Use UNION ALL whenever you know duplicates are impossible or acceptable.

Both require the same number of columns with compatible types across all branches.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — memory hierarchy

Q85. Which memory is fastest and smallest, and sits inside the CPU?

  • A) Cache
  • B) Registers
  • C) RAM
  • D) SSD
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Registers

Speed order (fastest → slowest): Registers → L1 → L2 → L3 cache → RAM → SSD → HDD. Size and cost per byte run the other way.

Level Size Speed
Registers bytes fastest
L1 cache 32–64 KB ~1 ns
L3 cache 8–32 MB ~15 ns
RAM 8–32 GB ~100 ns
SSD 256 GB+ ~100 µs

The exam sentence: 'Registers are the fastest and smallest memory, located inside the CPU. Cache is faster but smaller than RAM.'

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — SRAM vs DRAM

Q86. Which memory type requires periodic refreshing, and where is it used?

  • A) SRAM — used as main memory
  • B) DRAM — used as cache
  • C) DRAM — used as main memory
  • D) SRAM — used as secondary storage
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) DRAM — used as main memory

DRAM stores each bit in a capacitor that leaks charge, so it must be REFRESHED constantly. It is cheaper and denser → used for main memory (RAM).

SRAM uses flip-flops — no refresh needed, much faster, but larger per bit and far more expensive → used for cache.

The exam question is almost always 'which needs refreshing?' → DRAM.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — RAM vs ROM

Q87. Which statement about ROM is TRUE?

  • A) It is used as the primary working memory
  • B) It is faster than cache
  • C) It loses its contents when power is removed
  • D) It is non-volatile and retains its contents without power
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) It is non-volatile and retains its contents without power

RAM ROM
Volatile Yes No
Read/Write both primarily read
Purpose working memory firmware, BIOS, bootstrap

ROM holds the boot firmware — which must survive power-off, or the machine could never start.

ROM family: PROM (write once) → EPROM (UV-erasable) → EEPROM (electrically erasable) → Flash (a type of EEPROM — SSDs, USB drives).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — program counter

Q88. What does the Program Counter (PC) hold?

  • A) The address of the NEXT instruction to execute
  • B) The address of the top of the stack
  • C) The current instruction being executed
  • D) The result of the last ALU operation
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) The address of the NEXT instruction to execute

PC → address of the NEXT instruction. IR (Instruction Register) → the CURRENT instruction. Swapping these two is the most common wrong answer.

Register Holds
PC/IP address of next instruction
IR current instruction
MAR address being accessed
MDR/MBR data read from / written to memory
AC intermediate arithmetic results
SP top of stack
PSW/Flags zero, carry, sign, overflow bits

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — instruction cycle

Q89. What is the correct order of the instruction cycle?

  • A) Execute → Fetch → Decode
  • B) Decode → Fetch → Execute
  • C) Fetch → Decode → Execute
  • D) Fetch → Execute → Decode
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Fetch → Decode → Execute

Fetch the instruction at the address in the PC → Decode it in the Control Unit → Execute it in the ALU → optionally write back the result.

Pipelining overlaps these stages across different instructions, increasing throughput (not the latency of any single instruction). A 5-stage pipeline approaches 5× throughput ideally.

Pipeline hazards: structural (resource conflict), data (result not ready), control (branches) — mitigated by forwarding, stalling and branch prediction.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — cache hit ratio

Q90. Cache access takes 10 ns, main memory 100 ns, and the hit ratio is 0.9. What is the average access time?

  • A) 55 ns
  • B) 10 ns
  • C) 90 ns
  • D) 19 ns
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) 19 ns

Formula: hit_ratio × cache_time + (1 − hit_ratio) × memory_time

0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 9 + 10 = 19 ns ✅ computed

The insight worth carrying: a 90% hit ratio does not give you 90% of cache speed — the 10% of misses dominate, contributing 10 of the 19 ns. This is why hit ratios are pushed toward 99%.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — locality of reference

Q91. Why do CPU caches work?

  • A) Because programs are single-threaded
  • B) Because of locality of reference — programs reuse recent data and nearby addresses
  • C) Because caches compress data
  • D) Because RAM is unreliable
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Because of locality of reference — programs reuse recent data and nearby addresses

Temporal locality — recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon (a loop variable). Spatial locality — addresses near a recent access are likely next (walking an array).

Spatial locality is why caches fetch whole cache LINES (typically 64 bytes) rather than single bytes.

It is also why row-major array traversal is dramatically faster than column-major in C — one respects spatial locality and the other defeats it.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — address space

Q92. How many memory locations can be addressed with a 32-bit address bus?

  • A) 32
  • B) 2³² (about 4 billion)
  • C) 2¹⁶
  • D) 32 × 1024
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) 2³² (about 4 billion)

n address lines address 2ⁿ locations. With byte addressing, 2³² bytes = 4 GB — which is exactly why 32-bit systems cap out at 4 GB of usable RAM.

Bus width Locations Bytes
16-bit 65,536 64 KB
32-bit 4,294,967,296 4 GB
64-bit 2⁶⁴ 16 EB (theoretical)

✅ All conversions computed.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — units

Q93. How many bytes are in 1 KB (binary convention)?

  • A) 2048
  • B) 1024
  • C) 1000
  • D) 512
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) 1024

1 KB = 2¹⁰ = 1024 bytes in the binary convention used for memory.

1 KB = 1024 B    = 2¹⁰
1 MB = 1024 KB   = 2²⁰
1 GB = 1024 MB   = 2³⁰
1 TB = 1024 GB   = 2⁴⁰

1 byte = 8 bits. A nibble is 4 bits.

⚠️ Storage manufacturers use decimal (1 GB = 10⁹ bytes), which is why a '1 TB' drive shows as ~931 GB in the OS.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — RISC vs CISC

Q94. Which characteristic describes RISC architecture?

  • A) Few simple fixed-length instructions and many registers
  • B) No pipelining support
  • C) Many complex variable-length instructions
  • D) Instructions that each take many clock cycles
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Few simple fixed-length instructions and many registers

RISC (ARM, RISC-V) — a small set of simple fixed-length instructions, many registers, mostly one cycle each, pipelines extremely well. Complexity moves to the compiler. CISC (x86) — many complex variable-length instructions, fewer registers, multi-cycle. Complexity lives in the hardware.

Fixed-length instructions are the key enabler of pipelining — the CPU knows where the next instruction starts without decoding the current one.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — von Neumann

Q95. What is the von Neumann bottleneck?

  • A) Disks are slower than RAM
  • B) Instructions and data share one bus, limiting throughput
  • C) The CPU is slower than the GPU
  • D) Cache is too small
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Instructions and data share one bus, limiting throughput

In the von Neumann architecture, instructions and data live in the SAME memory and share ONE bus, so the CPU cannot fetch an instruction and its operand simultaneously — the bus becomes the limit.

Harvard architecture uses separate instruction and data memories/buses, allowing simultaneous access. Modern CPUs are effectively hybrid: unified main memory (von Neumann) with split L1 instruction and data caches (Harvard-like).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

CPU — interrupt vs polling

Q96. Why are interrupts generally preferred over polling?

  • A) Polling cannot detect device events
  • B) The CPU can do other work instead of repeatedly checking device status
  • C) Interrupts use less memory
  • D) Interrupts are simpler to program
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) The CPU can do other work instead of repeatedly checking device status

Polling wastes CPU cycles repeatedly asking 'are you ready yet?'. An interrupt lets the device signal the CPU, which suspends its work, runs an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine), and resumes.

When polling still wins: when events are extremely frequent, the interrupt overhead (context save/restore) can exceed the cost of just checking — which is why high-throughput network drivers sometimes switch to polling.

DMA goes further, letting devices write to memory without the CPU at all.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DS — stack vs queue

Q97. Which pair correctly describes a stack and a queue?

  • A) Stack is LIFO; queue is FIFO
  • B) Both are LIFO
  • C) Stack is FIFO; queue is LIFO
  • D) Both are FIFO
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Stack is LIFO; queue is FIFO

Stack = Last In, First Out (push/pop) — undo history, function-call stack, expression evaluation, DFS. Queue = First In, First Out (enqueue/dequeue) — print spooling, CPU scheduling, BFS.

Where each shows up: the call stack is why deep recursion causes a stack overflow; queues are why BFS finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DS — binary search

Q98. What is the time complexity of binary search, and what does it require?

  • A) O(log n), requires a sorted array
  • B) O(n), requires a sorted array
  • C) O(1), requires a hash table
  • D) O(log n), works on any array
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) O(log n), requires a sorted array

Binary search halves the search space each step, giving O(log n) — but it is only correct on sorted data.

The trade-off worth stating: if you must sort first, that costs O(n log n), so for a single lookup a linear O(n) scan is better. Binary search pays off across many lookups on data that stays sorted.

Implementation trap: compute the midpoint as low + (high-low)/2, not (low+high)/2, to avoid integer overflow.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DS — array vs linked list

Q99. Which is an advantage of a linked list over an array?

  • A) It uses less memory per element
  • B) Random access by index is O(1)
  • C) It has better cache locality
  • D) Insertion and deletion at a known position is O(1)
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) Insertion and deletion at a known position is O(1)

Array Linked list
Access by index O(1) O(n)
Insert/delete at known node O(n) (shifting) O(1)
Memory contiguous, compact extra pointer per node
Cache locality excellent poor

The other three options are all array advantages — arrays use less memory per element (no pointers) and have far better cache locality because they are contiguous.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DS — hash table complexity

Q100. What is the average-case time complexity of lookup in a hash table, and the worst case?

  • A) O(1) average, O(log n) worst
  • B) O(n) average, O(n) worst
  • C) O(log n) average, O(n) worst
  • D) O(1) average, O(n) worst
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) O(1) average, O(n) worst

Average O(1) — the hash function distributes keys evenly across buckets. Worst O(n) — if every key collides into one bucket, the structure degenerates to a linked list.

Collision handling: chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probe for the next free slot).

Real-world relevance: hash-collision attacks deliberately force the worst case; modern languages randomise hash seeds to prevent it.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DS — complexity of sorting

Q101. What is the average time complexity of Quicksort, and its worst case?

  • A) O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst
  • B) O(n log n) average, O(n log n) worst
  • C) O(n²) average, O(n log n) worst
  • D) O(n) average, O(n log n) worst
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst

Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but degrades to O(n²) when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element — classically, on already-sorted input with a first-element pivot.

Mitigation: randomised or median-of-three pivot selection.

Algorithm Average Worst Stable
Quicksort O(n log n) O(n²) No
Mergesort O(n log n) O(n log n) Yes
Heapsort O(n log n) O(n log n) No
Bubble/Insertion O(n²) O(n²) Yes

Mergesort guarantees O(n log n) but needs O(n) extra space — that is the trade.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Programming — compiler vs interpreter

Q102. What is the key difference between a compiler and an interpreter?

  • A) A compiler executes code without producing output files
  • B) An interpreter is always faster at runtime
  • C) A compiler translates the whole program before execution; an interpreter translates and executes line by line
  • D) They are the same
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) A compiler translates the whole program before execution; an interpreter translates and executes line by line

Compiler (C, C++) — translates everything up front, reports all errors before running, produces a fast standalone executable. Interpreter (Python, JavaScript) — translates and runs statement by statement, stops at the first error, slower at runtime but more portable and easier to debug.

Java uses both: javac compiles source to bytecode, and the JVM interprets it (with a JIT compiler that compiles hot paths to native code at runtime).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Programming — SDLC

Q103. Which SDLC model is best suited to requirements that change frequently?

  • A) Waterfall
  • B) Big Bang
  • C) Agile
  • D) V-model
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Agile

Agile delivers in short iterations (sprints) with continuous feedback, so changing requirements are expected rather than resisted.

Waterfall is strictly sequential — each phase completes before the next begins — so a late requirement change is extremely expensive. It suits fixed, well-understood requirements (regulatory or safety-critical work).

The V-model pairs each development phase with a corresponding test phase.

The placement deck lists 'Software Development concepts' among the technical topics, and DevOps is the practice layer built on top of Agile.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

SQL — GROUP BY output

Q104.

SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp
GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Departments: Eng(2), Sales(2), Finance(1). Which appear in the result?

  • A) Eng, Sales and Finance
  • B) Finance only
  • C) Eng and Sales
  • D) None
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: C) Eng and Sales

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filters GROUPS after grouping. Finance has only one employee, so its group fails the test and is removed.

Execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Groups do not exist until GROUP BY runs, which is exactly why the count test must live in HAVING and not WHERE.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

OS — context switch

Q105. What is saved during a context switch?

  • A) The entire hard disk state
  • B) Nothing — processes restart
  • C) The process's registers, program counter and state in its PCB
  • D) Only the program counter
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) The process's registers, program counter and state in its PCB

The OS saves the full CPU context into the process's PCB — general registers, program counter, stack pointer, memory-management info and state — then loads the next process's context.

A context switch is pure overhead: no useful work happens during it. This is why threads are cheaper to switch between than processes — threads within one process share the address space, so the memory mappings and TLB need not be swapped.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Security — least privilege

Q106. What does the principle of least privilege state?

  • A) Every user and process should have only the minimum access needed to do its job
  • B) All users should share one account for simplicity
  • C) Administrators should have no access
  • D) Privileges should be granted permanently to avoid re-requests
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Every user and process should have only the minimum access needed to do its job

Least privilege limits the BLAST RADIUS. If an account is compromised, the attacker inherits only that account's limited rights.

In practice: developers do not get production database write access by default; services run as unprivileged users, not root; admin rights are granted just in time and revoked.

It pairs with defence in depth (layered controls) and zero trust (never trust based on network location alone).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Cloud — shared responsibility

Q107. Under the cloud shared-responsibility model, who is responsible for securing customer DATA?

  • A) The cloud provider, always
  • B) The customer, always
  • C) It depends on the region
  • D) Neither — data is secured automatically
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) The customer, always

The provider secures the cloud; the customer secures what they put IN the cloud.

Provider: physical datacentres, hardware, the hypervisor, and the managed-service infrastructure. Customer: their data, access management (IAM), encryption choices, network configuration, and — under IaaS — the guest OS and patching.

Data classification, encryption and access control never transfer to the provider, regardless of service model. Misconfigured public storage buckets are the classic failure.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

DevOps — monitoring

  • A) Maven
  • B) Ansible
  • C) Terraform
  • D) Prometheus
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Prometheus scrapes and stores time-series metrics and evaluates alerting rules, typically paired with Grafana for dashboards.

The wider toolchain: Terraform provisions infrastructure · Ansible configures machines · Maven/Gradle build Java projects · ELK/EFK aggregates logs · Jaeger/Zipkin handle distributed tracing.

The three pillars of observability: metrics, logs and traces.

Pseudocode & OOPs

10 of 45 — the hardest section

First-hand: 'Pseudocode + OOPs — 10 questions. Included bitwise operations and logic-heavy pseudocode (10–12 lines). No pen and paper allowed, so you need to visualise carefully.' Practise tracing these in your head.

Sub-topics covered: Bitwise — AND/OR/XOR · Bitwise — shifts · Bitwise — check odd/even · Bitwise — count set bits · Bitwise — precedence trap · Loops — mutated loop variable · Loops — uninitialised variable · Loops — digit sum · Loops — do-while overshoot · Loops — nested count · Loops — iteration count · Arrays — in-place update · Arrays — reverse in place · Arrays — sum of even indices · Recursion — base case · Recursion — call count · Recursion — string reverse · Arithmetic — integer division · Arithmetic — ASCII · Arithmetic — pre/post increment · Functions — pass by value vs pointer · Functions — static locals · OOPs — four pillars · OOPs — overloading vs overriding · OOPs — diamond problem · OOPs — abstract class vs interface · OOPs — access modifiers · OOPs — static · OOPs — constructor · OOPs — polymorphism · OOPs — composition vs aggregation · OOPs — encapsulation in practice

Bitwise — AND/OR/XOR

Q109.

Set x = 29, y = 13
Print (x AND y), (x OR y), (x XOR y)

(bitwise operators)

  • A) 12 29 17
  • B) 13 31 18
  • C) 13 29 16
  • D) 9 29 20
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) 13 29 16

29 = 11101
13 = 01101
AND  01101 = 13
OR   11101 = 29
XOR  10000 = 16

13's bits are a subset of 29's, so AND collapses to 13 and OR to 29.

Two free checks: (a&b)+(a|b) = a+b → 13+29 = 42 = 29+13 ✓ and a^b = (a|b)−(a&b) → 29−13 = 16 ✓

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Bitwise — shifts

Q110.

Set n = 40
Set a = n >> 2
Set b = n << 1
Print a + b
  • A) 80
  • B) 70
  • C) 100
  • D) 90
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) 90

>>k divides by 2ᵏ, <<k multiplies by 2ᵏ.

a = 40 >> 2 = 40/4 = 10 · b = 40 << 1 = 80 → 10 + 80 = 90.

Binary check: 40 = 101000. Shift right 2 → 1010 = 10 ✓. Shift left 1 → 1010000 = 80 ✓

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Bitwise — check odd/even

Q111. What does if (n & 1) test?

  • A) Whether n is negative
  • B) Whether n is odd
  • C) Whether n is even
  • D) Whether n is zero
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) Whether n is odd

n & 1 isolates the least-significant bit, which is 1 exactly when n is odd. It is faster than n % 2 and works for any n.

Related idioms: n >> 1 halves · n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit (used to count set bits) · n ^ n = 0 · x ^ 0 = x.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Bitwise — count set bits

Q112.

Set n = 12, count = 0
while (n > 0)
    Set n = n AND (n - 1)
    Set count = count + 1
End while
Print count
  • A) 2
  • B) 4
  • C) 1
  • D) 3
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) 2

n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit — this is Brian Kernighan's algorithm for counting 1-bits.

12 = 1100 → two set bits. Trace: 12 & 11 = 8 (count 1) → 8 & 7 = 0 (count 2) → loop ends. count = 2

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Bitwise — precedence trap

Q113. In C, how does the compiler parse a & 1 == 0?

  • A) a & (1 == 0)
  • B) (a & 1) == 0
  • C) It is a syntax error
  • D) (a & 1) == (0)
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) a & (1 == 0)

All bitwise operators bind LOOSER than comparison operators. So == runs first: 1 == 0 is 0, and the expression becomes a & 0, which is always 0.

To test the low bit you must write (a & 1) == 0 with explicit parentheses. This is one of the most commonly set traps in the pseudocode section.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Loops — mutated loop variable

Q114.

Integer x
for (each x from 1 to 11)
    x = x + 2
End for
Print x
  • A) 13
  • B) 12
  • C) 10
  • D) 11
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) 13

The body adds 2 AND the loop header adds 1 — so x rises by 3 per iteration.

1 → 4 → 7 → 10 → 13. At 13 the test 13 <= 11 fails and the loop exits.

The answer is the value that BROKE the condition (13), not the last value inside the range. A loop variable always overshoots.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Loops — uninitialised variable

Q115.

Integer value, n, num
Set value = 1, n = 45
num = num >> 1
num = num + value
Print num
  • A) 12
  • B) 1
  • C) 44
  • D) 0
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: B) 1

num is declared but never assigned, so under Accenture's pseudocode convention it holds 0. Then 0 >> 1 = 0 and 0 + 1 = 1.

n = 45 is a pure decoy — never used. These questions routinely include an unused variable to see whether you actually trace.

⚠️ In real C an uninitialised local is indeterminate; only the pseudocode dialect defines the 0 default.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Loops — digit sum

Q116.

Set n = 3527, s = 0
while (n > 0)
    Set s = s + (n mod 10)
    Set n = n / 10      // integer division
End while
Print s
  • A) 15
  • B) 17
  • C) 18
  • D) 3527
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) 17

The digit-sum idiom: n mod 10 peels the last digit, n / 10 removes it.

pass n digit s
1 3527 7 7
2 352 2 9
3 35 5 14
4 3 3 17

Recognise the sibling: r = r*10 + n%10 reverses the number instead of summing it. These two look identical at a glance.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Loops — do-while overshoot

Q117.

Set i = 10, s = 0
do
    Set s = s + i
    Set i = i - 3
while (i > 0)
Print s, i
  • A) 22 1
  • B) 22 -2
  • C) 18 1
  • D) 25 -2
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) 22 -2

A do…while tests AFTER the body, so i is already decremented when the check runs.

iter s i after test
1 10 7 true
2 17 4 true
3 21 1 true
4 22 −2 false → exit

The trap is 22 1 — right sum, but reporting i at the start of the last pass. Report the value that caused the exit.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Loops — nested count

Q118.

Set count = 0
for (i = 1 to 5)
    for (j = i to 5)
        if ((i + j) mod 2 == 0)
            count = count + 1
    End for
End for
Print count
  • A) 10
  • B) 9
  • C) 15
  • D) 8
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) 9

Note the inner loop starts at j = i, so only pairs with j ≥ i are visited.

i+j is even exactly when i and j have the same parity. Odds in 1..5 = {1,3,5} (3 of them) · Evens = {2,4} (2 of them). Pairs with j ≥ i from a set of size k number k(k+1)/2:

  • odd–odd: 3×4/2 = 6 · even–even: 2×3/2 = 3 → total 9

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Loops — iteration count

Q119. How many times does for (i = 0; i <= n; i++) execute when n = 5?

  • A) 7
  • B) 4
  • C) 5
  • D) 6
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) 6

i <= n runs n+1 times (i = 0,1,2,3,4,5). i < n runs n times.

Off-by-one here is the second most common loss in this section after in-place array updates. Always ask whether the bound is inclusive.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Arrays — in-place update

Q120.

Integer arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
for (i = 0; i < 4; i = i + 1)
    arr[i] = arr[i] + arr[i+1]
End for
Print arr
  • A) 3 5 7 9 10
  • B) 3 5 7 9 5
  • C) 1 3 5 7 9
  • D) 3 8 15 24 5
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: B) 3 5 7 9 5

i reads array after
0 1+2 3 2 3 4 5
1 2+3 3 5 3 4 5
2 3+4 3 5 7 4 5
3 4+5 3 5 7 9 5

The trap is 3 8 15 24 5 — you get that by carrying the updated value forward. Wrong: arr[i+1] is to the right of the cursor and has not been touched yet. Only positions left of the cursor are modified.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Arrays — reverse in place

Q121.

Integer a[5] = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}
Set i = 0, j = 4
while (i < j)
    swap(a[i], a[j])
    i = i + 1
    j = j - 1
End while
Print a[1]
  • A) 4
  • B) 6
  • C) 2
  • D) 8
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) 8

Two-pointer reversal: after the loop the array is 10 8 6 4 2, so a[1] = 8.

Trace: swap(a0,a4) → 10 4 6 8 2 · swap(a1,a3) → 10 8 6 4 2 · now i=2, j=2 so i < j fails and the loop stops — the middle element is never swapped, which is correct.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Arrays — sum of even indices

Q122.

Integer a[6] = {5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2}
Set s = 0
for (i = 0; i < 6; i = i + 2)
    s = s + a[i]
End for
Print s
  • A) 6
  • B) 28
  • C) 22
  • D) 16
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) 22

i steps by 2, so only indices 0, 2, 4 are visited: a[0]=5, a[2]=8, a[4]=9.

5 + 8 + 9 = 22.

Trap: even index is not even value. The values at those indices here are 5, 8 and 9 — two of them odd.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Recursion — base case

Q123.

fn(a, b)
    if (a < b) return fn(b, a)
    elseif (b != 0) return a * fn(a, b-1)
    else return 1

What is fn(5, 5)?

  • A) 3125
  • B) 15625
  • C) 625
  • D) 525
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: A) 3125

The function computes aᵇ. Unwinding: fn(5,5) = 5·fn(5,4) = … = 5⁵ = 3125.

⚠️ A widely-copied prep-site version writes the base case as return 0 while still offering 3125. With return 0 the whole product collapses to 0, which is not among the options — that published question is unanswerable as printed.

Rule: if a recursive function multiplies and the base case returns 0, the answer is 0. Check the base case FIRST.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Recursion — call count

Q124.

fib(n)
    if (n <= 1) return n
    return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)

What is fib(6)?

  • A) 6
  • B) 5
  • C) 13
  • D) 8
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) 8

Naive Fibonacci with fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1:

0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 → indices 0…6, so fib(6) = 8.

Worth knowing for a follow-up: this runs in exponential time O(2ⁿ) because subproblems are recomputed. Memoisation or an iterative loop makes it O(n).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Recursion — string reverse

Q125.

rev(s)
    if (length(s) <= 1) return s
    return rev(substring(s, 1)) + s[0]

What does rev("ABCD") return?

  • A) ABCD
  • B) ACBD
  • C) DCBA
  • D) DABC
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) DCBA

Each call peels the first character and appends it AFTER the reversed remainder — which reverses the string.

rev("ABCD") = rev("BCD") + 'A' = (rev("CD")+'B') + 'A' = ((rev("D")+'C')+'B')+'A' = "DCBA".

Trap: if the concatenation were s[0] + rev(...) the string would come back unchanged. The order of concatenation is the whole question.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Arithmetic — integer division

Q126. In C, what does printf("%d %d %d", 7/2, -7/2, 7%3) print?

  • A) 3.5 -3.5 1
  • B) 3 -3 1
  • C) 3 -4 1
  • D) 4 -3 2
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: B) 3 -3 1

Integer division truncates TOWARD ZERO in C, so 7/2 = 3 and -7/2 = **-3** (not −4 — that would be flooring, which is Python's behaviour).

7 % 3 = 1.

This is the highest-frequency trap in the section — any division of integers discards the fraction, it does not round.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Arithmetic — ASCII

Q127.

char c = 'f', a = 's', b = 'x';
int sum = c + a + b;
printf("%d", sum);
  • A) 315
  • B) 324
  • C) 337
  • D) 320
Answer & explanation — 🟡 PYQ

Answer: C) 337

char is an integer type — adding chars adds their ASCII codes.

Anchor: 'a' = 97. So 'f' = 97+5 = 102, 's' = 97+18 = 115, 'x' = 97+23 = 120. Total 102+115+120 = 337.

Other anchors: 'A' = 65, '0' = 48, 'a' − 'A' = 32.

Trap: with %c instead of %d, C would wrap 337 mod 256 = 81 = 'Q'.

Provenance: Memory-based previous-year question republished on a prep site; treated as unverified and re-derived.

Arithmetic — pre/post increment

Q128.

int i = 5;
int x = i++;
int y = ++i;
printf("%d %d %d", i, x, y);
  • A) 6 5 6
  • B) 7 6 7
  • C) 7 5 7
  • D) 7 5 6
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) 7 5 7

i++ returns the OLD value then increments; ++i increments then returns the NEW value.

  • x = i++ → x gets 5, i becomes 6
  • y = ++i → i becomes 7, y gets 7

Final: i = 7, x = 5, y = 7.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Functions — pass by value vs pointer

Q129.

void modify(int a, int *b) { a = a + 10; *b = *b + 10; }
int main() { int x = 5, y = 5; modify(x, &y); printf("%d %d", x, y); }
  • A) 15 15
  • B) 5 5
  • C) 15 5
  • D) 5 15
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) 5 15

a is passed by value — the function gets a private copy, so x in main is untouched: 5. b is passed by pointer — &y hands over the address, so *b = *b + 10 writes through: 15.

Rule: in C a function can only change a caller's variable if it receives the address. No */& pair means no change sticks.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Functions — static locals

Q130.

int counter() { static int c = 0; c++; return c; }
int a = counter(); int b = counter(); int d = counter();
printf("%d %d %d", a, b, d);
  • A) 0 1 2
  • B) 3 3 3
  • C) 1 1 1
  • D) 1 2 3
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) 1 2 3

static inside a function allocates once, initialises once, and keeps its value between calls. So c goes 1, 2, 3.

Drop the static and c becomes an ordinary local, re-initialised to 0 every call — the output would be 1 1 1. That single keyword is the entire question.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — four pillars

Q131. Which OOP principle is described by 'exposing only what is necessary and hiding the internal implementation'?

  • A) Abstraction
  • B) Encapsulation
  • C) Inheritance
  • D) Polymorphism
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Abstraction

Abstraction hides COMPLEXITY — you expose what an object does, not how. Encapsulation hides DATA — bundling fields with methods and restricting access via modifiers.

The two are routinely confused. Memory hook: Abstraction = design-level (what), Encapsulation = implementation-level (data protection).

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — overloading vs overriding

Q132. Which statement about method overloading is TRUE?

  • A) It requires inheritance
  • B) Different name, same parameters, resolved at compile time
  • C) Same name, different parameter list, resolved at compile time
  • D) Same name, same parameter list, resolved at runtime
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) Same name, different parameter list, resolved at compile time

Overloading Overriding
Where same class subclass
Signature different params identical
Binding compile time (static) runtime (dynamic)
Inheritance needed No Yes

Trap: return type alone cannot distinguish overloads — int f() and double f() will not compile as an overload pair.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — diamond problem

Q133. Why does Java NOT support multiple inheritance of classes?

  • A) Because interfaces are faster
  • B) It does support multiple class inheritance
  • C) To avoid the diamond problem (ambiguity of inherited members)
  • D) Because it is slower to compile
Answer & explanation — 🔴 REDDIT

Answer: C) To avoid the diamond problem (ambiguity of inherited members)

The diamond problem: if B and C both extend A, and D extends both B and C, D would inherit two copies of A's members with no rule for which to use.

Java forbids multiple CLASS inheritance but allows multiple interface implementation. Java 8 default methods reintroduce the ambiguity, so the compiler forces you to override and disambiguate explicitly.

C++ solves it differently — with virtual inheritance, which keeps a single shared copy of the base.

Provenance: Question type reported first-hand for the Oct-2025 assessment.

OOPs — abstract class vs interface

Q134. Which is TRUE of an abstract class but NOT of a (pre-Java 8) interface?

  • A) All its methods are implicitly public
  • B) It supports multiple inheritance
  • C) It can have constructors and instance fields
  • D) It cannot contain concrete methods
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) It can have constructors and instance fields

Abstract class Interface
Constructors Yes No
Instance fields Yes No (only public static final constants)
Concrete methods Yes Only default/static, Java 8+
Multiple inheritance No Yes

Neither can be instantiated. Use an abstract class for shared state and partial implementation; an interface for a capability contract.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — access modifiers

Q135. Order the Java access modifiers from most restrictive to least restrictive.

  • A) public → protected → default → private
  • B) private → protected → default → public
  • C) private → default → protected → public
  • D) default → private → protected → public
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) private → default → protected → public

Modifier Same class Same package Subclass (other pkg) Anywhere
private ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗
default ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗
protected ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗
public ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓

The subtlety: protected is wider than default only because it adds subclass access from other packages.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — static

Q136. Which statement about a static method is TRUE?

  • A) It can use this
  • B) It is resolved at runtime
  • C) It cannot access instance variables directly
  • D) It must be overridden in a subclass
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) It cannot access instance variables directly

A static method belongs to the CLASS, not to any instance. With no instance, there is no this and no instance state to reach — so it can only touch other static members directly.

Static methods cannot be overridden — redeclaring one in a subclass hides it, and the call is resolved by the reference type at compile time.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — constructor

Q137. Which is TRUE about constructors in Java?

  • A) A constructor can be declared static
  • B) A constructor must declare a return type
  • C) A default constructor is provided only if you define no constructor
  • D) Constructors can be overridden
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: C) A default constructor is provided only if you define no constructor

The compiler supplies a no-arg default constructor ONLY when the class declares none. Define any constructor and the default disappears — which is why adding a parameterised constructor can break new MyClass().

Constructors: no return type, name matches the class, can be overloaded but never overridden, and cannot be static, final or abstract.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — polymorphism

Q138. Runtime polymorphism in Java is achieved through:

  • A) Method overriding
  • B) Method overloading
  • C) Constructor overloading
  • D) Static methods
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: A) Method overriding

Overriding is resolved at runtime by the actual object type (dynamic dispatch), which is what runtime polymorphism means. Overloading is resolved at compile time by the declared parameter types, so it is compile-time (static) polymorphism.

Classic form: Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak(); calls Dog's version.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — composition vs aggregation

Q139. Which relationship implies that the contained object CANNOT exist independently of its container?

  • A) Inheritance
  • B) Association
  • C) Aggregation
  • D) Composition
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) Composition

Composition is a strong has-a: destroy the whole and the parts die with it (a House and its Rooms). Aggregation is a weak has-a: the parts survive (a Department and its Professors). Association is a general 'uses' link.

In UML: composition = filled diamond, aggregation = hollow diamond.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

OOPs — encapsulation in practice

Q140. Which combination correctly implements encapsulation?

  • A) private fields with private methods
  • B) protected fields with no methods
  • C) public fields with public methods
  • D) private fields with public getters and setters
Answer & explanation — ⚪ BUILT

Answer: D) private fields with public getters and setters

Encapsulation = restrict direct access to data, expose controlled access through methods. Making fields private and providing public accessors lets you validate input, make a field read-only (getter but no setter), and change the internal representation later without breaking callers.

Public fields break encapsulation — any code can write any value with no validation.

Provenance: Written to match the observed style and difficulty. Not a real exam question.

Excel — operators

Q141. In Excel, if cell A2 is "max" and cell B2 is "Yahoo.com", which formula returns "max@yahoo.com" in C2?

  • A) =A2# "@" #B2
  • B) =A2$ "@" $B2
  • C) =A2+ "@" +B2
  • D) =A2& "@" &B2
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

Answer: D) =A2& "@" &B2

& is Excel's concatenation operator. =A2&"@"&B2 joins text. + is arithmetic and errors on text; # and $ are not concatenation ($ locks a reference). CONCATENATE(A2,"@",B2) and TEXTJOIN do the same job.

Provenance: Real Accenture question from the placement deck (year-tagged where shown). Answer derived by me — the deck ships no answer key.

Excel — absolute reference

Q142. Which sign makes a cell reference absolute in MS Excel?

  • A) &
  • B) #
  • C) @
  • D) $
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

Answer: D) $

$ locks the part that follows it. $A$1 never moves when copied; $A1 locks the column only; A$1 locks the row only. F4 cycles through all four forms while editing.

Provenance: Real Accenture question from the placement deck (year-tagged where shown). Answer derived by me — the deck ships no answer key.

Excel — text functions

Q143. PROPER, LOWER and UPPER functions in MS Excel are used to:

  • A) Change the font of the text
  • B) Change the cell reference
  • C) Change the position of the text
  • D) Change the case of the text
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL

Answer: D) Change the case of the text

All three change letter case. UPPER→ALL CAPS, LOWER→all lowercase, PROPER→Title Case Of Each Word. They change the value, not the formatting — font and position are formatting, not functions.

Excel — counting functions

Q144. Which function in MS Excel is used to count blank cells?

  1. COUNT() 2. COUNTIF() 3. COUNTIFS()
  • A) 2 and 3
  • B) 1 and 3
  • C) 1 and 2
  • D) 1, 2 and 3
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2022

Answer: A) 2 and 3

COUNTIF/COUNTIFS can count blanks using the criterion "" or "=", e.g. =COUNTIF(A1:A10,""). COUNT only counts numeric cells and can never count blanks. (The dedicated function is COUNTBLANK, but of the three offered, only 2 and 3 can do it.)

Provenance: Real Accenture question from the placement deck (year-tagged where shown). Answer derived by me — the deck ships no answer key.

Excel — VLOOKUP

Q145. Which statement is correct for VLOOKUP?

  1. Looks for a value in the leftmost column of the selected table
  2. Looks for a value in the rightmost column
  3. Cannot find a value in a previous (left) column
  • A) 1 and 3
  • B) 2 and 3
  • C) Only 2
  • D) Only 1
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL

Answer: A) 1 and 3

VLOOKUP searches only the FIRST (leftmost) column of the table array, and can only return values to the right of it. So statement 1 is true and statement 3 is true; statement 2 is false. To look leftward you need INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP.

Provenance: Real Accenture question from the placement deck (year-tagged where shown). Answer derived by me — the deck ships no answer key.

Excel — NOW()

Q146. If you use the NOW function in MS Excel, it returns:

I. Current time II. Current date

  • B) Both I and II
  • C) Only I
  • D) Neither I nor II
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2020

Answer: B) Both I and II

NOW() returns date AND time; TODAY() returns the date only. Both are volatile — they recalculate on every worksheet change.

Excel — insert object

Q151. An attachment can be inserted into a worksheet by using:

  • A) Insert > Scatter

All three are true. AutoRecover exists precisely to survive crashes (1); the interval is user-configurable in File → Options → Save (2); and the default interval is 10 minutes (3). Statements 2 and 3 are consistent — 10 minutes is the default of a configurable setting.

Provenance: Real Accenture question from the placement deck (year-tagged where shown). Answer derived by me — the deck ships no answer key.

DBMS — file system limits

Q201. Which are limitations of a File Management System?

  • A) All of the mentioned options
  • B) There is no concurrent access
  • C) It is difficult to access data
  • D) There is no backup and recovery option available
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL · Acc-2021

Answer: A) All of the mentioned options

All are genuine limitations — and they are precisely the problems a DBMS was invented to solve: data redundancy and inconsistency, difficulty accessing data, isolation, no concurrent access control, no backup/recovery, and no integrity or security enforcement.

Provenance: Real Accenture question from the placement deck (year-tagged where shown). Answer derived by me — the deck ships no answer key.

DBMS — limitations

Q202. Which are limitations of a database system?

  1. Setup is complex 2. Complexity may result in poor performance 3. Requires more cost
  • A) Only 2 and 3
  • B) All 1, 2 and 3
  • C) Only 1 and 2
  • D) Only 1 and 3
Answer & explanation — 🟢 REAL

Answer: B) All 1, 2 and 3

All three are standard disadvantages of a DBMS: high setup and licensing cost, complexity of installation and administration, and the performance overhead that generality brings. This is the mirror image of the file-system question — know both directions.

Real paper — questions from a recent Accenture test, worked
